text.2: -​ Undefined burden - affects other individual -​ Hidden burden - “stigma” (mark of shame) and violation of human rights -​ Future burden - next generation Clients of Community Health Nurses Individual - considered as the “entry point” (primary care) Family - collection of people who are integrated, interacting and interdependent (basic unit of service/care) Group/Aggregated/Population - a group of people who share common characteristics, developmental stage or common exposure to particular environment factors and consequently common health problems, issues and concerns Community - a group of people sharing common geographic boundaries and/or common values and interests within a specific social system Goal of PHC -​ Self-reliance in health Goal of COPAR -​ Community Health Development (social transformation) Health 1.​ Viewed as a continuum, is considered as the goal of public health in general and community health nursing 2.​ A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease (WHO) 3.​ An integrated method of functioning which is oriented toward maximizing the potential which the individual is capable (Dunn & Pender) 4.​ Quality of life involving social, emotional, mental, spiritual and biological fitness on the part of the individual which results from adaptations to the environment (Dubos) 5.​ Health and illness in relation to the environment (Florence Nightingale) 6.​ A state characterized by soundness and wholeness of human structures and bodily and mental functions (Dorothea Orem) Determinants of Health - factors that make an individual healthy or not -​ Genetics -​ Income -​ Education -​ Behavior -​ Health care delivery system

restore the health of individuals, families, groups and communities. (1) public sector which is largely financed through tax-based budgeting system at both national and local levels and where health care generally given free at the point of service (2) the private sector which is largely market-oriented and where health care is paid through user fees at the point of service. Levels of Health Care (1)​ Primary level of care (Accessible) - health care provided by center physicians, PHNs, RH midwives, BHWs, traditional healers and others at the barangay health stations (BHS) and RHU. The primary health facility is usually the first contact between the community members and the other levels of the health facility. Provides basic health care services. (2)​ Secondary level of care - usually given in health facilities either privately owned or government operated such as infirmaries, municipal and district hospitals and out-patient departments or provincial hospitals, It is capable of performing minor surgeries and performing some simple laboratory examinations. (3)​ Tertiary level of care - rendered by specialists including medical centers as well as regional and provincial hospitals and specialized hospitals. Complicated cases and intensive care requires tertiary care. 2 way referral system - Intrasectoral linkage Facilities -​ BHS - satellite station/extension; manned by PHM, BHW -​ HC/RHU - main center/intermediate primary center; complete health care team -​ Frontline: PHM -​ Supervisor: PHN -​ Manager: RHP (overall activities of the center) -​ Sanitary inspector: environment sanitation -​ Medtech: laboratory -​ Dentist: Dental Health Program Levels of Primary Health Care Workers (1)​ Village or BHWs - trained community health workers or health auxiliary volunteer or a traditional birth attendant or healer (2)​ Intermediate level health workers - general medical practitioners or their assistants. PHNs, Rural sanitary inspectors and midwives may compose these groups Health Worker to Patient Ratio (DOH) Category Ratio Legal Basis PHN 1:10,000 RA 7160, RA 7305

Phases of Nursing Process (1)​ Assessment: process of collecting, organizing and analyzing data/information about the client -​ Interview, observation -​ First level assessment: determine “what” are the problems -​ 4 categories of health problem: -​ Wellness state (healthy) -​ Health deficit (disability & disease) -​ Health threat (increase risk for illness & injury) -​ Foreseeable crisis/Stress points (anticipated problems that are developmental or social in nature - ADJUST) -​ Second level of assessment: determine “why” (reason behind the problem) - INABILITY to recognize the presence of the problem (2)​ Planning: a logical step-by-step process in designing a plan of action to accomplish specific goal and objectives (Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Reliable,Time bound) -​ Goal setting -​ Construct plan of action -​ Choose nursing intervention -​ Prioritization (Maglaya - 4 Criteria) - highest score is 5 -​ The highest score, the highest priority; the lowest score, the lowest priority -​ Nature of the problem (Wt: 1) - type of nursing problem -​ Wellness state: 3 -​ Health deficit: 3 -​ Health threat: 2 -​ Foreseeable crisis - 1 -​ Modifiability of the problem (Wt: 2) - the solution of the problem (most important) -​ Easily modifiable: 2 -​ Partially modifiable: 1 -​ Not modifiable: 0 -​ Preventive potential (Wt: 1) - future re-occurence of the problem -​ Highly preventable: 3 -​ Moderately preventable: 2 -​ Low preventive potential: 1 -​ Salience (Wt: 1) - perception of the client about the problem -​ Immediate: 2 -​ Not immediate: 1 -​ Not a problem: 0 -​ Formula: score/highest score x wt (3)​ Implementation: consists of doing or carrying out the interventions specified in the care plan in partnership with client-partners and/or other members of the team -​ Independent - text.19: -​ Family Coping Index -​ This tool is based on premise that nursing action may help a family in providing for a health need or resolving a health problem by promoting the family’s coping capacity Nine Areas of Assessment of the Family Coping Index I.​ Physical Independence - family members’ mobility and ability to perform activities of daily living II.​ Therapeutic Competence - ability to comply with prescribed or recommended procedures and treatment to be done at home III.​ Knowledge of Health Condition - understanding of the health condition or essentials of care according to the developmental stages of family members IV.​ Application of Principles of Personal and General Hygiene - practice of general health promotion and recommended preventive measures V.​ Health Care Attitudes - family’s perception of health care in general VI.​ Emotional Competence - degree of emotional maturity of family members according to their developmental stages VII.​ Family Living Patterns - interpersonal relationships among family members, management of the family finances, and the type of discipline in the home VIII.​ Physical Environment - includes home, school, work, and community environment that influence the health of family members IX.​ Use of Community Facilities - ability of the family to seek and utilize, as needed both environment-run and private health Community Organizing Participatory Action Research (COPAR) Community Organization - plan solution Participatory Action Research - active participation Action Research - promotes development, the people are the researcher themselves Role of the nurse: Facilitator, assist, teach Role of the people: leader, assess, plan, implementation, evaluation Emphases of Community Organizing in PHC (1)​ People from the community working together to solve their own problems (2)​ Internal organizational consolidation as a pre-requisite to external expansion (3)​ Social movement first before technical change (4)​ Health reforms occurring within the context of broader social transformation Community organizing as a process -​ Development of the community’s collective capacities -​ Continuous process of educating the community -​ Process of education and mobilizing members of the community Community Development entails a process of assessment of the current situation, the identification of needs, deciding on appropriate courses of actions or response, mobilization of resources to address these needs, and monitoring and evaluation by the people Community organizing is a value-based process -​ Human rights -​ Social justice -​ Social responsibility Community organizing is people-centered -​ The people are the means and ends of development and community empowerment is the process and the outcome Community organizing is participative -​ Participation of the community in the entire process is considered as the prime mover and determinant rather than beneficiaries and recipients of development efforts including health care Community organizing is democratic -​ It is a process that allows the majority of people to recognize and critically analyze their difficulties and articulate their aspiration Community organizing is developmental -​ Should be directed towards changing current undesirable conditions Community organizing is process-oriented -​ It is dynamic and goals of empowerment and development are achieved through a process of change Phases of COPAR -​ Pre-Entry -​ Simplest phase -​ Initial steps involved in establishing partnership with the people and identifying the needs, problems, issues affecting the community -​ Preliminary Social Investigation - collection of information in a systematic manner to generate community profile (different barangays) -​ Site selection -​ Site Selection Criteria: GIDA -​ Geographically inaccessible disadvantaged area -​ A community with a population of 100 or more families -​ Marginalized or in need -​ text.30: -​ Nosocomial (Hospital/Facility-based) - develop during a client’s stay in a facility or manifest after discharge (48 hours after admission/discharge) -​ Iatrogenic (procedure-based) - the direct result of diagnostic or therapeutic or invasive procedures The Epidemiological Triad -​ disease result from the interaction between the agent and the susceptible host in an environment that supports transmission of the agent from a source to that host -​ Host - influences an individual exposure, susceptibility or response to causative agent. Host can be the patient, carrier, suspect or contact -​ Environment - the sum total of all external conditions that affects the development of an organism and serves as the opportunity of the hosts exposure to harmful microorganisms. -​ Physical -​ Biological -​ Socio-economic -​ Infectious Agent - are the microorganisms or pathogen that cause infection -​ Factors influencing the Cause of Disease -​ Pathogenicity - ability of an organism to cause a disease, create damage to the host (immune system) -​ Infectivity - ability of an organism to infect (multiple within the host) -​ Virulence - ability of an organism to produce disease (severity) -​ Infective dose - number of organism and amount of toxin released by the organism to induce disease -​ Influenza - high infectivity, moderate pathogenicity, low to moderate virulence -​ Rabies - low infectivity, very high pathogenicity, extremely virulent -​ HIV - low to moderate infectivity, high pathogenicity, high virulence over time Stages of Disease Incubation period - time interval between the initial infection and the first appearance of any signs and symptoms -​ Start - upon exposure -​ End - first signs and symptoms Prodromal period - early, mild symptoms of disease -​ Start - first signs and symptoms -​ End - general signs and symptoms
text.31: Period of illness - overt signs and symptoms of disease -​ All signs and symptoms appear -​ Peak/acme -​ Pathognomonic sign - specific Period of convalescence - signs and symptoms are disappearing (recovery) Period of Defervescent - onset of complications leading to death Chain of Infection -​ conditions that must be met in order for the infectious diseases to spread Pathogen or Causative Agent -​ Biologic agent (organism) capable of causing disease -​ Bacteria - most common (DPT) -​ Virus - most microscopic (MMRV) -​ Fungi - least common (buni, alipunga, had had, anan) -​ Parasites - protozoans, helminths, flukes (filariasis and malaria) -​ Eliminate organism by: -​ Sterilizing surgical instruments and anything that touches sterile spaces of the body -​ Using good food safety methods -​ Providing safe drinking water -​ Vaccinating people so they do not become reservoirs of illness -​ Treating people who are ill Reservoir -​ Any persons, animal, arthropod, plant, soil, or substance in which a causative agent normally lives and multiples, on which it depends primarily for survival, and where it reproduces in such numbers that it can be transmitted to a susceptible host -​ Eliminate reservoir by: -​ Treating people who are ill -​ Vaccinating people -​ Handling and disposing body fluids responsibly -​ Monitoring soil and contaminated water in sensitive areas of the hospital and washing hands carefully after contact with others Portal of Exit -​ The way the causative agent gets out of the reservoir -​ Reduce risk from portal of exit by: -​ Covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue -​ Handling body fluids with gloves, then doing hand hygiene -​ Keeping draining wounds covered with a dressing -​ Not working when you have exudative (wet) lesions or weeping dermatitis Mode of Transmission -​ Any mechanism by which a pathogen is spread from a source or reservoir to a person, unwashed hands, things which are not cleaned between patients, droplets, or, for a few diseases, air -​ Eliminate the mode of transmission by: -​ Hand hygiene -​ Wearing gloves to minimize contamination of hands and discarding them after each patient -​ cleaning , disinfection, or sterilization of equipment used by more than one patient -​ Cleaning of the environment, especially high-touch surfaces -​ Contact Transmission -​ Direct contact - person to person transmission of an agent by physical contact between its source and susceptible host -​ Horizontal Transmission - immediate transfer from person to person -​ Vertical Transmission - refers to pathogen that is passed from mother to child either from utero (placenta) or during child birth -​ Indirect contact - reservoir to susceptible host by means of non-living object -​ Vehicle Transmission - through fomites -​ Vector-borne Transmission - occurs when a living organism carries a disease pathogen and passes it to another living organism -​ Droplet Transmission - can occur when a person comes within 1 meter of an infected person -​ Source and the host are within 1 m (3ft) -​ >5 microns -​ PIMP - Pertussis, Influenza, Meningitis, Pneumonia -​ Airborne Transmission - occurs when infectious agents are carried in the air via aerosol -​ Occurs regardless of distance -​ <5 microns -​ MTV - Measles, Tuberculosis and Varicella -​ Enteric Transmission - involves infectious agents that are spread via from feces of an infected individual to the mouth of another individual -​ Blood-borne transmission - occur from the introduction of pathogen via blood transfusion Portal of Entry -​ Hole in the skin that allows the infectious agent to get into the body (mouth, nose, eyes, rashes, cuts, needlestick injuries, surgical wounds and IV sites) -​ Protect portals of entry by: -​ Dressing on surgical wounds -​ IV site dressings and care -​ Elimination of tubes as soon as possible -​ Masks, goggles, and face shields -​ Keeping unwashed hands and objects away from mouth -​ Actions and devices to prevent needlesticks -​ Food and water safety

text.70: -​ Instruments with lenses should be sterilized after use on AIDS patient -​ Needles should not be bent after use, placed it under puncture-resistant -​ Patients with active AIDS should be isolated -​ Care of thermometer - wash with warm soapy water, soak in 70% alcohol for 10 minutes, dry and store Integumentary System Chicken Pox -​ other term: Varicella zoster -​ Description: acute infectious disease of sudden onset with slight fever, mild constitutional symptoms and eruptions which are maculopapular for a few hours, vesicular for 3-4 days and leaves granular scabs -​ Etiologic agent: Human (alpha) herpes 3 (Varicella-zoster virus) -​ Sources of infection: -​ secretions of respiratory tract of infected persons -​ Lesions (little consequences) -​ Scabs are not infective -​ MOT: -​ Direct contact -​ contact with contaminated linen and fomites -​ Airborne -​ Incubation Period: -​ 2-3 weeks -​ Period of communicability: -​ Cases are infectious up to 2 days before the onset of the rash until 5 days after the first crop of vesicles -​ Diagnostic Test: -​ Isolation of the virus from the vesicular fluid within the 3 to 4 days of the rash -​ Serum antibodies is present in 7 days after onset -​ Congenital varicella results in: -​ Hypoplastic, deformities and scarring of limb -​ Retarded growth -​ CNS and ophthalmic manifestation -​ Nursing considerations: -​ strict isolation -​ exclusion from school for 1 week after eruption first appears and avoid contact with susceptible
text.71: -​ Concurrent disinfection if throat and nose discharge -​ Tell the patient not to scratch the lesions -​ Teach the child and family to apply topical antipruritic medication correctly -​ Susceptibility, resistance and occurrence -​ Universal among those not previously attacked -​ Severe in adults -​ An attack covers long immunity -​ second attacks are rare -​ Prevention: -​ Vaccine: varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) it should be given within 10 days of exposure Measles -​ Other terms: Rubeola/Morbili/7-day measles -​ Description: it is an acute contagious and exanthematous disease that usually affects children who are susceptible to URTI -​ Etiological agent: filterable virus of measles (paromyxoviridae) -​ Source of infection: secretions of nose and throat infected persons -​ MOT: -​ Droplet spread/direct contact with infected person -​ Indirect contact (articles with secretions) -​ Airborne -​ IP: 1-2 weeks -​ Period of communicability: starts just before the prodrome and lasts until 4 days after the rash appear -​ Clinical manifestations: Koplik’s spots (pathognomonic sign -​ Pre-eruptive stage -​ Fever -​ catarrhal symptoms (cough, conjunctivitis, coryza) -​ Photophobia -​ stimson’s line (red line on the lower conjunctiva) -​ Eruptive stage -​ maculo-papular rash -​ High grade fever -​ Anorexia and irritability -​ throat is red and extremely sore -​ Convalescence stage -​ rashes fade away -​ Fever subsides

text.74: -​ Clinical observation -​ cell cultures of the throat, blood, urine and CSF confirm the presence of the virus -​ Convalescent serum that shows a fourfold rise antibody titer supports the diagnosis -​ Treatment: -​ Acetaminophen for fever and joint pain -​ Isolation -​ Complications: -​ Encephalitis -​ Neuritis -​ Arthritis -​ Arthralgias -​ Rubella syndrome -​ Microcephaly -​ mental retardation -​ Cataract -​ Deaf-mutism -​ Heart disease -​ Nursing considerations: -​ Provide comfort -​ Make sure female patients understand how important it is to avoid exposure to this disease when pregnant -​ Report confirmed cases of rubella to local public health officials -​ Warn the patient about possible mild fever, slight rash, transient arthralgia and arthritis -​ If lymphadenopathy persists after the initial 24 hours, suggest a cold compress to promote vasoconstriction and prevent antigenic cyst formation -​ Patient's room must be darkened to avoid photophobia -​ Patient’s eyes should be irrigated with warm saline to relieve irritation -​ Good ventilation is necessary -​ Prevention: -​ administration of live attenuated vaccine (MMR) -​ Pregnant women should avoid exposure to patients infected with rubella virus -​ Administration of immune serum globulin one week after exposure to rubella Pediculosis -​ Description: any human infestation of lice anywhere on the body -​ Types: -​ Pediculosis capitis - text.90: Uterus Menstrual Hormones -​ Estrogen: Produced by the ovaries, estrogen is crucial for developing and thickening the uterine lining (endometrium) and plays a role in follicle development. -​ Progesterone: Also produced by the ovaries (specifically after ovulation), progesterone maintains the uterine lining and prepares the uterus for a potential pregnancy. -​ Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH): Released by the pituitary gland, FSH stimulates the growth of follicles (which contain eggs) in the ovaries. -​ Luteinizing Hormone (LH): Another hormone released by the pituitary gland, LH triggers ovulation (the release of an egg from the ovary). -​ Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH): Produced by the hypothalamus (a part of the brain), GnRH stimulates the pituitary gland to release FSH and LH, initiating the menstrual cycle. Phases of Menstruation -​ Follicular Phase (1-14): Follicles in the ovaries start to develop, and the uterine lining begins to thicken. This phase begins with the end of menstruation and ends with ovulation. (FSH) -​ Menstrual - bleeding (day 1-6) decreased estrogen and progesterone -​ Proliferative - thickening (day 7-13) increased estrogen and decreased progesterone -​ Ovulation: An egg is released from an ovary and travels down the fallopian tube, making it available for fertilization. If fertilization doesn't occur, the uterine lining sheds, and the cycle restarts. This phase is characterized by rising progesterone levels. the fetus -​ Molding - change in the shape of fetal skull produced by the force of uterine contractions pressing the vertex of the head against the not-yet-dilated cervix -​ Attitude - describes the degree of flexion a fetus assumes during labor or the relation of the fetal parts to each other -​ Engagement - refers to the settling of the presenting part of a fetus far enough into the pelvis to be at the level of the ischial spines, a midpoint of the pelvis -​ Fetal Station - refers to the relationship of the presenting part of the fetus to the level of ischial spines -​ Fetal lie - the relationship between the long (cephalocaudal) axis of the fetal body and the long (cephalocaudal) axis of a woman’s body -​ Fetal Presentation - denotes the body part that will first contact the cervix or be born first -​ Cephalic Presentation - the fetal head is the body part that will first contact the cervix -​ Breech Presentation - either the buttocks or the feet are the first body parts that will contact the cervix -​ Complete breech presentation - fetus has thighs tightly flexed on the abdomen, both the buttocks and the tightly flexed feet present to the cervix -​ Frank breech presentation - the hips are flexed but the knees are extended to the rest on the chest -​ Footling - neither the thighs nor lower legs are flexed -​ Shoulder Presentation - presenting part is usually the shoulders, iliac crest, a hand or elbow -​ Fetal Position - relationship of the presenting part to a specific quadrant of the woman's pelvis -​ Vertex Presentation (Occiput) -​ Left occipitoanterior (LOA) -​ Left occipitoposterior (LOP) -​ Left occipitotransverse (LOT) -​ Right occipitoanterior (ROA) -​ Right occipitoposterior (ROP) -​ Right occipitotransverse (ROT) -​ Breech Presentation (Sacrum) -​ Left sacroanterior (LSaA) -​ Left sacroposterior (LSaP) -​ Left sacrotransverse (LSaT) -​ Right sacroanterior (RSaA) -​ Right sacroposterior (RSaP) -​ Right sacrotransverse (RSaT) -​ Face Presentation (mentum) -​ Left mentoanterior (LMA) -​ Left mentoposterior (LMP) -​ Left mentotransverse (LMT) -​ Right mentoanterior (RMA) -​ Right mentoposterior (RMP) -​ Right mentotransverse (RMT) -​ Shoulder Presentation (acromion process) -​ Left scapuloanterior (LAA) -​ Left scapuloposterior (LAP) -​ Right scapuloanterior (RAA) -​ Right scapuloposterior (RAP) Management for Fetal Malposition: to help rotate the head from posterior to anterior -​ Hands and knees position -​ All four position -​ Squatting -​ Knee-chest Leopold’s Maneuver - series of four abdominal palpations performed by HP to assess fetal position, presentation, and engagement within the uterus during pregnancy -​ Fundal grip - fetal lie -​ Umbilical grip - fetal position -​ Pawlik’s grip - fetal presentation -​ Pelvic grip - fetal attitude Power - force supplied by the fundus of the uterus, implemented by uterine contractions, a natural process that causes cervical dilatation and then expulsion of the fetus from the uterus -​ Uterine contractions - begin at a pacemaker point located in the uterine myometrium near one of the uterotubal junctions -​ Cervical changes -​ Effacement - shortening and thinning of the cervical canal -​ Dilatation - refers to the enlargement or widening of the cervical canal from an opening a few millimeters wide to one large enough to permit passage of the fetus Psyche - a woman’s psychological outlook refers to the psychological state or feelings that a woman brings into labor Stages of Labor First Stage of Labor -​ Latent Phase/Preparatory - begins at the onset of regularly perceived uterine contractions and ends when the rapid cervical dilatation begins -​ Active Phase - cervical dilatation occurs more rapidly, increasing from 4-7 cm -​ Transition Phase - contractions reach their peak of intensity, occurring every 2 to 3 minutes with the duration of 60-90 seconds and causing maximum cervical dilatation of 8-10 cm Latent (6 hours for Primi; 4.5 hours for Multi) Active (3 hours for Primi; 2 hours for Multi) Transition Dilatation 0-3 cm 4-7 cm 8-10 cm Frequency Every 5-10 minutes Every 3-5 minutes Every 2-3 minutes Duration 20-40 secs 40-60 secs 60-90 secs Intensity Mild Moderate Strong Behavior Excited Fear of losing control Resistance to touch Considerations Give instructions Give analgesia Reassurance Monitor Fetal Heart Rate Every 15-30 minutes Unnecessary Interventions during Labor (WHO protocol) -​ fundal pushing -​ Perineal shaving -​ IV infusion -​ NPO -​ Strict supine position -​ Artificial ROM -​ Enemas -​ Episiotomy Second Stage of Labor - period from full dilatation and cervical effacement to birth of the infant (FETAL EXPULSION STAGE - 1 HOUR) Temperature of delivery room 25-28C Transfer to delivery room Primi: 10 cm Multi: 7-8 cm Wear Double sterile gloves Most common birthing position lithotomy Surest sign that the baby is about to be delivered Bulging of the perineum When to push: during contractions, fully dilated cervix When not to push: not fully dilated cervix, intervals, delivery of the head Mechanisms (Cardinal Movements) of Labor -​ Descent - downward movement of the biparietal diameter of the fetal head to within the pelvic inlet -​ Flexion - the head bends forward onto the chest making the smallest anteroposterior diameter present to the birth canal -​ Internal rotation - head flexes as it touches the pelvic floor and the occiput rotates to bring the head into the best relationship to the outlet of pelvis -​ Extension - the back of the neck stops beneath the pubic arch and acts as a pivot for the rest of the head -​ External rotation - the head rotates back to the diagonal or transverse position of the early part of the labor -​ Expulsion - end of pelvic division of labor Third Stage of Labor/Placental Stage (3-10 minutes) - begins with the birth of the infant and ends with the delivery of placenta -​ Signs of placental separation -​ Lengthening of the umbilical cord -​ Sudden gush of vaginal blood -​ Change in the shape of uterus -​ Firm contraction of the uterus -​ Appearance of the placenta at the vaginal opening -​ Placental presentation -​ Schultz - appearing shiny and glistening from the fetal membrane -​ Duncan - raw, red and irregular, with ridges or cotyledons that separate blood collection spaces showing (maternal surface) -​ Active Management (WHO-DOH) - decreases the risk of postpartum hemorrhage -​ Administration of uterotonic - 10 units oxytocin IM, administered to the mother within 1 minute of baby’s birth -​ Controlled cord traction with counter traction - wait a strong contraction (2-5 minutes), push the fundus upward with one hand while applying continuous, steady, non-directional traction on the cord with the other hand -​ uterine massage - after placental delivery NOTE: do not wait for signs of placental separation Fourth Stage of Labor (1-2 hours)) - critical stage/recovery stage -​ VS checking for the first 2 hours every 15 minutes Temperature 36.2-38C for the first 24 hours due to dehydration BP Should remain consistent with baseline BP during pregnancy RR 16-22 cpm PR May be bradycardia (50-70 bpm) for one week Report: -​ Hypo - tachy- tachy = shock -​ Increased temperature after 24 hours = infection Normal characteristics of fundus after delivery: Firm, contracting, midline, below the umbilicus Fundus is soft, relaxed and boggy Uterine Atony Deviated to the side Full bladder Palpable above the umbilicus Over distention of the uterus Firm but there is steady trickle of blood Laceration

text.116: -​ All contraception with estrogen are not safe for lactating mothers -​ Progesterone only pill is safe for lactating mothers -​ Women who have rubella titer of less than 1:10 are usually given rubella vaccine in the postpartum period and instruct the mother that pregnancy is not allowed for 3 months -​ All Rh negative women who meet specific criteria should receive RhoGAM -​ Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for women with uncomplicated vaginal birth and for those women with episiotomy and 1st and 2nd degree lacerations -​ Hunger will start to increase 1-2 hours after birth -​ First bowel movement normally occurs by 2-3 days postpartum -​ Immediate weight loss after delivery 12-15 lbs -​ Weight loss in the 1st week 5 lbs -​ Loss in the next 6 weeks 10 lbs -​ Most women return to their pre-pregnant weight by 6 months -​ The best schedule for breastfeeding per demand -​ 3E’s of breastfeeding -​ Early (ASAP) -​ Exclusive (1st 6 months) -​ Extended (up to 2 years or beyond) Phases of the Puerperium -​ Taking-in - a time of reflection, 2-3 day period, mother is passive -​ Taking-hold - initiate action, expressed interest in caring for the child -​ Letting-go - mother redefines her new role, requires some grief work and readjustment of relationships Taking-In (first 3 days) Dependent phase (passive) Personal care Taking-Hold (4th-6th day) Independent phase (active) Newborn care Letting Go (7th day and above Interdependent phase (collaborative) Parenting and family planning 1st Trimester Complications Abortion -​ Medical term for any interruption of a pregnancy before a fetus is viable (20 weeks) -​ Spontaneous - miscarriage between 16-24 weeks -​ Threatened - begins as vaginal bleeding, initially only scant and usually bright red, no cervical dilatation -​ Imminent/Inevitable - (+) uterine contractions and cervical dilation, no FHT -​ Complete - entire products of conception are expelled without assistance -​ Incomplete - part of the conceptus is expelled, but the membrane or placenta is retained in the uterus -​ Missed - fetus dies in utero but is not expelled -​ Septic - due to infection -​ Habitual - recurrent, with dilation -​ Induced -​ Therapeutic -​ Intentional/elective Methods of Abortion -​ Medical termination -​ Avoids an anesthesia -​ More effective at earlier gestation (49 days or earlier) Surgical Termination -​ Suction evacuation (menstrual extraction) -​ Performed 5-7 weeks after LMP -​ A rigid or flexible suction is used -​ Dilatation and Curettage -​ If the AOG is less than 13 weeks -​ Needs anesthetic block and cervical dilators -​ Dilatation and Vacuum Extraction -​ Those between 12 and 16 weeks -​ Dilatation of the cervix is begun -​ Negative pressure of suction pump Ectopic/Tubal Pregnancy -​ implantation occurs outside the uterine cavity -​ most common site - ampulla of the fallopian tube Type Duration Ampullar 6-12 weeks Isthmic 6-8 weeks Fimbriated 6-12 weeks Interstitial 12-14 weeks -​ Risk factors -​ Previous PID (pelvic inflammatory disease) -​ Previous ectopic pregnancy, previous BTL, previous tubal or pelvic surgeries

bluish navel/hematoperitoneum indicative of internal bleeding -​ Kehr’s sign - referred pain (shoulders) due to stimulation to phrenic nerve Management: -​ Unruptured ectopic pregnancy: oral administration of methotrexate (anti-folic acid) and followed by Leucovorin (to decrease toxic effects of methotrexate) -​ Prerequisites: -​ Ectopic sac is smaller than 3.5 cm in diameter -​ Serum hCG levels <5000mIU/ml -​ Normal kidney and liver functions -​ No evidence of thrombocytopenia -​ Hysterosalpingography or ultrasound is performed after therapy - to check tubal patency Second Trimester Complications Hydatidiform Mole/Gestational Trophoblastic Disease -​ Abnormal proliferation and then degeneration of the trophoblastic villi developing into avascular transparent grapelike vesicles -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Big uterus -​ Snowstorm pattern in the ultrasound -​ No FHT -​ Excessive hCG (1-2 million IU) -​ Hyperemesis gravidarum -​ Hypertension before 20 weeks -​ Ovarian enlargement -​ Dark brown vaginal discharge -​ Passage of clear fluid-filled vesicles Types of H-Mole -​ Partial -​ Localized areas of chorionic villi -​ 69, (XXY, XXX, XYY) triploid karyotype -​ 1 set of chromosomes of maternal in origin and 2 sets of paternal in origin (Dispermy) -​ Complete -​ Generalized areas of the chorionic villi -​ A sperm fertilizes an ovum with no genetic material -​ Androgenesis -​ 46 diploids karyotype -​ History of clomid therapy -​ 20% risk for developing cancer Diagnostic Test: transvaginal ultrasound and serum hCG Management -​ Remove the moles - suction evacuation -​ Oxytocin after evacuation -​ follow up visit - check hCG levels monthly for 6-12 months -​ Regular chest X-ray and regular pelvic examination -​ DOC: methotrexate -​ If metastasis occurs, dactinomycin is added to the regimen -​ Other considerations: -​ No pregnancy for at least 1 year -​ Recommend to use contraception -​ Abdominal hysterectomy (optional) Premature Cervical Dilatation/Incompetent Cervix -​ refers to a cervix that dilates prematurely and therefore cannot hold a fetus until term -​ Usually painless, occurring before 20 weeks -​ Due to -​ Congenital incompetence: short cervix (<2cm) -​ Acquired incompetence: trauma, laceration, infection -​ First symptom - bloody show before 20 weeks -​ Best diagnostic tool to detect: transvaginal ultrasound -​ Management: Cervical Cerclage (12-14 weeks) under regional anesthesia -​ McDonald - simple procedure (temporary) -​ Shirodkar - complicated operation -​ Success rate 85-90% either technique -​ NOTE: following the Shirodkar operation, the sutures may be left in place and CS delivery performed -​ After Cerclage: -​ Position: modified/slight trendelenburg for few days to reduce pressure -​ Observe ROM, contraction, VS, infections -​ No sex, heavy lifting
text.120: -​ No prolonged sitting and standing Third Trimester Complications Placenta Previa -​ A condition of pregnancy in which the placenta is implanted abnormally in the uterus -​ Cannot be diagnosed on the first 5months of pregnancy due to placental migration -​ Low-lying placenta - implantation in the lower rather than in the upper portion of the uterus -​ Marginal placenta - the placenta edge approaches that of the cervical os -​ Partial placenta - implantation occludes a portion of the cervical os -​ Total placenta - implantation totally obstructs the cervical os Management -​ Sufficient migration of placenta away from the cervix -​ prevent and control bleeding -​ Bed rest -​ Bethamethasone may be administered -​ Double set up Abruptio Placenta -​ Premature separation of placenta -​ Partial Abruption: The placenta detaches partially from the uterine wall. -​ Complete Abruption: The placenta detaches completely from the uterine wall. -​ Revealed Abruption: Bleeding is visible, meaning blood escapes through the cervix. -​ Concealed Abruption: Bleeding is hidden behind the placenta, and blood does not escape through the cervix. text.126: Vulvovaginal Infections -​ Candida -​ Vulvar itching and reddening -​ Thick white, cheese-like vaginal discharge -​ Management: Nystatin, Myconazole, Fluconazole -​ Trichomonas -​ Thin, irritating, frothy, gray green discharge -​ Strong rotten odor -​ Itching -​ Management: metronidazole (Flagyl), douching with vaginal solution -​ Gardnerella -​ Edema and reddening of the vulva -​ Milky gray discharge -​ Fish-like odor -​ Management: metronidazole and clindamycin -​ Chlamydia trachomatis -​ Watery graywhite vaginal discharge -​ Vulvar itching -​ Management: tetracycline/doxycyline -​ During pregancy:erythromycin -​ Neisseria gonorrhea -​ Possibly symptomless -​ May hve profuse yellow-green vaginal discharge -​ Management: oral ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and doxycycline -​ Treponema pallidum -​ Painless ulcer on vulvar or vagina -​ Management: benzathine penicillin -​ Streptoccocus -​ Vaginitis, vulvar itching -​ Edema and reddening of vulva -​ Management: amoxicillin -​ Herpes virus -​ Painful pinpoint vesicles on an erythematous base with watery vaginal discharge -​ Voiding maybe irritating and painful -​ Management: acyclovir helps heal lesions, bathing with dilute sodium bicarbonate solution, oral analgesics
text.127: Essential Intrapartum and Newborn Care -​ a set of evidence-based practices focused on improving newborn care and reducing infant mortality. -​ Core Principles: -​ EINC emphasizes immediate and thorough drying of the newborn, followed by skin-to-skin contact with the mother, delayed cord clamping (1-3 minutes after birth), and the initiation of breastfeeding without separating the baby from the mother. -​ Evidence-Based: -​ These practices are supported by research and recommended by organizations like the Department of Health (DOH) and the World Health Organization (WHO). -​ Impact: -​ EINC aims to reduce neonatal mortality rates by ensuring consistent and high-quality care for newborns during the critical first moments after birth. -​ Implementation: -​ The program is designed to be implemented by skilled birth attendants in all settings, including both government and private facilities. -​ "Unang Yakap": -​ EINC is also known as "Unang Yakap" in the Philippines, where it is a key component of the Department of Health's efforts to improve maternal and newborn health. -​ Four time-bound interventions: 1.​ Immediate drying a.​ Using a clean, dry cloth, thoroughly dry the baby, wiping the face, eyes, head, front, back, arms and legs 2.​ Skin-to-skin contact a.​ If a baby is crying and breathing normally, avoid any manipulation such as routine suctioning that may cause trauma or introduce infection. Place the newborn prone on the mother’s abdomen or chest skin-to-skin b.​ Cover the newborn’s back with a blanket and head with a bonnet. Place identification band on ankle 3.​ Proper cord clamping and cutting a.​ Clamp and cut the cord after cord pulsations have stopped (1-3 minutes) b.​ Put ties tightly around the cord at 2cms and 5cms from the newborn’s abdomen c.​ Cut between the ties with sterile instrument d.​ Observe for oozing blood e.​ Do not milk the cord towards the newborn f.​ After cord clamping, ensure oxytocin 10IU IM given to the mother 4.​ Non-separation of baby from mother & breastfeeding initiation
text.128: a.​ Observe the newborn. Only when the newborn shows feeding cues (opening mouth, tonguing, licking, rooting), make verbal suggestions to the mother to encourage her newborn to move toward the breast b.​ Counsel on positioning and attachment c.​ When the baby is ready, advise the mother to: i.​ Make sure the newborn’s neck is neither flexed nor twisted ii.​ Make sure the newborn is facing the breast, with the newborn’s nose opposite her nipple and chin touching the breast iii.​ Hold the newborn’s body close to her body iv.​ Support the newborn’s body, not just the neck and shoulder v.​ Wait until her newborn’s mouth is opened wide vi.​ Move her newborn into her breast, aiming the infant’s lower lip well below the nipple vii.​ Look for signs of good attachment and suckling: 1.​ Mouth wide open 2.​ Lower lip turned outward 3.​ Baby's chin touching the breast 4.​ Suckling is slow, deep and some pauses 5.​ If the attachment or suckling is not good, try again and reassess Notes: -​ Health workers should not touch the newborn unless there is a medical indication -​ Do not give sugar water, formula or other prelacteals -​ Do not give bottles or pacifiers -​ Do not throw away colostrum Teratogenicity of Drug Drug Drug Use Teratogenic Effect Isotretenoin (Accutane) Etritinate (Tegison) Acne Psoriasis Craniofacial, cardiac and CNS anomalies Wine, whiskey Social use Fetal alcohol syndrome Acetylsalicylic acid (Aspirin) NSAIDs Minor pain relief Prolonged pregnancy, maternal bleeding, ductus arteriosus Methotrexate Cyclophosphamide Chemotherapy Multiple anomalies Danazol Endometriosis Masculinization of female fetus

physical change and quantitative increase in size of the whole body or any of its parts -​ Development - changes that mark an increase in function, complexity and progression of skill -​ Maturation - involves intrinsic processes of development that are genetically or organically programmed -​ Concepts: -​ Asynchronous growth -​ Whole body does not grow at once -​ Different regions and systems develop at different rates and times -​ The pace of growth and development is uneven -​ Growth is greater/very rapid in two periods: infancy and adolescence -​ All body systems do not develop at the same rate -​ Neurologic tissues grow during the first year of life while genital tissue grows until puberty -​ Development proceeds from gross to refined skills -​ This principle parallels the preceding one, once children are able to control distal body parts such as fingers, they are able to perform fine motor skills -​ Principles of Growth and Development: -​ Growth and development are continuous processes from conception until death -​ At all times a child is growing new cells and learning new skills -​ Growth and development proceed in an orderly sequence -​ Growth in height occurs in only one sequence from smaller to larger -​ Development proceeds from gross to refined skills -​ There is an optimum time for initiation of experiences or leaning -​ Children cannot learn new tasks until their nervous system is mature enough to allow that particular learning -​ All body systems do not develop at the same rate -​ Certain body tissues mature more rapidly than others -​ Development is cephalocaudal -​ Development proceeds from the head to tail -​ Development proceeds from proximal to distal body parts -​ Development starts from the midline of the body and progresses towards the extremities Basic Division of Childhood Neonate First 28 days Infant 1 month to 1 year Toddler 1 to 3 years Preschooler 4 to 6 years School-aged child 7 to 12 years

involves the capacity for true intimacy Developmental Theories Psychosocial Stages of Development -​ Erik Erikson views psychosocial growth occurs in sequential phases and each stage is dependent on completion of the previous stage or life task Stage Virtue Task Trust vs. Mistrust (Infant) Hope Viewing the world as safe and reliable; relationships as nurturing, stable and dependable Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt (Toddler) Will Achieving a sense of control and free will Initiative vs. Guilt (Preschool) Purpose Beginning development of a conscience; learning to manage conflict and anxiety Industry vs. Inferiority (School Age) Competence Emerging confidence in own abilities; taking pleasure in accomplishments Identity vs. Role Confusion (Adolescence) Fidelity Formulating a sense of self and belonging Intimacy vs. Isolation (Young Adult) Love Forming adult, loving relationships and meaningful attachments to others Generativity vs. Stagnation (Middle Adult) Care Being creative and productive; establishing the next generation Ego Integrity vs. Despair (Maturity) Wisdom Accepting responsibility for one’s self and life Cognitive Stages of Development -​ Human intelligence progresses through series of stages based on age, with the child at each successive stage demonstrating a higher level of functioning than of previous stages -​ Jean Piaget’s Four Stages of Cognitive Development (1)​ Sensorimotor (birth to 2 years old): the child develops a sense of self separate from the environment and the concept of object permanence; that is, tangible objects do not cease to exist just because they are out of sight. He/she begins to form mental images (2)​ Preoperational (2-6 years old): the child develops the ability to express self with language, understands the meaning of symbolic gestures, and begins to classify objects (3)​ Concrete operational (6-12 years): the child begins to apply logic to thinking, understands spatially and reversibility and is increasingly social and able to apply rules; however thinking is still concrete (4)​ Formal operational (12-15 years old): the child learns to think and reason in abstract terms, further develops logical thinking and reasoning, and achieves cognitive maturity Moral Development -​ Lawrence Kohlberg recognized moral reasoning helps determine whether children can be depended on to carry out self-care activities Age (Year) Stage Description Preconventional (Level I) 2-3 1 Punishment/Obedience orientation: child does right because a parent tells him or her to and to avoid punishment 4-7 2 Individualism: instrumental purpose and exchange. Carries out actions to satisfy own needs rather than society’s Conventional (Level II) 7-10 3 Orientation to interpersonal relations of mutuality: Child follows rules because of a need to be a “good” person in
text.134: own eyes of others 10-12 4 Maintenance of social order, fixed rules and authority: child finds following rules satisfying Postconventional (Level III) Older than 12 5 Social contract, utilitarian law-making perspective: follows standards of society for good of all people 6 Universal ethical principle orientation: follows internalized standards of conduct Growth and Development Infant Month Motor Development Fine Motor Development Socialization and Language Play 0-1 Largely reflex Keeps hands fisted; able to follow object to midline Enjoys watching face of primary caregiver, listening to soothing sounds 2 Holds head up when prone Has social smile Makes cooing sounds; differentiates cry Enjoys bright-colored mobiles 3 holds head and chest up when prone Follows object past midline Laughs out loud spends time looking at hands or uses them as toy during the month (hand regard) 4 Grasp, stepping, tonic neck reflexes are fading needs space to turn 5 Turns front to back, no longer has head lag when pulled Handles rattles well upright; some infants take first step holds cup and spoon well; helps to dress says two words Likes toys that fit inside each other; nursery rhymes; will like pull toys as soon as walking -​ Fear: Stranger and anxiety -​ Play: solitary -​ Toys: mobile, rattle, musical toys, crib (sensory toys) -​ Rapid growth and development -​ Birth until 1 year -​ Freud’s psychoanalytic theory: oral phase -​ Meet the oral needs of the infant: provide safe and washable toys such as pacifier -​ Feed on demand: feed according to the child’s biologic need for food -​ When oral feeding is contraindicated but sucking is not, give a pacifier to suck -​ Piaget’s cognitive development -​ 1-4 months: primary circular reaction (body is center of attention) -​ 4-8 months: secondary circular reaction (from body to environment) -​ 8-12 months: coordination of secondary reaction -​ 12-18 months: tertiary circular reaction (trial and error) -​ Kolhberg’s theory of moral development -​ The infancy period is pre-religious state. Infants learn that when they do certain actions, parents give them affection and approval; for other actions, parents scold and label the behavior “bad” Toddler -​ Fear: separation anxiety -​ Play: parallel -​ Toys: push and pull toys -​ Age 1-3 years old -​ Characterized by alternating rapid and slow rate of growth and development -​ Pot-belly -​ Bow-legged -​ Ask questions constantly, up tp 400 a day -​ A consistent bedtime ritual helps prepare the toddler for sleep -​ Security object at bedtime may assist in sleep -​ Children generally have 20 of their deciduous teeth by 3 years of age -​ Signs of readdinesss for toilet training -​ Child is able to stay dry for 2 hours -​ Child is waking up dry from a nap -​ Child is able to sit, squat, and walk -​ Child is able to remove clothing -​ Child recognizes urge to defecate or urinate -​ Child expresses willingness to please parent -​ Child is able to sit on toilet for 5-10 minutes without fussing or getting off -​ Negativism - toddlers often say “no” when asked to do something or may not obey request from people other than their parents because they do not view their authority as being at the same level as their parents’ authority -​ Nursing intervention -​ Offer choices to them -​ Avoid using close-ended questions, use open-ended questions instead -​ Freud’s psychoanalytic theory: anal phase -​ Focus on the anal region as they begin toilet training -​ Piaget’s cognitive development -​ Preoperational thought: 2-7 years -​ Thought becomes more symbolic; can arrive at answers mentally instead of through physical attempt. Comprehends simple abstractions but thinking is basically concrete and literal. Child is egocentric (unable to see the viewpoint of another) -​ Kolhberg’s moral development -​ Pre-conventional (2-3 years old): stage 1 -​ Morals are thought to be motivated by punishment and rewards Preschooler -​ Fear: mutilation and castration -​ Play: Associative and imitation/make-believe -​ Toys: a simple puzzle, dolls, coloring book -​ Age 3-5 years -​ The preschool grows 2 ½ to 3 inches per year -​ By 5 years old, the child tends to focus on social aspects of eating, table conversations, manners and willingness to try new foods -​ Oedipus complex: refers to strong emotional attachment a preschool boy demonstrates toward his mother -​ Electra complex: attachment of a preschool girl to her father -​ Centering -​ Children tend to look at an object and see only one of its characteristics -​ They see that a banana is yellow but not notice it is also long -​ Magical thinking: perceive animals and even inanimate objects capable of thought or feeling -​ Egocentrism: perceiving one’s thoughts and needs are better or more important than those of other -​ Kolhberg’s moral development -​ Pre-conventional (4-7) stage 2 -​ Individualism carries out actions to satisfy own needs rather than society’s School Age -​ Fear: displacement from school -​ Play: indoor competitive -​ Toys: computer games and table games -​ Age 6-12 years old -​ Characterized by having a slow period of growth and development patterns -​ Freud’s psychosexual stage: latent phase - a time which children’s libido appears to be diverted into concrete thinking -​ Piaget’s cognitive development: concrete operational (7-12 years old) -​ Include systematic reasoning. Classifications involve sorting objects according to attributes such as color. Child is aware of reversibility, an opposite operation or continuation of reasoning back to a starting point -​ Kolhberg’s moral development: Level II: conventional (7-10 years old) -​ Orientation to interpersonal relations of mutuality. Child follows rules because of the need to be a “good” person in own eyes and others -​ Reasoning during school age tends to be inductive, proceeding from specific to general: school-age children tend to reason that a toy they are holding is broken, the toy is made of plastic so all plastic toys break easily Adolescence -​ Fear: displacement from peers -​ Play: outdoor competitive (atheletic and sports) -​ Toys: basketball, etc. -​ Age 13-18 years old -​ Accelerated growth and maturation -​ Influeced by hormonal changes characterized by growth spurt which begins early in girls, about 1-2 years ahead than boys -​ Sebaceous and sweat glands become active and fully functional -​ Freud’s psychosexual stage: genital phase - establishment of new sexual aims and finding of new love objects -​ Piaget’s cognitive development: formal operational: 12 years -​ Can solve hypothetical problems with scientific reasoning -​ Understands thought casualty and can deal with past, present and future -​ Adult or mature thought, good activity this period “talk time” to sort through attitudes -​ Kolhberg’s moral development: post-conventional (older than 12 years old) -​ Social contract: utilitarian law-making perspective, follows standard of society for the good of all people -​ Universal ethical principle: orientations, folowss internalized standards of conduct -​ Adolescents can be responsible for self-care because they view this as a standard of adult behavior -​ Many adult do not reach this level of moral development

Completely covered minora and clitoris Profile -​ Normal birth weight: 2.5-4 kg -​ Doubles at 6 months -​ Triples at 12 months -​ Quadruplets at 2 ½ years -​ Second born usually weights more than first born, continues to increase with each succeeding child in a family -​ During the first few days after birth, a newborn loses 5% to 10% of birth weight due to newborn is no longer under the influence of salt and fluid retaining maternal hormones -​ Low birth weight: <2500 g -​ Large for gestational age: >4000 g -​ Birth length: 46-54 cm -​ Head circumference: 33-35 cm -​ Chest circumference: 31-33 cm Neurological Assessment Reflexes -​ Extrusion -​ Food placed on infant’s tongue is thrust forward and out of the mouth -​ Tonic neck -​ As head is turned to one side, arm and leg on that side extends and opposite extremities in flexion -​ Response usually disappears within 3-4 months -​ Palmar grasp -​ Elicited by placing finger in newborn’s palm -​ Palmar response lessens within 3-4 months -​ Moro -​ Place the newborn on a flat surface and strike the surface or make a lout abrupt noise to startle the newborn -​ The newborn systematically abducts and extends the arms -​ A persistent response lasting more than 6 months may indicate occurrence of brain damage during pregnancy -​ Sucking and rooting -​ Touch the newborn’s lip, cheek or corner of the mouth with a nipple -​ Newborn turns head toward the nipple, opens the mouth, takes hold of the nipple and sucks -​ Usually disappears after 3-4 months but may persist for up to 1 year -​ Stepping or walking -​ Hold the newborn in a vertical position, allowing one foot to touch a table surface -​ The newborn stimulates walking, alternately flexing and extending the feet -​ Present for 3-4 months -​ Babinski Sign: Plantar Reflex -​ Beginning at the heel of the foot, gently stroke upward along the lateral aspect of the sole, and then move the finger along the ball of the foot -​ The newborn’s toes hyperextend while the big toe dorsiflexes -​ Disappears after the newborn is 1 year old -​ Absence of this reflex indicates the need for neurological examination Vital Signs -​ Temperature: Axillary - 97.9-98F -​ Apical rate: 120-160 bpm -​ Respirations: 30-60 cpm -​ Blood pressure: 73/55 mmHg Newborns can conserve heat by constricting blood vessels and moving away from the skin. Brown fat, a special tissue found in mature newborns, apparently helps to conserve or produce body heat by increasing metabolism Physical Assessment -​ Head -​ Anterior fontanel -​ Soft, flat, diamond shaped 3-4 cm wide by 2-3 long -​ Closes between 12-18 months -​ Posterior fontanel -​ Triangular shaped 0.5-1 cm -​ Closes at 2-3 months -​ Caput succedaneum -​ Swelling of scalp caused by prolonged labor crosses over the suture line -​ Gradually disappears at about third day of life -​ Cephalhematoma -​ Collection blood caused by increased pressure of birth -​ Caused by rupture of periosteal capillary -​ Absorbed within 3-6 weeks -​ Craniotabes -​ Localized swelling of the cranial bones caused by pressure of the fetal skull against the mother’s pelvic bone in uterus -​ Condition corrects itself without treatment -​ Eyes -​ Infant eyes assume their permanent color between 3-12 months of age -​ Lacrimal ducts do not fully mature until about 3 months of age -​ Strabismus is normal until 6 months -​ Subconjunctival hemorrhage - a red spot on sclera on inner aspect of eye due to pressure at birth (absorbed 2-3 weeks) -​ Ears -​ The pinna normally align from inner to outer canthus of the eye -​ The low set ears indicate chromosomal disease -​ Trisomy 21 (down syndrome) -​ Kidney anomaly -​ Test newborn hearing by ringing a bell held 6 inches from each ear -​ Nose -​ Nasal flaring is the enlargement of the opening of the nostrils during breathing -​ Nasal flaring indicates respiratory distress -​ Test for choanal atresia (blockage at the rear of the nose) by closing the newborn’s mouth and compressing one nares at a time with fingers -​ Note any discomfort or distress while breathing this way -​ Neck -​ Short chubby with creases skin folds -​ Rigidity of the neck may indicate congenital torticollis/meningitis -​ The trachea may be prominent on the front of the neck, and the thymus gland may be enlarged because of the rapid growth of glandular tissue -​ The thymus gland will triple in size by 3 years of age; it remains at the size until the child is about 10 years old, and then shrinks -​ Chest -​ It is approximately 2 inches smaller than head circumference -​ Retractions or drawing in of the chest during inspiration should not be observed, it could indicate respiratory distress -​ Abdomen -​ The abdomen of the child should look slightly protuberant, a scaphoid or sunken appearance could indicate missing abdominal contents -​ Bowel sounds should be present 1 hour after birth -​ Umblical cord -​ Stump should appear as a white, gelatinous structure with blue and red streaks of the umbilical vein and arteries -​ 2 arteries and 1 vein -​ Single artery could signify congenital heart or kidney anomaly -​ Umbilical cordd should break free by day 6 to 10 -​ If umbilical hernia is present, taping or putting buttons or coins on the cord do not help defects to close -​ Anogenital Area -​ Inspect the anus of a newborn to be certain it is present, patent and not covered by a membrane (imperforate anus) -​ If a newborn does not do so in the first 24 hours, suspect imperforate anus or meconium ileus -​ Male genitalia -​ Both testes should be present in the scrotum -​ If one or both testicles are not present (cryptorchidism) caused by agenesis (absence of an organ) -​ Ectopic testes (the testes cannot enter the scrotum because the opening to the scrotal sac is closed) or undescended testes -​ Newborns with agenesis of the testes are usually referred for investigation of kidney anomalies because the testes arise from the same germ tissue as the kidneys -​ Elicit a cremastetic reflex - a test for the integrity of spinal nerves T8-T10. The response may be absent in newborns who are younger than 10 days -​ Urethral opening should be on the tip of the glans, not on the dorsal surface (epispadias) or on the ventral surface (hypospadias) -​ Female genitalia -​ The vulva in female newborns may be swollen because of the effect of maternal hormones -​ Pseudomenstruation: female newborns have a mucus vaginal secretion which is sometimes blood tinged which is normal -​ Back -​ Inspect the base of the newborn’s spine carefully to be sure there is no pinpoint opening, dimpling, or sinus tract in the skin which would suggest a dermal sinus or spinal bifida occulta -​ Extremity -​ Unusually short arms may signify achondroplastic dwarfism -​ Inspect the palm for a simian crease (down syndrome) -​ Assess webbing (syndactyly) -​ Extra toes or fingers (polydactyly) -​ Both hips can flexed and abducted to such an extent (180 degrees) that the knees touch or nearly touch the surface of the bed if the hip joint seems to lock short of this distance (160-170 degrees), hip subluxation (a shallow and poorly formed acetabulum) is suggested
text.144: Congenital Anomaly Appraisal Procedure Abnormalities Considered Inquire for hydramnios or oligohydramnios Presence of hydramnios suggests congenital gastrointestinal obstuction Oligohydramnios suggests genitourinary obstruction or extreme prematurity Appearance of abdomen Distended abdomen suggests ascites, possible bowel obstruction or tumor Empty abdomen suggests diaphragmatic hernia Passage of nasogastric tube through nares into stomach Failure to pass nasogastric tube through nares on either side establishes choanal atresia Failure to pass into the stomach confirms presence of esophageal atresia Counting of umbilical arteries The presence of one artery suggests possible congenital urinary or cardiac anomalies, chromosomal trisomy Breast feeding facts -​ Almost all drugs pass into breastmilk. A breastfeeding mother must be certain not to take any medication without contacting her primary care provider to be certain it is compatible with breastfeeding -​ If a baby will be formula fed, be certain the parents understand the potential danger of warming bottles in a microwave oven (the inner core of milk may grow very hot) -​ Caution parents not to prop bottles, because it increases the risk for aspiration and otitis media. It also deprives infants of the pleasure of being held for feedings -​ To avoid baby bottle syndrome (cavities of the lower teeth), infants should not be put to bed with a bottle Neurologic Disorders Increased Intracranial Pressure -​ Normal: 5-15 mmHg; >20 mmHg (life-threatening) -​ Cushing’s triad -​ Hypertension -​ Bradycardia -​ Bradypnea -​ Widened pulse pressure: difference between systolic and diastolic -​ Normal: 30-40 mmHg -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Bulging fontanels: aggravated by crying -​ Anterior: diamond, closes 12-18 months -​ Posterior: triangle, closes 2-3 months -​ High pitch/shrill/irritable cry: early sign -​ Increased head circumference: tape measure every shift (8 hours) -​ Headache: initial sign -​ Projectile vomiting: compression of medulla (chemoreceptor trigger zone: vomiting center) -> cerebral edema -​ Diplopia (double vision): increased ICP = increased IOP (proximity of brain and eyes) -> optic nerve damage -> blurring of vision -> blindness -​ Pupillary changes (Pupil Equally Round and Reactive to Light and Accomodation (normal) - consensual) -​ Anisocoria: uneven pupils -> brain damage -​ Dilated pupils -> shock -​ Constricted -> narcotic overdose -​ Sunset eyes: black portion of the eyes is pushed downwards -​ Anorexia, nausea, weight loss -​ Weight: important indicator of health -​ Seizures -​ Increased neuronal firing -> erratic transmission of electrical impulses -​ Vomiting -> decreased fluid levels -> dehydration -> increased temperature -> convulsions -​ Management: -​ Position: semi-fowler (decreased ICP = gravity) -​ Where sodium goes, water follows -​ Increased fluid = Increased pressure -​ Avoid coughing and sneezing -​ Limit fluid intake: 1200-1500 ml/day -​ Pharmacotherapy -​ Diuretics (potassium wasting -> monitor for hypokalemia) -​ Lasix (loop diuretic) -> loop of Henle -> localized -​ Mannitol (osmotic diuretic) -> osmosis (pulling pressure) -> generalized -​ Decadron (dexamethasone) -> anti-inflammatory -> prevent cerebral edema -​ Anti-convulsants: prevent seizure episodes -​ Antacids: neutralizes acidity -​ Stress -> GI compensates and increases HCl -​ Counteract the effects of decadron -​ Types: -​ Magnesium hydroxide: diarrhea -​ Aluminum hydroxide: constipation -​ Anticoagulants: prevents clumping of blood -​ Increased ICP -> damage the brain blood vessel walls -> bleeding -> clotting of blood -> formation of thrombus -> dislodges (emboli) -> CVA -> multiple organ failure -​ Types: -​ Heparin: IV/SQ - text.193: -​ ACE inhibitors (captopril) -​ Beta blockers (metoprolol) -​ Angiotensin II receptor blockers (lozartan) -​ Calcium - channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) -​ Increase cardiac contractility -​ Cardiotonic drugs -​ Phosphodiesterase inhibitors (milrinone, amrinone - IV through infusion pump) (+) inotropic effect (increased calcium in cardiac cells) -​ Peripheral vasodilation -monitor BP -​ Sympathomimetic (adrenergic agonist) - increased HR (+) chronotropic effect, (+) inotropic (dobutamine, dopamine) -​ Cardiac glycosides (digoxin, digitalis) -​ (+) Inotropic, (-) chronotropic -​ Nursing considerations: -​ Monitor HR prior to administration -​ Monitor serum potassium level (hypokalemia causes toxicity) -​ Monitor ECG -​ Maintain therapeutic level: 0.5 - 2 ng/ml -​ Do not combine with CCB -​ Do not combine with BB -​ Do not combine with amiodarone (anti-arrhythmic drug) -​ Monitor for signs of symptoms of toxicity -​ Bradycardia -​ GI toxicity -​ Visual disturbance -​ ECG changes -​ Withhold then refer -​ Antidote: digoxin immune Fab/digibind Oncology -​ A branch of medicine focused on the prevention,diagnosis, treatment and study of cancer -​ Oncology nursing are as diverse and complex as those of any nursing specialty -​ Nursing management of the patient with oncologic disorders includes care of patient throughout the cancer trajectory from prevention through end-of-life care
text.194: Cancer -​ A disease process that begins when an abnormal cell is transformed by the genetic mutation of cellular DNA -​ Uncontrolled cellular division -​ Cell Cycle: -​ Interphase: longest phase -​ G1: cellular growth -​ S: DNA synthesis -​ G2: Preparation for mitosis -​ Mitosis: cell division (one-way phase, irreversible) - 2 separate daughter cells -​ Karyokinesis: nuclear division -​ Cytokinesis: cytoplasmic division (fluid portion of the cell) -​ G0: resting phase (cells that do not regenerate - example: neurons, sensory cells) -​ Carcinogenesis: production of cancer, theory of cancer causation -​ Initiation (transformed cell): initial cell mutation occurs, spontaneous mutation, exposure to carcinogens, irreversible -​ Promotion (Neoplastic lesion): cancer cells stimulated to divide even further, reversible -​ Progression (malignant tumor): cancer cells compete with one another to survive, aggressive, malignant, poor prognosis -​ Oma: tumor -​ Carcinoma: epithelial tissues (lining organs; glands); 80-90% cases -​ Sarcoma: connective issues; osteosarcoma (bones); chondrosarcoma (cartilage); leiomyosarcoma (smooth muscle) -​ Leukemia: cancer of the blood -​ Lymphoma: cancer of lymphatic tissues, nodes -​ Myeloma: plasma cells (matured b cells); produced antibodies/immunoglobulin -​ Differentiation: cells are transformed into different and more specialized cell types as they proliferate from a single stem cell (1)​ Hyperplasia: irreversible increase number of cells in an organ or tissue, pre-malignant (BPH) (2)​ Metaplasia: substitution of one cell with another, one cell type is converted/replace/transformed into another cell (3)​ Dysplasia: deranged/bizarre cellular growth, complete alteration of cells in terms of size, shape, color, amount, etc., pre-malignant (4)​ Hypertrophy: increase in cell size (5)​ Atrophy: decrease in size (a)​ Decrease oxygen, nerve, blood, nutrient supply (b)​ Aging (c)​ Prolonged immobilization
text.195: (d)​ decreased use (6)​ Neoplasia/Anaplasia: automatic malignant Characteristics Benign Malignant Cell characteristics Well-differentiated cells that resemble normal cells of the tissue from which the tumor originated Cells are undifferentiated and often bear little resemblance to the normal cells of the tissue from which they arose Mode of growth Tumor grows by expansion and does not infiltrate the surrounding tissues; usually encapsulated Grows at the periphery and sends out processes that infiltrate and destroy the surrounding tissues Rate of growth Rate of growth is usually slow Rate of growth is variable and depends on level of differentiation; the more anaplastic the tumor, the faster its growth Metastasis Does not spread by metastasis Gains access to blood and lymphatic channels and metastasizes to other areas of the body General effects Usually a localized phenomenon that does not cause generalized effects unless its location interferes with vital functions Often causes generalized effects such as anemia, weakness, and weight loss Tissue destruction Does not usually cause tissue damage unless its location interferes with blood flow Often causes extensive tissue damage as the tumor outgrows its blood supply or encroaches on blood flow to the area; may also produce substances that cause cell damage Ability to cause death Does not usually cause death unless its location interferes with vital functions Usually causes death unless growth can be controlled Diagnosis of Cancer -​ A cancer diagnosis is based on assessment for physiological and functional changes and results of diagnostic evaluation
text.196: (1)​ Determine the presence of tumor and its extent (2)​ Identify possible spread (metastasis) of the disease or invasion of other body tissue (3)​ Evaluate the function involved and uninvolved body systems and organs (4)​ Obtain tissue and cells for analysis, including evaluation of tumor stage and grading Tumor Staging and Grading -​ Staging: determines the size of the tumor and the existence of metastasis, identify the extent of involvement of cancer -​ TNM system -​ T: refers to the extent of primary tumor -​ Tx: primary tumor cannot be assessed -​ T0: no evidence of primary tumor -​ Tis: carcinoma in situ -​ T1, T2, T3, T4: increasing size and/or local extent of primary tumor -​ N: refers to lymph node involvement -​ Nx: regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed -​ N0: No regional lymph node metastasis -​ N1, NP2, NP3: increasing involvement of regional lymph nodes -​ M: refers to extent of metastasis -​ Mx: distant metastasis cannot be assessed -​ M0: no distant metastasis -​ M1: distant metastasis -​ Most common metastatic sites: -​ Lungs, liver, lymph nodes, brain and bones -​ Grading: refers to the classification of the tumor cells (levels of differentiation) -​ Grade 0: grade cannot be assessed -​ Grade I (low): cells look relatively normal and well-differentiated (benign) -​ Grade II (intermediate): cells are moderately differentiated -​ Grade III (high): cells are poorly differentiated -​ Grade IV (high): cells are undifferentiated and are fast-growing (malignant) -​ Cancer General Clinical Manifestations (1)​ Pain: a complex sensation that reflects both damage to the body and the body’s response to the damage (a)​ Acute pain: starts suddenly (b)​ Chronic pain: lasts more than 6 months (2)​ Bleeding: a decrease in the circulating platelet count (3)​ Infection: streptococcus and staphylococcus species (4)​ Anorexia-Cachexia Syndrome: unexplained weight loss, wasted appearance Warning Signs of Cancer 1.​ Change in bowel or bladder movement/habit a.​ Alteration of diarrhea and constipation - colorectal cancer i.​ Blood in stool (hematochezia) ii.​ Dark starry stool (Melena) iii.​ Change in the shape of stool (Pencil shaped stool b.​ Urinary frequency, urgency, hesitancy, dysuria (burning sensation), hematuria, obstruction - bladder cancer (cigarette smoking - strongest risk factor) 2.​ A sore/wound that does not heal a.​ Oral cancer (risk factor: cigarette smoking, 30 y/o above) b.​ Melanoma (most severe skin cancer) i.​ ABCDE Assessment tool 1.​ Asymmetry 2.​ Irregular borders 3.​ Color 4.​ Diameter (N: <5 mm) 5.​ Evolving 3.​ Unusual bleeding or discharge a.​ Post menopausal bleed b.​ Post coital bleed c.​ Bleeding in between periods d.​ Abnormal nipple discharge e.​ Prolactinoma: benign pituitary gland tumor f.​ Breast Cancer g.​ Abnormal vaginal discharge (check color, smell) h.​ Abnormal penile discharge 4.​ Thickening of breast/lump or elsewhere (breast, testicles, lymph nodes) 5.​ Indigestion (dyspepsia)/difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) - head and neck cancer 6.​ Obvious change in wart/mole a.​ Elderly: scalp, face, behind the ear, nape b.​ Adults: upper back 7.​ Nagging/hoarseness a.​ Dry, persistent cough b.​ Lung, laryngeal, head and neck cancer 8.​ Unexplained anemia a.​ Colon cancer
text.198: 9.​ Sudden weight loss (cachexia) Cancer Prevention (1)​ Primary Prevention: health promotion and risk reduction strategies (a)​ Assisting patients to avoid known carcinogens (b)​ Adopting dietary and various lifestyle changes (c)​ Immunization (d)​ Limit consumption of alcohol beverages (2)​ Secondary Prevention: involves screening and early detection activities (a)​ Mammography: to detect cyst and tumors that are non-palpable during physical exam (b)​ Pap smear: for cervical cancer and HPV detection (c)​ Prostate exam: for BPH (d)​ Breast self-exam: do it every month, no BSE week before menstruation, only a week after menstruation (3)​ Tertiary Prevention (a)​ Preventing recurrence (b)​ Assessment for development of second malignancies Management of Cancer Surgery 1.​ Diagnostic: biopsy -​ Fine needle aspiration: solid tumors (breast, lungs, liver, thyroid, brain) -​ Punch: deeper tissue sample (skin, vulva) -​ Shave: superficial tissue sample -​ Incisional: very large tumors; portion of tumor removed -​ Excitional: entire tumor removed -​ Bone marrow aspiration: leukemia, lymphoma -​ Posterior iliac crest: most preferred site -​ Sternum/breast bone (avoid for pedia <12 years old) -​ Tibia: for pedia 2.​ Primary treatment: -​ Chemosurgery -​ Electrosurgery -​ Cryosurgery -​ Laser surgery 3.​ Prophylactic surgery: involves removing non-vital tissues or organs that are likely to develop cancer (risk reduction of symptoms) 4.​ Palliative surgery: when cure is not possible, the goals of treatment are to make the patient as comfortable as possible and promote a satisfying and productive life for as long as possible (improving the quality of life) 5.​ Reconstructive surgery: carried out in an attempt to improve function or obtain a more desirable cosmetic effect Radiation Therapy -​ Radiosensitive cancer cells: responsive to radiation -​ Normal cells: highly actively dividing cells -​ Hair cells: alopecia (improve self-esteem: offer wigs, scarves, hats); temporary hair loss (improve self-care: brush, shampoo, condition hair) -​ GI tract cells: stomatitis, oral mucositis, esophagitis (avoid alcoholic mouthwashes, avoid hot, rough, spicy , acidic foods: bland diet), radiation induced enteritis (diarrhea: low fiber diet) -​ Blood cells: Anemia (risk for fatigue, injury), leukopenia (risk for infection), thrombocytopenia (risk for bleeding) -> immunosuppression -​ Skin cells: radiation induced dermatitis (avoid wearing powders, lotions, cosmetics, etc., avoid extreme temperature -> promote dryness -> pruritus -​ Reproductive tract cells: sterility, decreased libido -​ Radioresistant cancer cells: difficult to kill; malignant -​ Normal cells: connective tissues, nerve cells, sensory cells, brain cells -​ External Radiation (Teletherapy): more common than internal; patient is not radioactive; happens in sessions -​ Internal Radiation (Brachytherapy): -​ Sealed: “implant”; localized; CBR w/o BP to avoid dislodgement; pick up the implant using long handled forceps and place it in a lead lined container -> refer; if not located: notify the safety radiation team -​ Unsealed: oral, IV; systemic; patient himself is radioactive, even body fluids; private CR; inform the patient to flush the toilet twice; 48 hours after radiation administration, patient is no longer radioactive -​ DTS Principles -​ Distance: 6 feet away; private room, away from the nurses station -​ Time: 30 mins/shift; cluster activities -​ Shield: Lead shield; dosimeter badge (indicator for radiation exposure) -​ Avoid elderly, pedia, pregnancy, immunocompromised visitors -​ Side effects: -​ Alopecia -​ Stomatitis -​ Immunosuppression -​ Dermatitis -​ Sterility -​ Anorexia -​ Cachexia -​ Fatigue (common of S/E) -​ Nausea and vomiting Chemotherapy -​ Administration of antineoplastic agents to manage cancer -​ Antineoplastic agents are used in attempt to destroy tumor cells by interfering with cellular functions and reproduction (photosensitive) -​ Cell cycle specific (S Phase) - DNA Synthesis -​ Topoisomease I inhibitor: Irinotecan, Tropotecan -​ Topoisomerase II inhibitor: Etoposide, Teniposide -​ Anti-metabolites: Cytarabine, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea, methotrexate -​ Cell cycle specific (M Phase) - Mitosis -​ Mitotic spindle inhibitors -​ plant alkaloids: Vinblastine, Vincristine, Vinorelbine -​ Taxane: Paclitaxel, Docetaxel -​ Cell cycle non-specific (all cell cycle - most dangerous) -​ Alkylating agent -​ Busulfan, Carboplatin, Cisplatin, Cyclophosphamide, Nitrogen mustard, Thiotepa -​ Nitrosureas -​ Carmustine, Lomustine -​ Anti-tumor antibiotics -​ Bleomycin, dactinomycin, daunorubicin, doxorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin -​ Hormonal agents -​ Tamoxifen, Fulvestrant, Goserelin -​ Side effects: -​ Alopecia (2nd) -​ Immunosuppression -​ Dermatitis -​ Sterility -​ Pulmonary toxicity -​ Nausea and vomiting (most common S/E) -​ Give ondansteron IV, metoclopramide IV push (30 minutes before chemotherapy) -​ Stomatitis
