STOP THE INFUSION -​ Irritants - localized tissue damage -​ Vesicants - permanent tissue damage -> tissue necrosis -> amputation Nursing Care for Patients with Cancer Risk for infection -​ Place patient in a private room -​ Inform patient to avoid contact with people who have known or recent infection -​ Instruct staff in careful hand hygiene before and after entering the room -​ Avoid rectal or vaginal procedures, IMs, insertion of urinary catheter -​ Encourage patient to ambulate in room unless contraindicated -​ Assess IV sites for evidence of infection Risk for Impaired Skin Integrity -​ avoid the use of soaps, cosmetics, perfumes, lotions, powders in erythematous area -​ Avoid rubbing or scratching skin -​ Avoid applying hot water bottles, heating pads -​ Avoid exposing the area to sunlight or cold weather -​ Avoid tight clothing;use cotton clothing Impaired Oral Mucous Membrane Integrity -​ assess oral cavity daily using the same assessment criteria or rating scale -​ Instruct patient to report oral burning, pain, areas of redness, open lessons on oropharyngeal mucosa and lips, pain associated with swallowing or decreased tolerance to temperature extremes of food -​ Encourage and assist as needed in oral hygiene -​ Advise patient to avoid irritants such as commercial mouthwashes, alcoholic beverages and tobacco -​ Avoid irritating foods (acidic, hot, rough and spicy) -​ Use water-based moisturizers to protect lips Impaired Tissue Integrity: Alopecia -​ Discuss potential hair loss and regrowth with patient and family; advise that hair loss may occur on body parts other than the head -​ Explore potential impact of hair loss on self-image, interpersonal relationships and sexuality -​ Explain that hair growth usually begins again once therapy is completed -​ Prevent or minimize hair loss through the following: -​ Use mild shampoo and conditioner, gently pat dry, and avoid excessive shampoo -​ Avoid excessive combing or brushing; use wide toothed comb -​ Suggest ways to assist in coping with hair loss: -​ Purchase wig or hairpiece before hair loss -​ Begin to wear wig before hair loss Impaired Nutritional Status (Anorexia, Cachexia, Malabsorption) -​ Assess and address factors that interfere with oral intake or are associated with increased risk of decreased nutritional status -​ Initiate appropriate referrals for interdisciplinary collaboration to manage factors that interfere with oral intake -​ suggest smaller, more frequent meals -​ Educate patient to avoid unpleasant sights, odors and sounds in the environment during mealtime -​ If patient desires, serve alcoholic beverage at mealtime with foods -​ Consider cold foods if desired Impaired Nutritional Status (Nausea and Vomiting) -​ Assess the patient’s previous experiences and expectations of nausea and vomiting, including causes and interventions used -​ Adjust diet before and after drug administration according to patient preference and tolerance -​ Prevent unpleasant sights, odors and sounds in the environment -​ Administer prescribed antiemetics, sedatives and corticosteroids before chemotherapy and afterward as needed -​ Ensure adequate fluid hydration before, during, and after drug administration; assess intake and output -​ Encourage frequent oral hygiene Fatigue -​ Encourage balance of rest and exercise; avoiding extended periods of inactivity. At minimum, promote patient’s normal sleep habits -​ Encourage protein, fat, calorie intake at least equal to that recommended for the general public -​ Encourage participation in planned exercise programs involving aerobic, resistance and flexibility training based on individual limitations and safety measures -​ Encourage the use of relaxation technique and guided imagery Chronic Pain -​ Use pain scale to assess pain and discomfort characteristics: location, quality, frequency, duration at baseline and on the ongoing basis -​ Assure patient that you know the pain is real and will assist them in reducing it -​ Address myths or misconceptions and lack of knowledge about the use of opioid analgesics -​ Collaborate with patient, primary provider, and other health care team members when changes in pain management are necessary -​ Explore nonpharmacologic and complementary strategies to relieve pain and discomfort: distraction, imagery, relaxation, cutaneous stimulation, acupuncture Grief -​ Encourage verbalization of fears, concerns and questions regarding the disease, treatment and future implications -​ Explore previous successful coping strategies -​ Encourage ventilation of negative feelings, including projected anger and hostility within acceptable limits -​ Involve spiritual advisor as desired by the patient and family -​ Allow for progression through the grieving process at the individual pace of the patient and family Disturbed Body Image -​ Identify threats to patient’s self-esteem, validate concerns with patient -​ Encourage continued participation in activities and decision making -​ Encourage patient to verbalize concern -​ Assist patient in self-care when fatigue, lethargy, nausea, vomiting and other symptoms prevent independence -​ Assist patient in selecting and using cosmetics, scarves, hair pieces, hats, and clothing that increase their sense of attractiveness
text.204: Common Cancers Worldwide Breast Cancer -​ Most common cancer worldwide -​ Terminal duct lobular unit (site of milk release - mature cells) -​ Upper outer quadrant -​ Risk factors: -​ Predisposing: -​ Gender: 99% Females; 1% Males (BRCA 2 Gene, Klinefelter syndrome: XXY chromosome) -​ Age (55-65 y/o) -​ Family history -​ Race: Caucasians -​ Precipitating: -​ Previous cancer of the breast, uterus or ovaries -​ Obesity -> increased subcutaneous fats -> increased estrogen hormones -​ Nulliparity -​ Early menarche (<12 y/o) -​ Late menopause (>55 y/o) -​ Pills -​ High-dose radiation exposure to chest -​ Smoking -​ Alcohol drinking -​ Diagnostic Test: -​ Mammography - initial screening test (X-ray of the breast) -​ 40-44 years old: option to start screening -​ 45-54 years old: required annually -​ >55 years old: biennially; every two years; every other year -​ High risk: on the age 30 years old annually -​ Tumor Marker test - CA 125; screening procedure only, unreliable; ovarian cancer -​ Genetic testing - BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 Gene (ovarian cancer, prostate cancer), HER 2 Gene -> HER 2 proteins -​ Imaging test -​ CT Scan: radio waves; fastest, least expensive -​ MRI: magnetic waves; provides detailed pictures than CT Scan; remove metallic objects (jewelries, implants), hearing aids; CI: pacemaker; if claustrophobic: sedate; braces are not magnetic (except head MRI) -​ PET Scan: radioisotopes; identifies metabolic abnormalities; most expensive -​ Ultrasound: sound waves; drink 6-8 glasses of water without voiding (pelvic/abdominal only) -​ Biopsy (confirmatory) -​ Signs and symptoms: Upper outer quadrant -​ Non tender, firm, fixed, irregular nodules -​ Peau D’orange (Orange peel skin) - large pores near the areola -​ Abnormal nipple discharge, inversion, retraction, ulceration -​ Skin dimpling -​ Pain (severe) -​ Interventions: -​ Radiation therapy -​ Chemotherapy -​ Progesterone therapy -​ Surgery -​ Mastectomy -​ Modified radical: removal of breast tissues, nipple areola complex and axillary lymph nodes; pectoralis major + minor intact -​ Radical: remove everything -​ Total: prophylactic purpose; benign - removal of breast tissues + nipple areola complex -​ Lumpectomy: everything is intact, tumor only removed -​ Post-operative complications: -​ Lymphedema: semi fowlers with affected arm elevated above the level of the heart; avoid BP taking, venipuncture -​ Hematoma formation: Jackson-Pratt drainage (negative pressure suction) -​ Infection: Culture first, antibiotics after (7-14 days) -​ Post-operative interventions: -​ Monitor VS -​ Encourage deep breathing -​ Assess for infection, color changes, bleeding in surgical site -​ Maintain F&E balance, diuretics and low salt diet for severe lymphedema -​ Breast Self Exam -​ Pre-menopausal: 5-7 days after menstrual period -​ Post-menopausal: same day each month -​ Irregular: same day each month -​ Stand in front of the mirror -​ Circular motion outer to inner, up down motion or spiral motion -​ If lying down, place a folded towel underneath the shoulders for even distribution of tissues across the chest wall Lung Cancer -​ Bronchogenic carcinoma (2nd common cancer) -​ Risk factors: -​ >60 y/o; M>F -​ Family history -​ Cigarette smoking -​ Secondhand smoke -​ Inhalational chemical carcinogens -​ Environmental and occupational pollutants (silica dust, asbestos, radon gas) -​ Diagnostic Test: -​ Tumor Marker - CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) initial screening; colon cancer -​ Imaging Test -​ Low Dose CT Scan - 50-80 y/o annually (smokers); 20 smoking pack year history -​ 1 pack year = 1 pack (20 cigarettes per day for a year) -​ 1 pack /day for straight 20 years -​ 2 packs/day for straight 10 years
text.207: -​ Bronchoscopic biopsy (confirmatory test) -​ Pre-endoscopy: suppresses gag reflex (administer lidocaine spray) -​ Post-endoscopy: assess return of gag reflex -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Nagging cough (dry persistent cough) -> hemoptysis -​ Dyspnea -> fatigue -> anorexia -> cachexia -​ Nausea and vomiting, dysphagia, hoarseness, chest pain -​ Diminished or absent breath sounds, respiratory changes -​ Interventions: -​ Surgery: -​ Thoracotomy: general surgical procedure; surgical incision into the thoracic cavity -​ Lobectomy: removal of a lung lobe; remaining lobes will re expand -​ Position: unaffected side to promote lung expansion -​ Pneumonectomy: removal of entire lung -​ Position: affected side to promote maximum lung expansion -​ Wedge resection: incision of a small part of of tissue (biopsy) -​ Radiation therapy -​ Chemotherapy -​ Incentive Spirometry -​ To prevent atelectasis -​ To strengthen intercoastal muscles -​ 10-15x/waking hours -​ Inhale & suck -​ Nursing management: -​ Monitor VS, breath sounds and oxygen saturation -​ Fowlers position and administer oxygen PRN -​ High calorie, high protein, high vitamin diet -​ Administer bronchodilators, corticosteroids, analgesics as prescribed -​ Provide activity and rest periods as tolerated Common Blood Cancers Hodgkin’s Lymphoma -​ Rare; high cure rate -​ Risk Factors: -​ 15-35 years old & >60 years old -​ Male -​ Family history -​ History of viral infections -​ Long term use of immunosuppressants -​ Diagnostic test: -​ Reed Sternberg Cells -​ PE: palpable lymph nodes -​ PET Scan -​ Bone marrow aspiration biopsy -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Painless, firm and large lymphatic nodules (cervical lymph node) -​ B symptoms: -​ Fever -​ Night sweats -​ Weight loss -​ Management: -​ Chemotherapy Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma: absence of Reed Sternberg cells Multiple Myeloma -​ Risk factors: -​ >65 y/o, male -​ Diagnostic test: -​ Bence Jones Proteins (urine) - WOF: infection, injures -​ Renal function test -​ Imaging test -​ X-ray -​ Bone marrow aspiration biopsy -​ Signs and symptoms: CRAB -​ Hypercalcemia (encourage increased OFI) -​ Renal dysfunction -​ Anemia -​ Bone destruction (osteoporosis, multiple fractures) -​ Management: SAFETY is the PRIORIT -​ Chemotherapy
text.209: Common Reproductive Cancers Prostate Cancer -​ Prostate gland: seminal fluid production; below the neck of the bladder -​ Risk factors: lifestyle related -​ Unclear cause -​ Advancing age (>50 y/o; average 67 y/o); men -​ Heavy metal exposure -​ Red meat diet -​ Smoking -​ History of STI -​ Race: African American descent -​ Diagnostic test: -​ Tumor marker: PSA (Prostate Specific Antigen) -​ Digital rectal exam -​ Imaging tests: rectal ultrasound -​ Biopsy -​ Clinical manifestation: -​ Asymptomatic in early stage -​ Changes in bladder habits (painless hematuria, nocturia, urinary obstruction) -​ Pelvic/abdominal/back pain -​ Management: -​ Surgery -​ Prostatectomy: removal of prostate gland -​ Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP): the procedure involves insertion of a scope into the urethra to excise prostatic tissue -​ Suprapubic prostatectomy: removal of prostate gland by an abdominal incision with a bladder incision -​ Retropubic prostatectomy: removal of prostate gland by a low abdominal incision without opening the bladder -​ Perineal prostatectomy: the prostate gland is removed through an incision made between the scrotum and anus (risk for sterility, bladder incontinence) -​ Continuous bladder irrigation -​ Decrease bleeding and to keep the bladder free from clots -​ 1 lumen is for inflating the balloon (30ml) -​ 1 lumen is for instillation (inflow) - PNSS -​ 1 lumen is for outflow -​ Maintain traction on the catheter, if applied. Instruct patient to keep the leg straight -​ Run the solution at a rate as prescribed to keep the urine pink (clear) -​ Avoid heavy lifting, stressful exercise, driving, the valsalva maneuver and sexual intercourse for 2 to 6 weeks to prevent strain and call the if bleeding occurs -​ Radiation therapy -​ Chemotherapy -​ Androgen suppression therapy -​ Orchiectomy - removal of testicles Testicular Cancer -​ Testicles: sperm production -​ One of the best prognosis: 95% chance recovery -​ Thermoregulation: 3 degrees less than the body temperature for the sperm to survive -​ Risk factors: -​ Young adult males 15-35/17-45 years old -​ Family history -​ Personal history -​ History of cryptorchidism (undescended testicles) - late pregnancy -​ Orchiopexy - surgical manipulation of testicles -​ Inguinal hernia -​ Klinefelter syndrome -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ Tumor marker test: HCG, AfP, LDH -​ Testicular self exam (after warm shower, same day each month) -​ Gently roll and palpate using the thumb and forefinger -​ Hold the penis upward -​ Imaging test: ultrasound -​ Biopsy -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Painless testicular swelling -​ Sudden feelings of heaviness sorotum -​ Fluid collection scrotum -​ Pelvic, abdominal, scrotal pain -​ Low back pain (bone metastasis) -​ Gynecomastia -​ Management: -​ Radiation therapy or chemotherapy as needed -​ Testosterone Replacement therapy (oral, IM, topical) -​ Unilateral orchiectomy (risk for sterility); radical orchiectomy; retroperitoneal lymph node dissection -​ Post-operative interventions: -​ Monitor for signs of bleeding, infection, I&O, pain management -​ Instruct patient to avoid lifting and strenuous activity -​ Discuss reproduction, sexuality, and fertility information and options with the client Cervical Cancer -​ Risk factors: -​ Average: 52 y/o; 35-45 y/o -​ Family history -​ Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection -​ HPV types 6, 11: STI -​ HPV types 16,18: Cervical cancer -​ Cigarette smoking -​ Risky sexual behavior (early coitus <17 y/o) -​ Unprotected sex, multiple sexual partners -​ Multiparity -​ Poor ulitilization of pap smear, HPV vaccine -​ Diagnostic Test: -​ Pap Smear: is not biopsy -​ Identify cervical lesions, inflammations -​ 25-65 y/o: with HPV test every 5 years -​ HPV test only: every 5 years -​ Pap smear only: every 3 years -​ Avoid sexual intercourse before pap smear (false positive) -​ Avoid douching, contraceptive creams for 2-3 days before pap smear (false negative) -​ Colposcopy: “acetowhite lesions” -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Unusual bleedings or discharge -​ Painless vaginal postmenstrual and postcoital bleeding -​ Foul-smelling or serosanguinous vaginal discharge -​ Pelvic, abdominal lower back, leg or groin pain, dyspareunia -​ Leg edema -​ Hydronephrosis -​ Anorexia and weight loss -​ Leakage of urine and feces from vagina (vesicovaginal fistula/rectovaginal fistula) -​ Changes of bladder habits -​ Dysuria and hematuria, urinary obstruction -​ Management: -​ Surgery -​ Cryosurgery: freezing the cancer tissues -​ Conization: cone-shaped cancerous area of cervix is removed; allows the woman to retain reproductive capacity -​ Hysterectomy: removal of whole uterus; discuss reproductive, sexuality, fertility issues -​ Pelvic exenteration: the removal of all pelvic contents, for recurrent cancer if no evidence of tumor outside the pelvis and no lymph node involvement exist -​ Types of pelvic exenteration -​ Anterior: removal of uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, vagina, bladder, urethra and pelvic lymph nodes -​ Posterior: removal of uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, descending colon, rectum and anal canal -​ Total: combination of anterior and posterior -​ Radiation and Chemotherapy -​ Laser therapy: boundaries of the lesions are visible during colposcopic examination -​ Prevention: -​ Pap smear -​ HPV vaccine -​ 9-14 y/o - 2 doses; day 0 - 6-12 months -​ 15-45 y/o - 3 doses; day 0, 1-2 months, 6 months -​ Gardasil: HPV Type 6, 11, 16, 18 -​ Cervarix: HPV Type 16, 18 Ovarian Cancer -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ abdominal discomfort or swelling -​ GI disturbance -​ Dysfunctional vaginal bleeding -​ Abdominal mass -​ Elevated tumor marker (CA 125) -​ Interventions:

caused by: -​ Trauma -​ twisting -​ Bone disease or degeneration -​ Assessment: -​ Pain or tenderness -​ Decrease or loss of muscular strength or function -​ obvious deformity and shortening -​ Crepitation -​ localized edema and ecchymosis -​ Diagnosis: -​ X-ray -​ MRI or arthroscopy -​ Types by exposure -​ Closed or simple - skin over fracture remains intact -​ Compound or open - bone is exposed to air through break in skin -​ Types by extent of break -​ Complete - bone is separated completely, breaks into two parts -​ Incomplete - fracture line does not extend through full transverse width of bone -​ Types by pattern -​ Comminuted - bone is shattered or crushed, creates numerous fragments -​ Compression - fractured bone is compressed by other bones -​ Depressed - bone fragments are driven inward, commonly seen in skull fractures -​ Greenstick - one side of the bone is broken and the other is bent, occurs mostly in children -​ Impacted - part of the fracture bone is driven into another bone -​ Oblique - fracture lines run at an angle across the axis of the bone -​ Pathological/Spontaneous - results from weakening of bone structure by pathological processes -​ Spiral - break partially encircles the bone caused by twisting bone -​ Stress - occurs in normal or abnormal bone exposed to repeated stress, common in athletes or military recruits -​ Transverse - bone is fractured straight across (horizontal line across the bone) -​ Emergency management (nonsurgical) -​ Immobilize immediately + apply splinting to prevent further injury -​ Open fracture -​ Cover wound with sterile dressing and splint the limb -​ Do not attempt to manually reduce the fracture outside of the hospital setting -​ In the ED, remove or cut the clothes around the injury and assess and treat -​ Surgical management -​ Fracture reduction - restoration of bone fragments to anatomic realignment and positioning with immobilization -​ Interventions:

text.234: Cast Complications Compartment Syndrome -​ Medical, painful emergency condition mostly in lower leg -​ Pressure increases within one or more compartments, usually in extremities = decreased blood flow -> tissue ischemia and neurologic impairment -​ Common among young adults; may take up to 48 hours for symptoms to be present -​ Neurologic damage may be irreversible if untreated within 4-12 hours -​ Assessment (6P’s): -​ Pain (severe, unrelieved by opioids, disproportionate) -​ Pallor -​ Poikilothermia (coolness) -​ Paralysis (loss of movement) -​ Paresthesia (tingling/numbness) -​ Pulselessness (late sign) -​ Intervention: -​ Univalve or bivalve the cast/dressing -​ Fasciotomy (anterolateral or posteromedial removal of fascia) -​ Wound left unclosed for 3-5 days -​ Cover with moist, sterile saline dressing or aseptic sheet -​ Negative-pressure wound therapy (VAC) -​ Splint in functional position + elevate + passive ROM -​ Once resolved, debride + close with skin graft Pressure Ulcer -​ Pressure on soft tissues causing anoxia and pressure ulcers -​ Typically reports very painful “hot spot” and tightness under cast -​ May feel warmth in affected area -​ Drainage may stain cast and emit unpleasant odor -​ Extensive loss of tissue with skin breakdown and necrosis -​ Intervention: -​ Windowing - ensure prevention of window edema Disuse Syndrome -​ Muscle atrophy and loss of strength = deterioration of body system -​ Intervention: -​ Isometric muscle contraction exercises/muscle setting exercises
text.235: -​ How: -​ Arm -​ Contract and relax arm muscles against resistance -​ Quadriceps & gluteal setting exercise -​ Position: supine (lying flat) -​ Push knee back onto mattress -​ How? Contract anterior thigh muscles -​ Or contract muscle of buttocks -​ Hold for 5 to 10 seconds -​ Relax and repeat 10 times each hour when awake Fracture Complications Fat Embolism Syndrome -​ Movement of fat globules/foreign particles into pulmonary circulation -​ Occurs within 24 - 72 hours of injury; mostly in males (10-40 years old) with closed fractures -​ Assessment (classic triad): -​ Hypoxemia -​ Neurologic changes -​ Petechial rash (upper body, conjunctiva, oral mucosa) -​ Sudden chest pain -​ Dyspnea/ difficulty breathing -​ Restlessness and confusion -​ Coughing with bilateral crackles -​ Diagnosis -​ Clinical suspicion (triad) + imaging (CXR, CT) -​ Intervention (supportive) -​ Immobilization of fracture -​ Oxygenation (humidified O2) -​ IV fluids to maintain perfusion -​ IV anticoagulant (heparin) -​ Intubation + mechanical ventilation if ABG indicates severe hypoxemia Infection & Osteomyelitis -​ Introduction of microorganisms into bone -> inflammation and localized bone infection -​ Assessment -​ Tenderness and fever -​ Edema and pain -​ Leukocytosis and elevated ESR -​ Intervention -​ Aggressive, long term IV antibiotics via central venous access -​ Surgery for resistant infection with sequestrectomy and/or bone grafts -​ Sequestrum = fragment of dead bone that has separated -​ Debridement with sterile irrigating solution in OR -​ Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) for unrelenting infection Avascular Necrosis (Osteonecrosis) -​ Loss of blood supply -> bony collapse and joint destruction -​ Common in: femoral head, scaphoid, talus, humeral head -​ Assessment: -​ Pain with movement -> progresses to pain at rest -​ Diagnosis: -​ X-ray, CT scan, bone scan -​ Interventions: -​ Joint preservation approach -​ Nonoperative: activity modification (reduced weight bearing) -​ Surgical: -​ Drilling avascular segment (core decompression) or bone marrow graft -​ Remove necrotic fragment + joint reconstruction Complex Regional Pain Syndrome -​ Disportionate regional pain in limb following fracture, soft tissue injury, or surgery -​ Chronic; may extend to adjacent areas -​ Common in women > 40 years -​ Types: -​ Type I - reflex sympathetic dystrophy (no confirmed nerve injury) -​ Type II - causalgia (confirmed nerve injury) -​ Assessment: -​ Severe burning pain -​ Vasomotor skin changes (mottled, shiny skin) -​ Hyperesthesia (increased sensitivity) -​ Local edema -​ Stiffness -​ Diagnosis: -​ Physical history and exam + ruling out other causes
text.237: -​ Interventions: -​ Pain relief: NSAIDs, opioids, topical anesthetics, corticosteriods -​ Neuropathic pain: anticonvulsants, antidepressants -​ Sympathetic nerve blocks, neural stimulation -​ Novel treatment: IVIG infusion, ketamine, hyperbaric oxygen therapy -​ Psychiatric nursing support + rehabilitation Hip Fracture -​ Risk factors -​ Age > 65 years old -​ Women (osteoporosis risk) -​ Higher risk for falls -​ Types: -​ Intracapsular - fracture of femoral head and neck -​ High risk of vascular damage on neck of femur = ischemia -> avascular necrosis -​ Extracapsular - fracture outside joint capsule = base of femoral neck to distal lesser trochanter -​ Assessment: -​ Pain over outer thigh or groin -​ Discomfort with hip flexion and rotation -​ Shortening, adduction, external rotation -​ Diagnosis: X-ray -​ Intervention: -​ Intracapsular fracture - broken femoral head within joint capsule -​ Preoperatively: reduce fracture and decrease spasms with skin traction -​ Surgical: hip replacement (hemi/total arthroplasty) or ORIF -​ Postoperatively: prevent dislocation -​ Avoid hip flexion >90 degrees -​ Avoid crossing legs or pointing toes inward -​ Ensure correct positioning -​ Extracapsular fracture - fracture outside joint capsule -​ Preoperatively: reduce pain and spasms with skin traction or balanced suspension -​ Surgical: ORIF with nail plate or intramedullary fixation -​ Postoperatively: -​ Institute safety precautions -​ Maintain leg and hip alignment -​ Prevent internal or external rotation -​ Turn only to unaffected side if needed -​ Elevate HOB 30 to 45 degrees
text.238: -​ Educate on walker use to avoid weight bearing -​ Keep operative leg extended, straight, elevated -> prevents hip flexion >90 degrees -​ Avoid low chairs, crossing legs, bending over -​ Use anti-embolism stockings or sequential compression devices -​ Encourage flexing and extending of feet Total Hip Arthroplasty -​ Replacement of severely damaged hip with an artificial joint -​ Indications: -​ Femoral fracture -​ Osteoarthritis -​ Rheumatoid arthritis -​ Avascular necrosis of hips -​ Interventions (postoperative): -​ Maintain femoral head in acetabular cup for approximately 4 months -​ Avoid hip full flexion, adduction and internal rotation -​ Position: -​ Supine -​ Abduction splint = wedge pillow or two pillows between legs -​ Continuous boot = prevents leg rotation and prevents pressure ulcer on heels -​ Never flex hip >90 degrees -​ Movement: turning or bedpan -​ Keep operative hip in abduction -​ Don’t turn on operative side -​ No bending forward -​ High seat (orthopedic) chairs -​ Hips higher (not lower) than knees -​ No leg crossing -​ Allowed to sit for <1 hour only -​ Activity resumptions -​ Stair climbing and driving resumes within 3-6 months -​ Sexual activity resumes at about 3 months Total Knee Arthroplasty -​ Interventions (postoperative): -​ General
text.239: -​ Compression bandage and cold packs -​ Assess neurovascular status every 2 hours -​ Infection -​ Monitor drainage and infection -​ Wound suction drain for 24-48 hours -​ Prophylactic antibiotic for 24 hours -​ Mobility -​ Ambulate by first postoperative day -​ Continuous passive motion started immediately if prescribed or active flexion of foot if awake = give analgesics -​ Avoid leg dangling, knee gatch position (flexed knee) and pillows behind knees -​ Protect with knee immobilizer and elevate legs when sitting -​ Administer tranexamic acid to reduce bleeding -​ Rehabilitation -​ Acute rehab: 1-2 weeks -​ Total recovery: approximately 6 weeks -​ Prosthesis may last 15-20 years Intervertebral Disc Herniation -​ Nucleus of disc protrudes into annulus -> nerve compression -​ Cervical disc herniation: most common at C5-C6 and C6-C7 -​ Assessment -​ Pain and paresthesia -​ Neck, top of shoulders, scapula -​ Arm, hand, pectoral muscles -​ Myelopathy - bilateral arm and leg weakness -​ Lhermitte’s sign - electric-like shock in extremities or spine with neck flexion -​ Diagnosis: cervical MRI -​ Intervention -​ Conservative management -​ Bed rest -​ Ice and heat compress -> hot, moist compress (10-20 mins) to back of neck, several times/day -​ Maintain head alignment -​ Pharmacological -​ Muscle relaxants -​ NSAIDs and corticosteroids -​ Head alignment -​ Cervical collar: limits neck movement and holds head neutral or slightly flexed -​ Wear intermittently or 24 hours/day -​ Inspect skin for irritation -​ After pain decreases -> cervical pain exercise to strengthen muscles -​ Other interventions -​ Minimize long sitting/standing (<30 mins) -​ Avoid neck twisting, flexion, extension, rotation -​ Avoid sleeping in prone; text.241: -​ Throat sprays or lozenges for sore throat; avoid anesthetic lozenges (mask swallowing difficulty) -​ Soft diet if dysphagia -​ Watch return of radicular pain -​ Lumbar -​ Assess/manage dressings and drains -​ Monitor lower extremities for neurovascular complications -​ Monitor for urinary retention, paralytic ileus, constipation -​ High fiber diet, fluids, stool softener as prescribed -​ Opioids and sedatives for pain/anxiety -​ Back brace or corset + cotton underwear to prevent skin irritation -​ Immediately lie supine post-op + pillow under neck and slightly flex knees -​ Avoid spinal flexion or twisting -​ Minimize sitting + avoid extreme hip flexion when lying on side -​ Avoid heavy work for 2-3 months Amputation -​ Surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb -​ Post-operative interventions -​ Evaluate for phantom limb sensation and pain -​ First 24 hours: elevate foot of bed (to reduce edema, not the stump -> prevents contracture) -​ After 24 to 48 hours: place in prone position (to prevent hip flexion contracture, especially in above-knee amputation -​ Types of amputation -​ Below-knee amputation (BKA) -​ Prevent knee flexion contracture -​ Encourage extension exercises and prone positioning -​ Above-knee amputation (AKA) -​ Prevent hip flexion contracture -​ Prone position several times a day -​ Emergency amputation (traumatic) -​ Obtain emergency medical assistance (call 911) and stay with the victim -​ Apply direct pressure with gauze or cloth + elevate injured part -​ If finger(s) amputated: -​ Place in waterproof sealed plastic bag -​ Then place the bag in ice water (not directly on ice -> prevents tissue damage) -​ Transport to emergency department with victim
text.242: Assistive Devices -​ Crutches -​ Principles -​ Client -​ Distance between axilla and axillary pad on crutch should be 2-3 finger widths in axilla -​ Elbow should be slightly flexed = 20-30 degrees -​ Should look up and outward when ambulating -​ Place crutches 6-10 inches diagonally in front of foot -​ Stop ambulating if with numbness or tingling in hands or arms -​ Nurse -​ Stand on affected side when ambulating with client -​ Crutch measurement -​ If standing: set crutch 5 cm (2 in) below axilla -​ If lying down: measure from axillary fold of axilla to sole + 2.5 cm (1 in) -​ If using patient’s height: subtract 40 cm (16 in), adjust hand grip to allow 20-30 degrees elbow flexion -​ Crutch gaits -​ 4-point gait: partial weight bearing both feet; provides maximal support; constant shift of weight -​ 2-point gait: partial weight bearing both feet; provides less support; faster than 4-point gait -​ 3-point gait: non-weight bearing; requires good balance and arm strength; faster gait -​ Swing-to-gait: for partial weight bearing limitations with bilateral lower extremities prostheses -​ Swing-through gait: requires adequate muscle power and balance in arms and legs -​ Crutch movement -​ Sitting and standing -​ Place unaffected leg against front of the chair -​ Move crutches at unaffected side -​ Grasp arm of chair with hand of affected side -​ Flex knee of unaffected leg to lower self into chair while placing affected leg straight out in front -​ Going up stairs “Up with the GOOD” (move unaffected leg first) -​ Going down stairs “Down with the BAD” (move affected leg first) -​ Canes -​ Principles

text.253: -​ Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) -​ Pectus deformities (excavatum/carinatum) -​ Kyphoscoliosis -​ Cardiovascular: aortic root dilation, aneurysm, dissection, mitral valve prolapse -​ Intervention -​ Cardiac: beta blockers or ARBS to reduce aortic dilation -​ Orthopedic: braces, surgery for scoliosis/pectus deformity -​ Opthalmic: corrective lens, lens surgery -​ Lifestyle: avoid high-intensity contact sports -​ Surgical: aortic root replacement if aneurysm develops Respiratology/Pulmonology Respiratology/Pulmonology - a medical specialty focused on respiratory system Respiratology nursing - focuses on the specialized care of patients with respiratory illnesses, encompassing both acute and chronic conditions Respiratory System Anatomy -​ comprised of the upper and lower airway structures, responsible for ventilation -​ Upper respiratory system - filters, moistens and warms air during inspiration -​ Nose - serves as a passageway for air to pass to and from the lungs. It filters impurities and humidifies and warms the air as it is inhaled -​ Paranasal sinuses - prominent function of the sinuses is to serve as resonating chamber in speech -​ Pharynx - throat, a tube-like structure that connects the nasal and oral cavities to the larynx -​ Larynx - voice organ, a cartilaginous epithelium lined structure that connects the pharynx and the trachea -​ Lower respiratory system - enables the exchange of gases to regulate serum PaO2, PaCO2 and pH -​ Trachea (windpipe) - serves as the passage between larynx and bronchi -​ Lungs - paired elastic structures enclosed in the thoracic cage, which is an airtight chamber with distensible walls -​ Pleural - serous membrane that lined the lungs and wall of the thorax -​ Bronchi and Bronchioles -​ Alveoli -​ Basic gas exchange unit of the respiratory system (simple diffusion)
text.254: -​ Alveolar stretch receptors respond to inspiration by sending signals to inhibit inspiratory neurons in the brain stem to prevent lung over distention -​ During expiration stretch receptors stop sending signals to inspiratory neurons and inspiratory is ready to start again -​ Oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged across the alveolar capillary membrane by process of diffusion -​ Neural control of respiration is located in the medulla. The respiratory center in the medulla is stimulated by the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood -​ Chemoreceptors, a secondary feedback system, located in the carotid arteries and aortic arch respond to hypoxemia. These chemoreceptors stimulate the medulla Gas Exchange -​ The delivery of oxygen from the lungs to the bloodstream and the elimination of carbon dioxide from the blood stream to the lungs. Occurs in the alveoli through passive diffusion -​ Types: -​ Normal ventilation - for healthy lungs -​ High ventilation-low perfusion ratio - dead space, pulmonary emboli, pulmonary infarction, cardiogenic shock -​ Low ventilation-high perfusion ratio - client with pneumonia, atelectasis, mucus plug, tumor, COPD -​ Low ventilation-low perfusion ratio - silent, pneumothorax, ARDS Arterial Blood Gas Analysis -​ Three parameters: -​ pH level: 7.35-7.45 -​ PCO2: 35-45 -​ HCO3: 22-26 -​ Steps: -​ Step 1: know the normal values -​ Step 2: look at the pH, it indicates presence of acidemia or alkalemia or normal pH -​ Step 3: look at the PCO2 - respiratory indicator (Respiratory Opposite) -​ Step 4: look at the HCO3 - metabolic indicator (Metabolic Equal) -​ Step 5: determine the compensation -​ if pH normal: fully compensated
text.255: -​ if pH abnormal, PCO2 or HCO3 abnormal: uncompensated -​ if pH abnormal, both PCO2 and HCO3 abnormal: partially compensated Metabolic Acidosis - an acid-base imbalance resulting from excessive absorption or retention of acid or excessive excretion of bicarbonate -​ Heart problem (ischemia) - production of lactic acid -​ Aspirin, metformin - lactic acid accumulation -​ Diabetes Mellitus Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis -​ Gastrointestinal - diarrhea, ileostomy, enema (excrete too much bicarbonate) -​ Rena problem/failure/damage - may not able to remove acid from the body Metabolic Alkalosis - occurs when your blood becomes overly alkaline -​ Vomiting/NGT suctioning = removes stomach acid which is rich in hydrogen ion causing increased pH level or bicarbonate in the body -​ Diuretics - increased pH level -​ Alkaline loading - water, nuts and seeds, apple, avocado and banana Respiratory Acidosis - when the lungs can’t remove enough carbon dioxide from the body, making the blood too acidic (hypoventilation) -​ Anesthesia -​ COPD - retention of carbon dioxide -​ Increased ICP - can affect the brain region which is responsible for respiration (medulla & pons) -​ Drug overdose - morphine (opioids) -> respiratory depression Respiratory Alkalosis - hyperventilation -​ Anxiety, fever, chest pain -​ Living in a high altitude -​ Pregnant mom - increased progesterone (stimulate respiratory center - increased ventilation, decreased carbon dioxide in the blood) -​ Analeptic overdose - stimulates CNS -> seizure (hyperventilation) Restrictive Disorders -​ The problem is with the parenchyma of the lungs, interstitial tissue also the inflammatory situation like fibrosis means lot of collagen deposited to lung parenchyma results in lungs stiffness and restrict expansion of lungs Pneumothorax -​ Accumulation of atmospheric air in the pleural space, which results in a rise in the intrathoracic pressure and reduced vital capacity -​ Types: -​ Spontaneous pneumothorax: entry of air in pleural space without obvious cause
text.256: -​ Open pneumothorax: air enters pleural space through an opening in the chest wall (stab/gunshot wound) -​ Tension pneumothorax: air enters pleural space with at inspiration and can’t escape leading to over distention of thoracic cavity resulting to shifting of mediastinum content to unaffected side (flail chest - paradoxical breathing pattern) -​ Predisposing factors: -​ Chest trauma -​ Inflammation lung conditions -​ tumor -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Sudden sharp chest pain -​ Unexplained dyspnea or SOB -​ Cyanosis -​ diminished or decreased breath sound of affected lung -​ Cool moist-skin - initial sign of shock -​ Mild restlessness/apprehension, anxiety -​ Resonance to hyperresonance -​ Decreased tactile fremitus -​ Diagnosis: -​ ABG -​ CXR - confirms pneumothorax/collapse of lung -​ Nursing management: -​ Assist in endotracheal intubation -​ Assist in thoracentesis -​ Administer meds: morphine sulfate due to pain, antimicrobial agents due to bacteria -​ Assist in test tube thoracotomy attached to water sealed drainage system Pleural Conditions Pleural Effusion -​ Is the collection of fluid in the pleural space -​ Causes: -​ Tumor -​ Heart failure -​ Pulmonary embolus -​ Chest injury -​ Kidney failure -​ Types: -​ Hemothorax - blood in pleural space -​ Pyothorax - pus in plural space -​ Hydrothorax - water in plural space -​ Signs and Symptoms -​ Chest pain (pleuritic pain) -​ DOB -​ Dry, unproductive cough -​ tachycardia -​ Elevated temperature (pyothorax) -​ decreased breath sounds -​ Diagnosis: CXR and CT Scan -​ Management: -​ Remain with the client, stay calm -​ High fowlers -​ O2 therapy -​ Thoracentesis -​ CXR -​ Antibiotics Hemothorax -​ Blood in pleural space as a result of penetrating or blunt chest trauma -​ Accompanies in high percentage of chest injuries -​ Can result in hidden blood loss -​ Patient may be asymptomatic, dyspneic, apprehensive or in shock -​ Management: -​ Assist with thoracentesis to aspirate blood from pleural space -​ Assist with chest tube insertion and set up drainage system for complete and continuous removal of blood or air -​ Auscultate lungs and monitor for relief of dyspnea -​ Monitor amount of blood loss in drainage -​ Replace volume with IV fluids or blood products Pleurisy (Pleuritis) -​ Inflammation of both layers of the pleurae (parietal and visceral) -​ May develop in conjunction with pneumonia or an upper respiratory tract, TB, or collagen disease -​ When the inflamed pleural membranes rub together during respiration (intensified on inspiration), the result is severe, sharp, knife-like pain -​ Clinical manifestations:
text.258: -​ Pleuritic pain during deep breath, coughing or sneezing -​ Pain is limited in distribution rather than diffuse -​ Pleural friction rub can be heard with stethoscope -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ CXR -​ Sputum analysis -​ Thoracentesis -​ Pleural biopsy -​ Management: -​ Treatment of underlying condition causing pleurisy -​ Topical applications of heat or cold -​ Indomethacin for pain relief -​ Intercostal nerve block if pain is severe -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Instruct the patient in heat/cold application for pain relief -​ Instrcut the patient to turn onto the affected side to splint the chest wall and reduce the stretching of the pleurae -​ Teach the patient to use hands or pillow to splint the ribcage while coughing Empyema Thoracis -​ Accumulation of purulent fluid in the pleural space -​ Occur as complication of bacterial pneumonia, lung abscess or chest trauma -​ Patient is acutely ill and has signs and symptoms similar to acute respiratory infection -​ Diagnostic test: chest CT -​ Main objective: to drain the fluid in the pleural cavity -​ Thoracentesis is done if the fluid is not too thick -​ Tube thoracostomy is done to patients with loculated or complicated pleural effusions -​ Open chest drainage via thoracotomy is done to remove thickened pleura, pus and debris -​ Nursing intervention: provide specific to the method of drainage of pleural fluid Upper Respiratory System Disorders Rhinitis -​ A group of disorders characterized by inflammation and irritation of the mucous membranes of the nose -​ Allergic rhinitis -​ Further classified as seasonal rhinitis (occurs during pollen seasons) or perennial rhinitis (occurs throughout the year) -​ Commonly associated with exposure to airborne particles such as dust, dander or plant pollens in people who are allergic to these substances -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Rhinorrhea (excessive drainage or runny nose) -​ Nasal congestion -​ Sneezing -​ pruritus of the nose, roof of the mouth, throat, eyes and ears -​ Management: -​ Antihistamines -​ corticosteroids nasal sprays -​ Desensitizing immunizations -​ Nursing Intervention: -​ Instruct the patient with allergic rhinitis to avoid or reduce exposure to allergens and irritants -​ instruct the patient in correct administration of nasal medications -​ To achieve maximal relief, the patient is instructed to blow the nose before applying any medication into the nasal cavity -​ Viral rhinitis (Common cold) -​ Most frequent viral infection in the general population caused by coronavirus -​ Highly contagious because the virus is shed for 2 days before the symptoms appear and during the first part of symptomatic phase -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Low grade fever -​ Nasal congestion -​ Rhinorrhea and nasal discharge -​ Halitosis, sneezing -​ Tearing watery eyes -​ Scratchy or sore throat -​ general malaise, chills -​ Headache and muscle aches -​ Management: -​ symptomatic therapy -​ adequate fluid intake and rest -​ Prevention of chilling -​ warm salt-water gargles to soothe the sore throat -​ NSAIDS to relieve aches and pains -​ antihistamines are used to relieve sneezing, rhinorrhea and nasal congestion -​ Inhalation of steam or heated, humidified air Acute Pharyngitis -​ a sudden painful inflammation of the pharynx, the back portion of the throat that includes the posterior third of the tongue, soft palate, and tonsils -​ Commonly referred as sore throat -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ fiery-red pharyngeal membrane and tonsils -​ Swollen lymphoid follicles -​ Enlarged and tender cervical lymph nodes -​ Fever -​ Malaise -​ sore throat -​ Pharmacologic therapy -​ Penicillin (DOC) -​ Celasphorin -​ Macrolides -​ Gargles with benzocaine may relieve symptoms -​ Nursing interventions -​ Liquid or soft diet is provided during the acute stage -​ Cool beverage , warm liquids and flavored frozen dessert such as popsicles are often soothing -​ Warm saline gargles or throat irrigations -​ Increase oral fluid intake -​ Ice collar can relieve severe sore throats -​ CBR during febrile stage -​ Instruct the patient about preventive measures Chronic Pharngitis -​ chronic pharyngitis is a persistent inflammation of the pharynx. It is common in adults who work in dusty surroundings, use their voice to excess, suffer from chronic cough, or habitually use alcohol and tobacco -​ Three types: -​ Hypertrophic - characterized by general thickening and congestion of the pharyngeal mucous membrane -​ Atrophic - late stage of the first type (the membrane is thin, whitish, glistening and at times winkled) -​ Chronic granular - “clergyman’s sore throat”, characterized by numerous swollen lymph follicles on the pharyngeal wall -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ constant sense of irritation or fullness in the throat -​ Mucus that collects in the throat -​ Difficulty swallowing -​ Pharmacological management: -​ Nasal sprays or medications containing ephedrine sulfate or phenylephrine hydrochloride -​ Antihistamine decongestant medications -​ Acetaminophen -​ Nursing management: -​ instruct patient to avoid contact with others until the fever subsides to prevent the spread of infection -​ Avoidance of alcohol, tobacco, secondhand smoke, and exposure to cold or to environment or occupational pollutants Tonsillitis and Adenoiditis -​ The tonsils are composed of lymphatic tissue and are situated on each side of the oropharynx -​ The adenoids or pharyngeal tonsils consist of lymphatic tissue near the center of the posterior wall of nasopharynx -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Sore throat, fever, snoring and difficulty swallowing -​ Enlarged adenoids may cause mouth-breathing, earache, draining ears, frequent head colds, bronchitis, foul-smelling breath, voice impairment and noisy respiration -​ Management: -​ Penicillin (first line) or cephalosporins -​ Tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy is indicated if the patient has had repeated episodes of tonsillitis despite antibiotic therapy -​ Nursing Intervention (post-op): -​ In the immediate post-operative period, the most comfortable position is prone, with head turned to the side to allow drainage from the mouth and pharynx -​ apply ice collar to the neck -​ assess for post op bleeding much as frequent swallowing -​ Ice chips may be given to the patient -​ Alkaline mouthwashes and warm saline solutions are useful in coping with the thick mucus and halitosis that may be present after surgery -​ Milk and milk products (ice cream and yogurt) may be restricted -​ provide soft, adequate diet -​ instruct the patient to avoid vigorous tooth brushing or gargling -​ Encourage the use of cool-mist vaporizer or humidifier in the home -​ Instruct patient to avoid smoking and heavy lifting or exertion for 10 days Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy) -​ Most common major suppurative complication of sore throat/tonsillitis. This collection of purulent exudate between the tonsillar capsule and the surrounding tissues including the soft palate, may develop after an acute tonsillar infection that progress to local cellulitis and abscess -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Severe sore throat, fever, trismus (inability to open the mouth), and drooling -​ Severe pain, raspy voice -​ Odynophagia (a severe sensation of burning, squeezing pain while swallowing) -​ Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) -​ Otalgia(pain in the air), tender and enlarged cervical lymph nodes -​ Airway obstruction may occur -​ Management: -​ Antimicrobial agents (penicillin) -​ corticosteroid therapy -​ needle aspirations are performed to decompress the abscess -​ Nursing interventions: -​ Assist in performing intubation, cricothyroidotomy or tracheotomy to treat airway obstruction -​ Assist in needle aspiration when indicated -​ Gentle gargling after the procedure with cool normal saline gargle may relieve discomfort -​ Provide cool liquids -​ Instruct patient to refrain from or cease smoking -​ it is also important to reinforce the need for good oral hygiene Laryngitis -​ An inflammation of the larynx, often occurs as a result of voice abuse or exposure to dust, chemicals, smoke, and other pollutants -​ Most common cause are viruses, bacterial invasion may be secondary -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Horseness of voice (initial sign) -​ Aphonia (complete loss of voice) -​ Severe cough -​ Throat feels worse in the morning and improves when the patient is in a warmer climate -​ Management: -​ Instruct the patient to rest the voice and avoid irritants (including smoking) -​ Inhaling cool steam or an aerosol is provided -​ Administer antibacterial therapy as ordered -​ Topical corticosteroids may be given by inhalation -​ Increased OFI Laryngeal Cancer -​ Etiology: -​ Most tumors of the larynx are squamous cell carcinoma -​ Men > women, age 60 - 70 -​ Cigarette smoking and alcohol consumption are associated with laryngeal cancer -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Hoarness of voice for more than 2 weeks -​ Persistent cough and sore throat -​ Dyspnea -​ Dysphagia -​ Pain radiating to ear and burning sensation in the throat -​ Weight loss -​ Enlarged cervical lymph nodes -​ Unilateral nasal obstruction -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ Virtual endoscopy -​ Optical imaging -​ CT Scan -​ MRI -​ Direct laryngoscopic examination -​ Management: -​ Radiation therapy -​ Chemotherapy -​ Surgery -​ Partial laryngectomy: a portion of the larynx is removed, aling with one vocal cord and the tumor -​ Complication: change in voice quality or hoarness of voice -​ Total laryngectomy: laryngeal structures are removed, including the hyoid bone, epiglottis, cricoid cartilage and two or three rings of the trachea -​ Complication: permanent loss of voice, salivary leak, wound infection, stomal stenosis, and dysphagia -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Arrange for clients with laryngectomies to meet with members of support groups -​ Establish a method for communication before surgery -​ Maintain airway, have suction equipment at bedside -​ Observe for signs of hemorrhage or infection -​ Teach about tracheostomy and stoma care
text.264: -​ Assist in period of grieving Lower Respiratory System Disorders Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) Three pathological processes: -​ Loss of alveoli attachment -​ Inflammatory obstruction of the airway -​ Excessive mucus production Obstructive Lungs Disorder -​ Chronic bronchitis - excessive mucus production and inflammatory obstruction of the airway -​ Emphysema - loss of alveoli attachment Etiogy: -​ Chronic cigarette smoking -​ Lalaki (male) -​ Exposure to irritants -​ Age (old) -​ Respiratory infection Emphysema -​ Destruction of alveoli, narrowing of airway, the alveoli lose their elasticity and cannot inflate and deflate as they used to. This then has an effect on the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Protease (inflammatory response) -> destruction of alveoli, elastic fiber, collagen -> loss of elastic recoil, deficiency in alpha 1 anti trypsin -> air trapping -> impaired gas exchange -> hypoxia/CO2 retention -> hyperinflation of lungs -> barrel chest -​ Risk factor: -​ Chronic cigarette smoking -​ working/living in highly polluted area -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Pink puffer (pathognomonic sign) -​ Barrel chest -​ Polycythemia (increased in RBC production) -​ Weight loss -​ Clubbing of fingers (chronic hypoxia) -​ Purse lip breathing (to exhale the retained or excess carbon dioxide) -​ Hypercapnia (excessive carbon dioxide) -​ Laboratory: -​ ABG (respiratory acidosis) -​ CXR -​ Pulse oximeter -​ spirometry -​ Nursing intervention: -​ O2, however low flow with the rate of 1-2LPM (hypoxic drive) via venturi mask/nasal cannula -​ Position: sitting/upright/orthopneic (to expand the lungs) -​ Increase fluid intake (liquify mucus secretions) -​ Diet: high CHO, CHON, vitamin C Chronic Bronchitis -​ Criteria: -​ Productive cough for 3 months for 2 consecutive years -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Increase function of goblet cells -> increased mucus production -> increase air volume -> hyperinflation of the lungs -> decrease oxygen level/CO2 retention -> respiratory acidosis -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Productive cough -​ Cyanosis -​ Crackles -​ Wheezing -​ Hypercapnia -​ Cor pulmonale -> right ventricular hypertrophy -​ Weight gain -​ Blue bloaters (pathognomonic sign) -​ Laboratory: -​ CXR -​ ABG -​ Pulse oximeter -​ Nursing Intervention: -​ O2 low flow 1-2LPM via venturi mask -​ Increase fluid intake -​ CPT (check for contraindication first) -​ Increased humidification Bronchial Asthma -​ Chronic inflammatory disease of the respiratory system -​ Inflammation of the airways -​ bronchospasm -​ Increased mucus secretion -​ Narrowing of airway -> impaired gas exchange -> hypoxia/CO2 retention (Respiratory Acidosis) -​ Risk factor: -​ Allergies -​ Smoking/Stress/Sports -​ Temperature -​ Hazardous materials -​ Microorganism -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Wheezing (upon expiration, prolonged exhalation) -​ Dyspnea -​ Tachypnea -​ Tachycardia -​ Cough -​ Hyperresonance -​ Restless -​ Laboratory: -​ ABG -​ CXR -​ Spirometry -​ Intervention: -​ Avoid exercise, emotional factor, environmental factors -​ Alert: -​ Can’t talk (obstructed) -​ Cyanosis (impaired gas exchange) -​ Inhaler won’t work (fully obstructed) -​ (-) breath sounds Treatment for COPD and Bronchial Asthma -​ Bronchodilators -​ selective beta 2 agonist (beta 2 - stimulates bronchodilation) -​ albuterol (Proventil) -​ salbutamol (Ventolin) -​ Non-selective beta agonist (beta 1 - stimulates increased HR) -​ Isoprotenarol (Isopril) -​ Terbutaline (Bricanyl) -​ Xanthine derivatives (with compounds of caffeine) -​ Aminophylline, theophylline -​ Side effect: palpitations -​ Anti-inflammatory -​ Corticosteroids -​ Hydrocortisone (Solu-cortef), Prednisone -​ Anti-histamine -​ Benadryl -​ Side effect: drowsiness -​ Avoid driving or machinery -​ Leukotriene (inflammatory mediator) inhibitor -​ Monteleukast -​ Expectorant -​ Gualafenesin, mucolytics -​ Antitussive given at night Bronchiectasis -​ Abnormal permanent dilation of bronchus leading to destruction of muscular and elastic tissues of alveoli -​ Predisposing factors: -​ Recurrent lower respiratory tract infections -​ Chest trauma -​ Congenital defects -​ Related to presence of tumor -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ productive cough -​ Dyspnea -​ cyanosis -​ anorexia and generalized body malaise -​ Hemoptysis -​ Diagnostic: -​ ABG -​ Bronchoscopy - direct visualization of bronchus using fiberscope -​ Pre: -​ Secure inform consent and explain procedure to client -​ Maintain NPO 6-8 hours prior to procedure -​ Monitor VS and breath sounds -​ Post: -​ Feeding initiated upon return of gag reflex -​ Avoid talking, coughing and smoking may cause irritation -​ Monitor signs of laryngeal spasm - prepare tracheostomy set -​ Treatment:
text.268: -​ Surgery (pneumonectomy, 1 lung removed and position on affected side) -​ Segmental wedge lobectomy (promote re expansion of lungs) - unaffected lobectomy facilitate drainage Occupational Lung Diseases -​ Asbestosis: diffuse interstitial fibrosis of the lung caused by inhalation of asbestos dust and particles -​ Found in workers involved in manufacture, cutting and demolition of asbestos-containing materials -​ Silicosis: chronic pulmonary fibrosis caused by inhalation of silica dust -​ Exposure to silica dust is encountered in almost any form of mining because the earth’s crust is composed of silica and silicates (gold, coal, tin, copper mining); also stone cutting, quarrying, manufacture of abrasives, ceramics, pottery, and foundry work -​ Sarcoidosis: granulomatous disease in which clumps of inflammatory epithelial cells occur in many organs, primarily in the lungs -​ Lymph node enlargement seen on chest x-ray -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Chronic cough; productive in silicosis -​ Dyspnea on exertion; progressive and irreversible in asbestosis -​ Susceptibility to lower respiratory tract infections -​ Bibasal crackles in asbestosis -​ Management: -​ There is no specific management; exposure is eliminated and the patient is treat symptomatically -​ Give prophylactic isoniazid (INH) to patient with positive tuberculin test because silicosis is associated with high risk of TB -​ Persuade people who have been exposed to asbestos fiber to stop smoking to decrease risk of lung cancer -​ Keep asbestos worker under cancer surveillance; watch for changing cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, melena -​ Bronchodilators may be some benefit if any degree of airway obstruction is present -​ Nursing interventions: -​ Administer oxygen therapy as required -​ Administer or teach self-administration of bronchodilators as ordered -​ Encourage smoking cessation -​ Advise patient on pacing activities to prevent fatigue -​ Provide information to healthy workers on prevention of occupational lung disease
text.269: Lower Respiratory Tract Infectious Diseases Pneumonia -​ Inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by various microorganisms, including bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi and viruses -​ Types: -​ Community -acquired pneumonia: occurs either in the community setting or within the first 48 hours after hospitalization or institutionalization -​ Hospital-acquired pneumonia: also known as nosocomial pneumonia, is defined as the onset of pneumonia symptoms more than 48 hours after admission in patients with no evidence of infection at the time of admission -​ Aspiration pneumonia: refers to the entry pulmonary consequences resulting from entry of endogenous or exogenous substances into the lower airway -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Sudden onset, rapidly rising fever 38.3-40.5C -​ Cough productive of purulent sputum -​ Pleuritic chest pain aggravated by deep respiration/coughing -​ Dyspnea, tachypnea accompanied by respiratory grunting, nasal flaring use of accessory muscles of respiration, fatigue -​ Rapid, bounding pulse -​ Orthopnea -​ Rusty, blood-tinged sputum -​ Poor appetite, diaphoresis -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ CXR: shows presence/extent of pulmonary disease typically consolidation -​ Gram stain and culture and sensitivity test may indicate offending organism -​ Blood culture detects bacterecemia (bloodstream invasion) occurring with bacterial pneumonia -​ Management: -​ Administration of the appropriate antibiotic as determined by the results of gram stain -​ S. pneumonia - macrolide antibiotic (azithromycin, clarithromycin or erythromycin) -​ Pseudomonas infection - anti pneumococcal, anti pseudomonal beta-lactam -​ Treatment of viral pneumonia is primarily supportive -​ Oxygen therapy if patient has inadequate gas exchange -​ Complications: -​ Shock and respiratory failure -​ Pleural effusion -​ Nursing interventions: -​ Encourage coughing and deep breathing after chest physiotherapy, splinting the chest if necessary -​ Maintain semi-fowlers position -​ Promote hydration (2-3L/day) to liquify secretions -​ Teach effective coughing techniques to minimize energy expenditures; plan rest periods -​ Suction if necessary -​ Instruct client to cover nose and mouth when coughing -​ Teach the need to continue entire course of antimicrobial therapy which is usually seven to ten days -​ Teach the patient about proper administration of antibiotics and potential side effects -​ Teach that findings are expected to be less within 48-72 hours of initial therapy -​ Nutritionally enriched drinks or shakes maybe helpful in maintaining nutrition Pulmonary Tuberculosis -​ Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease that primarily affects the lung parenchyma -​ It is also transmitted to other parts of the body, including meninges, kidneys, bones and lymph nodes -​ The primary infectious agent, M. tuberculosis is an acid fast aerobic rod that grows slowly and sensitive to heat and ultraviolet light spreads from person to person by airborne transmission -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, low grade fever, night sweats -​ Some patients have acute febrile illness, chills and flu-like symptoms -​ Cough (insidious onset) progressing in frequency and producing mucoid or mucopurulent sputum -​ Hemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnea (indicates extensive involvement) -​ Diagnostic test: -​ Sputum smear/sputum culture confirms a diagnosis of TB -​ CXR to determine presence and extent of disease -​ Tuberculin skin test (purified protein derivative PDD or Mantoux test) -​ Classification: -​ Data from the history, physical examination, TB test, CXR, and microbiologic studies are used to classify TB into one of five classes -​ A classification scheme provides public health officials with a systematic way to monitor epidemiology and treatment of the disease -​ Class 0: no exposure; no infection -​ Class 1: exposure; no evidence of infection -​ Class 2: latent infection; no disease -​ Class 3: disease; clinically active -​ Class 4: disease; not clinically active -​ Class 5: suspected disease; diagnosis pending -​ Management: -​ Pulmonary TB is treated primarily with antituberculosis agents for 6-12 months -​ The initial phase consists of a multiple medication regime of INH, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol and is administered daily for 8 weeks -​ Continuation phase of treatment include INH and rifampicin and lasts for additional 4-7 months -​ Vitamin B (pyridoxine) is usually administered with INH to prevent INH-associated peripheral neuropathy Commonly Used Agents Adult Daily Dosage Most common Side Effects Isoniazid (INH) 5 mg/kg (300 mg maximum daily Peripheral neuritis, hepatic enzyme elevation, hepatitis, hypersensitivity Rifampicin 10 mg/kg (600 mg maximum daily) Hepatitis, febrile reaction, purpura (rare), nausea and vomiting Pyrazinamide 15-30 mg/kg (2.0 g maximum daily) Hyperuricemia, hepatotoxicity, skin rash, arthralgias, GI distress Ethambutol 15-25 mg/kg (no maximum daily dose but based on lean body) Optic neuritis (may lead to blindness;very rare at 15 mg/kg), skin rash -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Instructs the patient to increase fluid intake and about correct positioning to facilitate airway drainage -​ Discuss the medications schedule and side effects of the drugs -​ Instructs the patient to take the medication either on an empty stomach or at least 1 hour before meals because food interferes with medication absorption -​ Patients taking INH should avoid food that contain tyramine and histamine because it may result in headache, flushing, hypotension, lightheadedness, palpitations, and diaphoresis -​ Monitors for side effects of anti-TB drugs -​ Encourage rest and avoidance of exertion -​ Provide nutritional plan that allows for small frequent meals -​ Instruct the patient about important hygiene measures including mouth care, covering the mouth and nose when coughing and sneezing, proper disposal of tissues and hand washing Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) -​ An acute condition characterized by bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and severe hypoxemia in the absence of evidence for cardiogenic pulmonary edema -​ Causes: -​ Viral -​ Trauma -​ Burns -​ Aspiration pneumonia -​ Overdose -​ Near drowning -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Viral infection -> initiation of immune inflammatory response -​ -> release of a-vasoactive substance -> increased capillary permeability -​ -> pulmonary edema -> hypoxia -​ -> atelectasis -> decreased ventilation -​ -> b-proteolytic enzymes -> decreased perfusion -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Tachypnea (earliest sign) -​ Crackles. Dyspnea, intercostal retractor -​ Cyanosis -​ Decreased breath sounds -​ hypoxia -​ Nursing management: -​ Identify and treat the cause of the ARDS -​ Administer oxygen as prescribed (8-10 LPM) -​ Position: High fowlers/orthopneic -​ Restrict fluid intake as prescribed (due to pulmonary edema) -​ Provide respiratory treatment as prescribed -​ Administer diuretics, anticoagulants or corticosteroids as prescribed -​ Prepare the client for intubation and mechanical ventilation using PEEP (to open up the collapsed alveoli) Diagnostic Tests ABG -​ Purpose: to detect the presence of acid-base imbalance and to assess ventilation (respiratory therapist) -​ Nursing responsibilities: -​ Heparinized syringe 10 ml -​ Allen’s test (Normal: 5-15 seconds) - to check the adequacy of collateral circulation -​ Artery “radial” - oxygenated blood -​ Pressure (5-10 minutes to prevent bleeding) -​ Ice - to prevent hemolysis (breakdown of red blood cells) -​ Educate/elevate the site of extraction to prevent bleeding -​ ML: 5-10 ml of blood -​ Avoid: suctioning before ABG (it suctions also the oxygen) Pulse Oximeter -​ Purpose: to determine oxygen saturation in the blood -​ Normal: 95-100% -​ Nursing key points: -​ Avoid exposure to sunlight -​ Blanch test - press the index finger (<2 secs) -​ Color removal of nails -​ Do not place the same arm with the BP monitoring -​ Edematous hand (-) Thoracentesis -​ Purpose: aspiration of fluid or air from the pleural space -​ Indication: pneumothorax & pleural effusion -​ Uses: diagnostic (10-20 ml) & therapeutic (to alleviate the symptoms) - 1000 ml/1L (standard) -​ Preprocedure: -​ Topical anesthesia (local) -​ Orthopneic position (sitting upward leaning forward) - 2-3 ICS midclavicular/4-5 ICS anterior axillary -​ Record initial vital signs (baseline: HR, RR, BP) -> hypovolemic shock (complication) -​ Avoid coughing/remain still (may lead to internal bleeding) -​ Consent (invasive procedure) -​ Post-procedure: -​ Position: unaffected side (to expand the lungs, prevent leakage of fluid at thoracic cavity) -​ Apply pressure (5-10 minutes to prevent bleeding) -​ Check for expectoration of blood - lung trauma (notify physician) -​ Monitor vital signs (BP/HR/RR) hypotachytachy = hypovolemic shock -​ Monitor complications: shock, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, air embolism Bronchoscopy -​ Purpose: direct inspection and observation of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi -​ Uses: Diagnostic (collect secretion - CS) & therapeutic (to alleviate the symptoms of client) -​ Preprocedure: -​ Consent (secure) -​ NPO (6-8 hours) to prevent aspiration and vomiting -​ Medication: -​ Atropine sulfate - reduce salivation -​ Anesthesia (local) - to reduce discomfort -​ Remove dentures (to prevent aspiration) -​ Post-procedure: -​ Position: side lying - for drainage -​ Check for return of gag reflex (tongue depressor) -​ if (+) gag reflex, they can eat -​ WOF: sign of bronchial perforation -​ Hemoptysis -​ Cyanosis -​ DOB/dyspnea -​ Tachycardia -​ Arrhythmias -​ Hypotension Sputum Collection -​ Purpose: to assess for gross appearance of the sputum -​ Color: -​ Rusty - pneumococcal or bacterial -​ Green - pseudomonas -​ Blood-tinged sputum - pulmonary tuberculosis -​ Confirmatory test for PTB: acid-fast bacillus staining -​ Culture and sensitivity -​ Cytologic study - to detect abdominal lung cell -​ Key points: -​ Best time: early morning (concentrated) -​ Rinse mouth with plain water only -​ Use sterile container -​ Assist client in expectorating sputum (chest physiotherapy, nebulization) -​ Secretion first before administering antibiotic -​ 15 ml pure sputum (no saliva) Tracheobronchial Suctioning -​ Purpose: to remove excess mucus secretion to maintain patent airway -​ To collect specimen for diagnostic studies -​ Indication: based on clinical findings -​ Nursing responsibilities: -​ Sterile technique - gloves -​ Hyperventilate: 100% oxygenation before and after the procedure -​ Insert catheter: 3-5 inches in length -​ Apply suction while withdrawal of catheter in circular motion with a duration of 5-10 secs but not more 15 seconds (can lead to hypoxia if prolonged) -​ Complications of over suctioning: -​ Hypoxia -​ Bleeding -​ Bradycardia (stimulated vagus nerve) -​ Hypotension -​ Interval: 2-3 minutes Chest Physiotherapy -​ Purpose: to help clear excessive bronchial secretions for airways -​ Three method: -​ Percussion: produce mechanical waves of energy that is transmitted through chest wall (with cupped hands) - upper lobe first before lower lobe to loosen secretions -​ Vibration: hand is paced on the client’s chest while rapid and vigorous vibration -​ Postural drainage: use of gravity to assist in the movement of secretion -​ Contraindication: -​ Lung trauma -​ Ribs and spinal cord injury -​ Pulmonary tuberculosis -​ Increased ICP -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Secure consent -​ Check area of accumulation of mucus -​ Place client in each position for 10-15 minutes -​ Change position gradually (postural hypotension) -​ procedure best done in the morning or before meals -​ Provide good oral hygiene Close Chest Tube -​ Purpose: to restore the negative pressure and re expand the lungs -​ Three types of closed chest tube: -​ One-bottle system -​ Serves as drainage bottle and water seal bottle -​ Immerse tip of the tube 3-5 cm of sterile NSS to create water seal -​ Note: observe for fluctuations of fluid along the tube, intermittent bubbling of the fluid -​ Continuous bubbling - indicate presence of air leak (apply tape) -​ Two-bottle system -​ Not connected to the suction apparatus -​ 1st bottle is drainage -​ 2nd bottle is water seal bottle (intermittent bubbling) -​ Connected to suction apparatus -​ 1st bottle is drainage and water seal bottle -​ 2nd bottle is suction control bottle (continuous bubbling) -​ Three bottle system -​ 1st bottle is drainage bottle -​ 2nd bottle is water seal bottle -​ 3rd bottle is suction-control bottle -​ 2-3 feet below the level of the chest -​ Absence of fluctuation in water seal -​ Obstruction or kink -​ Re-expansion (CXR) -​ Dislodgement: apply occlusive dressing at site, 3 side taped technique (to prevent tension pneumothorax) -​ Disconnected: submerge the tube to the water -​ Avoid clamping -​ Chest tube removal: physician -​ Criteria: -​ Negative fluctuation -​ Positive breath sounds -​ Positive XR (lung re-expansion) -​ Instruct: exhale deeply, hold and do valsalva maneuver -​ Position: semi-fowlers -​ Monitor RR, WOF: respiratory distress - tachypnea (1st hour after removal) - Notify MD
text.277: Hematology Hematology - a branch of medicine focused on the study of blood-forming organs and blood-related disorders Hematology nursing - specializing in caring for patients with blood disorders Hematologic System -​ The hematologic system consist of the blood and the and the sites where blood is produced, including the bone marrow and the reticuloendothelial system (RES) -​ Blood is a specialized organ that differs from the other organs in that it exists in a fluid state. Blood is composed of plasma and various types of cells -​ Plasma is the fluid portion of blood; it contains various proteins such as albumin, globulin, fibrinogen and other factors necessary for clotting as well as electrolytes, waste products, and nutrients. About 55% of blood volume is plasma -​ Serum is plasma minus the clotting factors Blood Cells Myeloid lineage: involved in innate immunity -​ Neutrophils -​ Macrophages -​ Monocytes -​ Eosinophil and Basophil -​ Platelets -​ RBCs Lymphoid lineage: involved in adaptive immunity -​ B lymphocytes -​ T lymphocytes -​ Natural Killer cells Cell Type Major Function WBC (Leukocyte) Normal: 4500-11000/mm3 Granulocytes Neutrophil Eosinophil Fights infection Essential in preventing or limiting bacterial infection via phagocytosis Involved in allergic reactions (neutralize histamine), digest foreign proteins
text.278: Agranulocytes Monocyte T lymphocyte Plasma cell Enters tissue as macrophage; highly phagocytic, especially against fungus, immune surveillance Responsible for cell-mediated immunity Secretes immunoglobulin (Ig/antibody) Most mature form of B lymphocytes RBC (Erythrocyte) Hemoglobin Male: 13-18 g/dl Female: 12-16 g/dl Hematocrit Male: 42-52% Female: 35-47% Carries hemoglobin to provide oxygen to tissues; average lifespan is 120 days Platelet (Thrombocyte) Normal: 150000-450000/mm3 Fragment of megakaryocyte; provides basis for coagulation to occur; maintains hemostasis; average lifespan is 10 days Hematologic Disorders Anemia -​ Decreased availability of oxygen to tissues -​ Causes: -​ Inadequate intake of vitamins and food rich in iron and RBC production -​ Decreased RBC production by the bone marrow (aplastic anemia) -​ Increased destruction of RBC due to severe infection (hemolytic anemia) -​ Acute, chronic blood loss -​ Diagnosis: -​ Low mean corpuscular volume (MCV): the size of RBC (Normal: 80-100 fL) macrocytic/microcytic -​ Low Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC): average amount of hemoglobin in every single red blood cell (Normal: 32-36 g/dL) hypochromic/hyperchromic Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) -​ Results when the intake of dietary iron is inadequate for hemoglobin synthesis -​ Causes: -​ chronic blood loss due to trauma, menorrhagia, GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena, hematochezia) -​ Inadequate Fe+2 in the diet -​ Impaired Fe+2 absorption due to: -​ Chronic diarrhea -​ Malabsorption syndrome -​ Gastrectomy -​ celiac disease -​ Clinical manifestation: -​ Fatigue/easy fatigability (Hallmark sign) -​ Brittle hair, spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) due to atrophy of epidermal cells -​ Palpitations, cold sensitivity -​ Pallor -​ Smooth, sore tongue -​ Plummer Vinson’s syndrome - atrophic glossitis, stomatitis, dysphagia due to atrophy of papilla of the tongue, mouth and pharyngeal cells -​ Pica - due to neuronal degeneration that affects cognitive function -​ Angular cheilosis - ulceration of the corner of the mouth -​ Cerebral hypoxia - dizziness, dyspnea -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ RBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit, reticulocyte count, serum iron, ferritin -​ Management: -​ Correction of chronic blood loss -​ Oral or parenteral iron therapy -​ Nursing -​ Monitor all signs of bleeding -​ CBR -​ Increase intake of iron rich foods: -​ green, leafy vegetables -​ Organ liver meat -​ Egg yolk -​ Legumes -​ california raisins -​ red meats -​ Molasses -​ Administer iron preparation as ordered -​ FeSO4, Fe+2 Gluconate, Fe+2 fumarate -​ Taken with vitamin C to increase absorption -​ Instruct patient to avoid taking antacids and dairy products (it decreases iron absorption) -​ Best absorbed on an empty stomach, in between meals to prevent GI upset -​ Monitor side effects: nausea and vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhea/constipation, black stools Megaloblastic: Pernicious Anemia -​ Most dangerous of all chronic anemia due to deficiency of intrinsic factor leading to vitamin B12 malabsorption -​ Predisposing factors: -​ Unknown cause -​ Subtotal gastrectomy -​ Hereditary -​ Inflammation disorders of the ileum -​ Crohn’s diseases -​ Absence of intrinsic factor -​ Strict vegetarian diet -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Headache, dizziness, dyspnea, palpitations, cold sensitivity, general body malaise, extreme pallor -​ Sore mouth, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, loss of weight, indigestion, epigastric discomfort, recurring diarrhea or constipation -​ Red beefy tongue/glossitis - pathognomonic sign -​ Paresthesia in the extremities, difficulty maintaining their balance, lose position sense (proprioception) (+) Romberg’s test -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ CBC (decreased hemoglobin and hematocrit) -​ blood smear (large and oval shaped - macroovalocytes) -​ Schilling’s test for absorption of vitamin B12 - patient receives small amount of radioactive B12 orally and 24 hour urine collection is obtained (definitive/confirmatory) -​ Positive: Vitamin B12 is absent in urine -​ Negative: Vitamin B12 is present in urine -​ Nursing management: -​ Enforce CBR and ensure safety -​ Administer vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) injections at monthly intervals for lifetime as ordered (IM) -​ Diet: -​ SFF, bland soft food -​ Increase CHO, CHON, iron (0.3 mg/day) & vitamin C, folic acid 1 mg/day -​ Avoid irritating mouthwashes, use of soft bristled toothbrush is encouraged -​ Avoid excessive heat and cold temperature -​ Blood transfusion PRN -​ Physical examinations every 6 months (hematologic studies & GI evaluation) -​ Administer parenteral iron preparations as ordered -​ Administer using Z-track method to prevent discoloration and leakage to tissues -​ Do not massage the injection site, encourage ambulation instead -​ Monitor side effects: -​ Pain at injection site -​ Localized abscess -​ Lymphadenopathy -​ Fever and chills -​ Skin rashes -​ Watch out for anaphylaxis due to parenteral iron supplement Megaloblastic: Folic Acid Deficiency -​ Occurs if there is folic acid deficiency within 4 months -​ Risk factors: -​ People who rarely eat uncooked vegetables -​ Alcoholism -​ Chronic hemolytic anemia -​ Pregnancy -​ Malabsorptive diseases of the small bowel such as sprue -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Fatigue, weakness -​ Pallor, dizziness, headache -​ Tachycardia -​ sore tongue, cracked lips -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ CBC will show decreased RBC, hemoglobin, and hematocrit with increased mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration -​ Management: -​ Administer 1mg folic acid daily -​ Folic acid IM for patients with malabsorption problems -​ SFF, bland soft food if sore mouth and tongue is present -​ Diet: food rich in folic acid such as beef liver, peanut butter, red beans, oatmeal, broccoli, asparagus Aplastic Anemia -​ A rare disease caused by a decrease in or damage to marrow stem cells, damage to the microenvironment within the marrow, and replacement of the marrow with fat resulting in pancytopenia (low RBCs, WBCs and platelets) -​ Hypoplasia of bone marrow -​ Predisposing factors: -​ Congenital -​ Viral infection -​ Chemicals (benzene & its derivatives, pesticides) -​ Radiation -​ immunologic injury -​ Drug causing bone marrow depression -​ Broad spectrum antibiotics: -​ Chloramphenicol -​ Sulfonamides (Bactrim) -​ Chemo therapeutic drugs: -​ Methotrexate -​ nitrogen mustard -​ Vincristine -​ Attack of T cells against bone marrow -​ Infections and pregnancy -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Decreased RBC: pallor, weakness, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, palpitations, fatigue -​ Decreased WBC: Infections associated with leukopenia: fever, headache, malaise, abdominal pain, diarrhea, erythema, pain, exudates at wounds or sites of invasive procedures, lymphadenopathies, and splenomegaly -​ Decreased Platelets: Thrombocytopenia - bleeding from gums, nose, GI or GU tracts, purpura, petechiae, ecchymosis, retinal hemorrhages, oozing of blood from venipuncture sites -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ Bone marrow aspiration shows an extremely hypoplastic or even aplastic (very few to no cells) marrow replaced with fat -​ CBC and peripheral blood smear shows decreased RBC, WBC and platelets (pancytopenia) -​ Therapeutic Management: -​ Removal of causative agent or toxin -​ Bone Marrow Transplantation (BMT) or Peripheral Blood Stem Cell Transplant (PBSCT) -​ Immunosuppressive therapy -​ Corticosteroids -​ Sandimmune (cyclosporine) -​ Cytoxan -​ Imuran -​ Supportive treatment includes platelet and RBC transfusions, antibiotics and antifungal administration -​ Blood transfusion (depends on what blood cell is low) -​ Nursing Management: -​ Low RBC -​ O2 administration -​ Rest -​ Low WBC -​ Practice hand hygiene -​ Avoid raw food -​ Administration of immunosuppressants as ordered -​ Teach patient how to minimize risk for infection -​ Reverse isolation due to leukopenia -​ Monitor for signs of infection -​ Limit visitors -​ Avoid crowded places -​ Low Platelets -​ Minimize risk of bleeding -​ Avoid SQ, IM. Use only soft toothbrush and electric razor -​ Avoid invasive procedures, contact sports Sickle Cell Anemia -​ Is a severe hemolytic anemia that results from inheritance of the sickle hemoglobin gene. This gene causes the hemoglobin molecule to be defective. The abnormal sickle hemoglobin (HbS) acquires a crystal-like formation when exposed to low oxygen tension -​ Autosomal recessive disorder -​ If both parents have trait: 25% -​ If 1 parent have trait and other have the disease: 50% -​ If both have disease: 100% -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Severe pain in various parts of the body -​ Tachycardia, murmurs and cardiomegaly -​ Chest pain and dyspnea -​ Jaundice -​ Delayed growth -​ Fatigue -​ enlarged skull and facial bones due to bone marrow expansion -​ Complications: -​ Hypoxia, ischemia, infection, poor wound healing -​ Impotence -​ CVA -​ Renal failure -​ Heart failure -​ Pulmonary hypertension -​ Types of Cell Crisis: -​ Sickle crisis - results from tissue hypoxia and necrosis due to inadequate blow to a specific region of tissue or organ -​ Aplastic crisis - results from infection with the human parvovirus -​ Sequestration crisis - results when other organs pool that sickled cells -​ Vaso-occlusion crisis - severe pain, hypoxia
