or ischemia -​ Eye -​ Lungs (pulmonary hypertension) -​ Kidney (kidney damage) -​ Brain (CVA) -​ Spleen (splenomegaly) -​ Hypovolemia -​ Bone weakening -​ Diagnosis: -​ CBC (low RBC, hemoglobin) -​ Hemoglobin electrophoresis - to detect hemoglobin S -​ Stem cell - to produce health RBC -​ Treatment: -​ bone marrow transplant -​ Hydroxyurea - anti metabolite, avoids RBC to become sickle cell -​ Long term RBC transfusion -​ Splenectomy -​ peripheral blood stem cell transplant -​ Nursing management: -​ Managing pain -​ Treat the triggering factors -​ Hypoxia: provide oxygen support -​ dehydration: infuse IV, encourage increased OFI -​ Infection control -​ Pain reliever: PRN (NSAIDS) -​ Support and elevate acutely inflamed joint -​ Relaxation techniques -​ Prevent and manage infection -​ Monitor patient for signs and symptoms of infection -​ Initiate prompt antibiotic therapy -​ Monitor and prevent potential complications -​ Always provide adequate hydration -​ Avoid cold temperature that may cause vasoconstriction -​ Protect leg from trauma and contamination to prevent leg ulcer -​ Aseptic technique -​ Avoid high altitude -​ Diet: -​ High calorie, high protein, folic acid supplements Thalassemia -​ Group of hereditary anemias characterized by hypochromia (an abnormal decrease in the hemoglobin content of erythrocytes), extreme monocytosis (smaller than normal erythrocytes), destruction of blood elements (hemolysis) and variables degrees of anemia -​ Associated with defective synthesis of hemoglobin; the production of one or more globulin chains within the hemoglobin molecule is reduced -​ 2 classifications: -​ Alpha-thalassemia -​ Occur mainly in people from Asia and Middle East -​ Milder than the beta forms and often occurs without symptoms; the erythrocytes are extremely microcytic, but the anemia if present is mild -​ Beta-thalassemia -​ Most prevalent in people from Mediterranean regions -​ Patients with mild forms have microcytosis and mild anemia -​ Severe beta-thalassemia (thalassemia major or Cooley’s anemia) can be fatal within the first few years of life if untreated -​ Management: -​ Bone marrow transplant -​ Blood transfusion of PRBCs -​ Thalassemia major (Cooley’s anemia) -​ Characterized by severe anemia, marked hemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis -​ With early regular transfusion therapy, growth and development through childhood are facilitated -​ Management: PBSCT before liver damage occurs -​ WOF iron overload which results to excessive iron in multiple packed RBCs -​ Management: regular chelation therapy Polycythemia Vera (Primary Polycythemia) -​ Proliferative disorder of the myeloid stem cells -​ The bone marrow is hypercellular (hyperplasia) -​ Elevated levels of blood cells (erythrocytes, leukocytes, thrombocytes) -​ Blood = concentration -​ -> increased blood viscosity -> thromboembolism -> coronary artery disease/CVA -​ -> organ involvement -> cerebral hypoxia/arthralgia/splenomegaly/hepatomegaly -​ -> capillary over distention -> rupture -> bleeding -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Chest pain -​ Ruddy complexion -​ Splenomegaly/Hepatomegaly -​ headache and dizziness -​ Tinnitus, fatigue, paresthesia -​ Blurred vision -​ Increased blood viscosity: angina, claudication, dyspnea, and thrombophlebitis -​ elevated BP -​ Uric acid may be elevated resulting in gout and renal stone formation -​ Generalized pruritus -​ Erythromyalgia (burning sensation in fingers and toes) -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ CBC -​ Bone Marrow aspiration -​ Complications: -​ CVA -​ MI -​ bleeding due to dysfunctional large amount of platelets -​ Management: -​ Phlebotomy - removing enough blood (initially 500 ml once or twice a week) to reduce blood viscosity and to deplete the patient’s iron stores -​ Chemotherapeutic agents (hydroxyurea) can be used to suppress marrow function -​ Anagrelide (Agrylin) - inhibits platelet aggregation -​ Interferon alfa-2b (Intron-A) - for management or pruritus (WOF: flu-like symptoms and depression) -​ Antihistamine -​ Allopurinol -​ Analgesic for pain -​ Nursing management: -​ Monitor sign of thromboembolism
text.287: -​ Increase fluid intake to reduce blood viscosity -​ Instruct the patient to avoid sedentary behaviors, crossing legs, wearing tight or restrictive clothing -​ avoid aspirin and aspirin-containing medications -​ Minimize alcohol intake -​ Instruct patient to avoid iron supplements -​ Avoid activity in high altitude (low level of oxygen -> stimulates kidney (erythropoietin) -> stimulates bone to produce blood -> increased blood viscosity) -​ For pruritus: -​ Bathing in tepid or cool water -​ Use cocoa butter or oat meal based lotions and bath products -​ Dissolved baking soda in bath water Bleeding Disorders Hemophilia -​ Inherited bleeding disorder -​ Hemophilia A (Classic Hemophilia) - caused by genetic disease that results in deficient or defective factor VIII -​ Hemophilia B (Christmas Disease) - genetic defect that causes deficient or defective factor IX -​ Both types of hemophilia are inherited as X-linked recessive traits, so almost all affected people are males; females can be carriers -​ Recognized in early childhood, usually in the toddler age group -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ hemorrhages into various parts of the body -​ hemarthroses and hematomas -​ 75% of all bleeding occurs into joints -​ Chronic pain or ankylosis (fixation) of the joints occurs -​ spontaneous hematuria and GI bleeding -​ Intracranial or extra cranial bleeding - most dangerous -​ Management: -​ Administration of factor VIII and factor IX concentration -​ Infusion of fresh frozen plasma -​ Plasmapheresis or concurrent immunosuppressive therapy -​ Aminocaproic acid inhibits fibrinolysis and therefore stabilize the clot -​ Desmopressin (DDVAP) - induce significant but transient rise in factor VII levels -​ Nursing management: -​ RICE: Rest, Ice/Immobilize, Compression/Elevate -​ Gentle massive exercise 48 hours after acute phaseA -​ Avoid immobility -​ Assist child in coping with the condition -​ Encouraged to be self-sufficient and to maintain independence by preventing unnecessary trauma that can cause acute bleeding episodes -​ Instruct patient to avoid OTC medications such as aspirin, NSAIDs, herbs, nutritional supplements and alcohol -​ Nasal packing should be avoided, because bleeding frequently resumes when the packing is removed -​ All injections should be avoided -​ Splints and other orthopedic devices may be useful in patients with joint or muscle hemorrhages -​ Warm baths promote relaxation, improve mobility -​ Provide genetic testing and counselling to female carriers Thrombocytopenia -​ Causes: -​ decreased platelet production -​ Increased platelet destruction (ITP, DIC) -​ Normal: 150,000-450,000 -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Petechiae -​ Ecchymosis -​ bleeding (GI, GU) -​ Management: -​ blood transfusion: platelet -​ Steroids - decreased production of anti platelet antibody (IgG) -​ Bleeding precaution: -​ Avoid contact sports -​ NSAIDs, aspirin Idiopathic Thrombocytopenia Purpura -​ Autoimmune -​ Management: -​ Platelet transfusion -​ Steroids -​ IV immunoglobulin - increases platelet count -​ Bleeding precautions
text.289: von Willebrand’s Factor Disease -​ Inherited or acquired blood disorder -​ Glycoprotein that plays a crucial role in blood clotting -​ decreased level of von Willebrand's factor (needed for formation of clotting factor VIII (Hemophilia A) -> bleeding -> bruising, abnormal menstrual bleeding, bleeding in gums, nose, GIT, excessive bleeding after procedure -​ Management: -​ Desmopressin - synthetic analogue of vasopressin (increase the level of von Willebrand’s factor -> reduced bleeding) -​ Reduced fluid intake -​ S/E: decreased urination (cerebral edema -> increased ICP) -​ Factor VIII replacement: cryoprecipitate -​ Antifibrinolytic agent: Amicar - to stabilize clot formation especially before procedure -​ Bleeding precaution Bleeding Precaution 1.​ Minimize trauma a.​ Avoid IM unless absolutely necessary b.​ Use the smallest gauge needle possible c.​ Use soft toothbrushes or oral swabs for oral care d.​ Avoid rectal temperatures, enemas, or suppositories e.​ Use electric razors instead of blades 2.​ Monitor for bleeding a.​ Check for signs of: i.​ Gum bleeding ii.​ Nosebleed iii.​ blood in urine or stool iv.​ Bruising or petechiae b.​ Report persistent bleeding immediately 3.​ Avoid medications that increase bleeding risk a.​ Avoid NSAIDS unless prescribed b.​ Only use prescribed anticoagulants with close monitoring c.​ Check herbal supplements that may interfere without (garlic, gingko) 4.​ Environmental safety a.​ Keep the patient’s environment clutter-free to avoid bumps and falls b.​ ensure adequate lighting to prevent injury c.​ Use bed rails if needed to prevent falls 5.​ Activity restrictions
text.290: a.​ avoid contact sports or vigorous activity b.​ Use protective equipment if mobility aids are used c.​ consider limiting straining during bowel movements (use stool softeners as needed) 6.​ Patient education a.​ Teach patients and caregivers: i.​ To recognize signs of internal and external bleeding ii.​ The importance of avoiding injury iii.​ When and how to seek medical help Infection Precaution 1.​ Standard precaution a.​ Frequent hand hygiene b.​ Use of PPE c.​ Safe injection practices and sterile techniques d.​ Proper waste disposal and handling of bodily fluids 2.​ Neutropenic precautions (<500 cells/mm3) a.​ Protective isolation or reverse isolation b.​ Limit visitors c.​ Staff and visitors must wear surgical masks, sanitize hands and possibly gown d.​ No fresh flowers/plants or raw fruits/vegetables e.​ Use bottled or sterile water if advised f.​ daily bathing with antimicrobial soap 3.​ Environmental controls a.​ Patient rooms clean daily with disinfectants b.​ HEPA filtration for bone marrow transplant units c.​ Avoid shared equipment unless thoroughly disinfected d.​ No humidifiers or standing water 4.​ Antimicrobial prophylaxis a.​ Antibacterial (levofloxacin) b.​ Antiviral (acyclovir) c.​ Antifungal (fluconazole) d.​ Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP) prevention (trimethoprim-sulfamethaxazole) 5.​ Vaccination precaution a.​ No live vaccines b.​ Ensure household contacts are up to date on vaccines c.​ Post-chemotherapy or transplant patients may need revaccination 6.​ Patient and family education a.​ Report fever >38C (100.4F) immediately (medical emergency in neutropenia) b.​ Avoid crowds and public spaces when counts are low
text.291: c.​ Maintain good oral hygiene but avoid dental procedures unless cleared d.​ Safe food handling e.​ Encourage wearing mask in public Perioperative/Surgery Perioperative nursing - a specialized area of nursing focused on the care of surgical patients before, during and after their procedure -​ Preoperative phase: begins when the decision to proceed with surgical intervention is made and ends with the transfer of the patient onto the operating room table -​ Visit the patient - the day or the night before the surgery; for additional queries -​ Interview/informed consent - one method of assessment (preoperative assessment) -​ Preoperative assessment: to identify and correct problems before surgery and establish a baseline data for postoperative comparison -​ Preparation - physical and psychological -​ Psychological preparation -​ Alleviate the fear of the unknown (anxiety) - most common -​ Physical preparation -​ Health teaching (deep breathing, performing early ambulation and coughing exercises, splinting the wound) -​ Preoperative checklist: tests or activities conducted before the procedure -​ What is to be removed and retained -​ Jewelries/contact lens/dentures/nail polish (removed) -​ Hearing aid (retained) -​ Methods of hair removal -​ Shaving -​ Clipping -​ Depilation (cream) -​ Intraoperative phase: begins when the patient is transferred onto the OR table and ends with admission to the PACU (Post Anesthesia Care Unit) -​ Safety -​ Aseptic-controlled environment -​ Traffic control in the OR -​ Movement of personnel - kept to a minimum -​ OR zones - installing signage to clarify requirements for what must be worn in each area -​ Cleaning in the OR -​ Routine cleaning -​ Cleaning first thing the morning - done before the patient is received in the OR -​ Damp dusting - performed before surgical supplies are brought to OR and are opened, use clean, low-linting cloth moistened with disinfectant -​ End of procedure cleaning - done between every patient during the day -​ Terminal cleaning and disinfecting/Turnover cleaning - done at the end of the day -​ Scheduled cleaning - depends upon institutional protocol -​ Coordinated cleaning - cleaning of equipment with the help of maintenance -​ Prevent sentinel events in the OR -​ Sentinel events - a patient safety event that may result in death, severe or permanent harm; wrong patient,wrong procedure; wrong site -​ Pre-procedure verification process - multiple times whenever necessary -​ Site marking - laterality (extremities), paired organs, specific levels (spine surgery) -​ Do not use X mark (ambiguous) -​ Time out/huddle - brainstorming led by the circulating nurse; recite the information of procedure to ensure the whole team know the procedure (everyone is on the same page); it may be performed as necessary -​ Temperature and humidity level in the OR -​ Temperature: 20-24C, Humidity: 50-55% -​ Microorganisms will proliferate if the temperature and humidity is not in the recommended range -​ Positioning -​ I&O (collaborative with anesthesiologist) -​ Postoperative phase: begins with the admission of the patient to PACU and ends with the follow-up evaluation in the clinical setting or home -​ Temperature and other VS -​ Oxygenation status -​ LOC -​ Drainage and dressing -​ Airway
text.293: Surgical Classification According to Magnitude -​ Major procedure -​ High risk for morbidity and mortality -​ Extensive or prolonged -​ Large amount of blood loss -​ Presence of complications -​ Minor procedure: procedures that are not included in the characteristics of major procedures Note: anesthesia is not a part of the characteristics of major or minor procedure According to Purpose -​ Diagnostic: to establish the disease or condition (biopsy) -​ Exploratory: to determine cause of unexplained symptoms; to determine the extent of a condition (exploratory laparotomy) -​ Preventive/Prophylactic: stops the development of a disease (removal of pre-cancerous lesions) -​ Curative -​ Ablative: removal of body part -​ Constructive: repair for congenital defects -​ Reconstructive or cosmetics: repair of a damaged or diseased organs (mammoplasty or facelift) -​ Palliative: to reduce distressful signs and symptoms According to the Degree of Urgency -​ Optional: surgery is scheduled completely at the preference of the patient -​ Elective: the approximate time for surgery is at the convenience of the patient; failure to have surgery is not catastrophic -​ Required: the condition requires surgery within a few weeks -​ Urgent: the surgical problem requires attention within 24 to 48 hours -​ Emergency: the situation requires immediate surgical attention without delay According to Invasiveness -​ Open surgery: requires cutting of skin and tissues for a full view of the organs or structures involved -​ Minimally invasive surgery: does not require large incision (keyhole surgery/laparoscopy surgery) Informed Consent Informed consent: the patient’s autonomous decision about whether to undergo a surgical procedure. It is the process of informing the patient about the surgical procedure; that is risks and possible complications of surgery and anesthesia -​ Consent is obtained by the surgeon; this is a legal requirement
text.294: -​ Purpose: -​ To ensure that the patient understands the nature of treatment, including potential complications -​ To indicate the patient’s decision was made without pressure -​ To protect the patient against unauthorized procedure is performed on the correct body part -​ To protect the surgical team and hospital against legal action by a patient who claims that an unauthorized procedure was performed -​ Information provided to the patient -​ Nature and magnitude of the procedure -​ Risks and benefits of the procedure -​ Alternative treatment -​ Prognosis -​ Role of Nurse -​ Witness client’s signature on the form -​ Advocate client by verifying that the client received adequate information to give consent -​ Important reminders -​ Right of consent also includes the right of refusal -​ Right to refuse continues even after signing the consent form -​ Document client concerns or questions and notify the HCP -​ Who cannot give consent -​ Minors -​ Unconscious -​ Mentally-ill -​ Conditions requiring Informed Consent -​ Minor and Major procedures -​ Anesthesia administration -​ Radiographic exam with the use of contrast medium -​ Entry to body cavity Surgical Team 1.​ Circulating Nurse a.​ Main responsibilities include: i.​ Verifying consent ii.​ Coordinating the team iii.​ Ensuring cleanliness iv.​ Proper temperature and humidity v.​ Light and safe function of equipment and availability of supplies and materials
text.295: b.​ The circulating nurse monitors aseptic practices to avoid breaks in technique while coordinating the movement of related personnel as well as implementing fire safety precautions c.​ Responsible for ensuring that the second verification of the surgical procedure and site takes place is documented 2.​ Scrub Nurse a.​ Performs surgical hand scrub b.​ Setting up the sterile tables c.​ Preparing sutures, ligatures and special equipments d.​ Assisting the surgeon and the surgical assistants during the procedure by anticipating the instruments and supplies that will be required such as sponges, drains, and other equipment e.​ Scrub nurse and circulating nurse count all needles, sponges and instruments to be sure they are accounted for and not retained as a foreign body in the patient 3.​ Surgeon a.​ performs the surgical procedure, heads the surgical team and is specially trained and qualified b.​ Has the ultimate responsibility for performing the surgery in an effective and safe manner 4.​ Anesthesiologist a.​ Assess the patient before surgery, selects anesthesia, administer it, intubates patient if necessary, manages any technical problems related to the administration of the anesthetic agents and supervises the patient’s condition throughout the surgical procedure b.​ During surgery, the anesthesiologist monitors the patient’s BP, PR, RR as well as ECG, O2 saturation, tidal volume, blood gas level, blood pH, alveolar gas concentration and body temperature Surgical Environment -​ The surgical suite is double doors, and access is limited to authorized personnel -​ External precautions include adherence to principles of surgical asepsis; strict control of the OR environment is required including traffic pattern restriction -​ To provide the best possible conditions for surgery, the OR is situated in a location that is central to all supporting services -​ To help decrease microbes, the surgical area is divided into three zones: -​ Unrestricted zone: where street clothes are allowed; area in operating room that interfaces with other departments, includes patient reception and holding area -​ Semi-restricted zone: area in the OR where scrub attire is required; may include area where surgical instruments are processed -​ Restricted zone: scrub clothes, shoe cover caps, and masks are worn, includes OR and sterile core area
text.296: -​ Other concepts in OR: -​ Time out -​ Sentinel events -​ Surgical conscience -​ Quintana Model of Surgical Conscience -​ Knowing what is sterile and safe -​ Accepting a moral obligation to advocate safety -​ Acting in accordance with the obligation to advocate safety Surgical Attire 1.​ Scrub suit a.​ Two piece pant suit b.​ Worn in the semi-restricted c.​ Must fit the body properly d.​ Waistline drawstrings must be tucked in e.​ Wet or soiled garments should be changed 2.​ Head cover a.​ Should cover the hair completely b.​ Worn in the semi-restricted c.​ Never comb your hair when wearing a scrub suit d.​ Disposable caps are preferred e.​ Bald head also causes contamination by shedding squamous cells f.​ Net caps do not prevent contamination 3.​ Shoes and Shoe cover a.​ Worn in semi-restricted area b.​ Should be comfortable and puncture resistant c.​ Shoe covers are worn during procedures with expected spills/splashes of blood or body fluid d.​ Street shoes are not used e.​ Shoe covers should be disposed before leaving OR 4.​ Surgical mask a.​ High filtration masks decrease the risk of post wound infection b.​ Worn inside the restricted area at all times c.​ Should cover nose and mouth completely d.​ Should fit tightly e.​ Double masking - a barrier not a filter f.​ Masks are changed between patients and should not be worn outside the OR g.​ Handle the mask by ties or strings h.​ Front of the mask is contaminated
text.297: i.​ Mask should never be hanged on the neck or place on top of cap j.​ It should not be kept in the pocket after use k.​ Should not interfere with breathing, speech or vision 5.​ Eye wear a.​ Eye wear or face shield protects the eyes from splashing of blood and body fluids or from debris when bone drilling is performed 6.​ Laser eyewear a.​ Protects the eyes from the intense light created by laser surgery 7.​ Gloves a.​ Nonsterile gloves: donned for clean procedures b.​ Sterile gloves: donned for sterile procedures Principles for Surgical Asepsis -​ All surgical supplies, instruments, needles, sutures, dressings, gloves, covers, and solutions that may come in contact with the surgical wound or exposed tissue must be sterilized before use -​ He surgeon, surgical assistants, and nurses prepare themselves by scrubbing their hands and arms with anti-septic soap and water or alcohol-based product or scrubless soap is used to prepare for surgery -​ During surgery, only personnel who have scrubbed, gloved, gowned touch sterilize objects -​ Requires meticulous cleaning and maintenance of the OR environment -​ An area of the patient’s skin larger than that requiring exposure during the surgery is meticulously cleansed, and an antiseptic solution is applied Basic Guidelines for Maintaining Surgical Asepsis -​ Only sterile surfaces/articles may touch other sterile surfaces/articles -​ Gowns of the surgical team are considered sterile in front from the chest to the level of the sterile field. The sleeves are also considered sterile from 2 inches above the elbow to the stockinette cuff -​ Only the top surface of a draped table is considered sterile -​ Sterile supplies including solutions are delivered to a sterile field or handed to a scrubbed person in such a way that the sterility of the object or fluid remains intact -​ The movements of the surgical team are from sterile to sterile areas and from unsterile to unsterile areas -​ Movement around the sterile field must not cause contamination of the field -​ Whenever a sterile barrier is breached, the area must be considered contaminated -​ Items of doubtful sterility are considered unsterile
text.298: Decontamination Process -​ Decontamination/Cleaning: removal of foreign material from the instrument by a combination of mechanical means (scrubbing) and chemical means (enzyme and detergents) -​ Mechanical/Physical: the use of physical force -​ Chemical: uses substances to loosen up the debris from the instrument -​ Disinfection: reduces or eliminates many pathogens but not necessarily all especially bacterial spores -​ Levels of Disinfection -​ Low level: limited/narrow spectrum (phenolic compounds) -​ Intermediate level: wide spectrum (70% isoproyl alcohol) -​ High level: 2% glutaraldehyde (high level disinfectant) -​ Recommended immersion time: 20 minutes (high level disinfectants); sterilization: 10 hours -​ Physical disinfection by boiling: uses 100C boiling water to destroy most pathogens except spores -​ Pasteurization: -​ Used for items such as reusable respiratory devices and anesthesia breathing circuit -​ Exposure to hot water with temperature of 60-80C for 30 mins -​ Chemical disinfection: -​ Items are soaked in disinfectant -​ Choice depends on compatibility and effectiveness of the instruments -​ Used for heat table instruments that cannot be boiled or sterilized -​ Sterilization: -​ Process which all pathogens are destroyed including spores -​ Highest level of decontamination -​ Methods of sterilization: -​ Physical sterilization -​ Exposure of instruments to radiation -​ Chemical sterilization -​ Ethylene oxide gas is used to sterilize items that are sensitive to heat or moisture -​ Heat and moisture labile instruments -​ Autoclaving (Steam under pressure sterilization) -​ Most common method -​ Uses steam with 120-121C temperature and 1 ATM pressure for 30 mins -​ Flush sterilization - emergency sterilization of unwrapped items -​ Dry heat sterilization -​ Dry heat in form of air is used
text.299: -​ Sterilizes anhydrous oils, petroleum products and talc powder -​ Indicators Used in Sterilization -​ Indicators never indicate sterility; it is only a parameter that instruments have undergone sterilization -​ Event related not based on time -​ Expiration date is only an estimate -​ Shelf life depends on: -​ Amount of handling -​ The quality of packaging materials used -​ Storage conditions General Risk Factors to Surgery -​ Age - older adults have reduced physiologic reserves -​ Obesity -​ Poor nutrition -​ Fluid and electrolyte imbalances -​ Pre-existing conditions (DM, respiratory conditions) -​ Alcoholism - can cause alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremors) -​ Severity and urgency of surgery Preoperative Medication -​ Reduce anxiety -​ Promote relaxation -​ Reduce pharyngeal secretions -​ Prevent laryngospasm -​ Inhibit gastric secretion -​ Decrease amount of anesthetic needed for induction and maintenance of anesthesia -​ Anesthesia a state of narcosis, analgesia, relaxation and reflex loss General Anesthesia -​ A reversible consisting of complete loss of consciousness that provides analgesia, muscle relaxation and sedation, protective reflex are lost -​ Lose the ability to maintain ventilator function and require assistance in maintaining a patent airway Administration of General Anesthesia -​ Inhalation -​ Inhaled anesthetic agents include volatile liquid agents and gases -​ Volatile liquid: anesthetic agents produce anesthesia when their vapors are inhaled -​ Halothane (Fluothane) -​ Enflurane (Ethrane) -​ Isoflurane (Forane) -​ Sevoflurane (Ultrane) -​ Desflurane (Suprane) -​ Gas anesthetic agents are administered by inhalation and are always combined with oxygen -​ Nitrous oxide -​ Intravenous -​ Barbiturates -​ Benzodiazepines -​ Non-barbiturate hypnotics -​ Dissociative agents -​ Opioid agents Stages of General Anesthesia -​ Stage 1 (Beginning Anesthesia/Induction) -​ Feeling of detachment -​ Drowsy/dizziness -​ Hallucinations occurs -​ Close OR doors -​ Ringing, roaring or buzzing in the ears -​ Keep quiet because exaggerated noises are heard by the patient -​ Standby to assist the client -​ Stage 2 (Excitement/Delirium) -​ Pupils are dilated, pulse rate is rapid, and may have irregular respirations -​ Because of uncontrolled movement of the patient, restraints are necessary -​ Stage 3 (Surgical Anesthesia) -​ Patient is unconscious and lies quietly -​ Pupils are small but reactive to light -​ Respirations are regular, the pulse and volume are normal -​ Skin is pink or slightly flushed -​ Stage 4 (Medullary Depression/Danger) -​ Too much anesthesia has been administered -​ Shallow respirations, weak and thread pulse -​ Widely dilated pupils -​ Death may occur -​ If this stage develops, discontinue anesthesia and initiate respiratory and circulatory support
text.301: Regional Anesthesia -​ anesthetic agents are injected around nerves so that the region supplied by these nerves is anesthetized -​ patient receiving regional anesthesia is awake and aware of his/her surroundings unless medications are given to produce mild sedation or to relieve anxiety Administration of Regional Anesthesia -​ Epidural Anesthesia -​ achieved by injecting a local anesthetic agents into the epidural space that surrounds the dura mater of the spinal cord -​ advantage: absence of headache -​ Disadvantage: greater technical challenge of introducing the anesthetic agents into the epidural rather than the subarachnoid space -​ Spinal Anesthesia -​ extensive conduction nerve block that is produced when a local anesthetic agents is introduced into the subarachnoid space at the lumbar level, usually between L4 and L5 -​ it produces anesthesia of the lower extremities, perineum, and lower abdomen -​ Moderate sedation -​ Previously referred to as conscious sedation, is form of anesthesia that involves the IV administration of sedative or analgesic medications to reduce patient’s anxiety and control pain during diagnostic or therapeutic procedures -​ Monitored Anesthesia Care (MAC) -​ Also referred to as monitored sedation is moderate sedation administered by an anesthesiologist or anesthetist who must be prepared and qualified to convert to general anesthesia if necessary -​ Local Anesthesia -​ Injection of a solution containing the anesthetic agents into the tissues at the planned incision site WHO Surgical Checklist Sign In -​ Before the actual start of surgery -​ Identifying the patient, site -​ Allergies, antibiotics, anticipated blood loss (if >500ml or 7ml/kg in children, need BT) -​ Pulse oximeter Time Out -​ Introduction of patient and procedure by doctor -​ Identify of team -​ Special concerns of anesthesiologist
text.302: -​ Completeness and sterility of equipment by scrub nurse -​ Done before skin incision Sign Out -​ Completeness of instruments -​ Proper endorsement of specimen -​ Must be labeled with name, age, gender, specimen/location, surgeon, pathologist -​ For normal histopathology -​ On buffered formalin solution -​ After 7-10 working days -​ Labeled properly -​ Frozen section -​ Clean plastic bag -​ Labeled properly -​ Labeled immediately and sent right away -​ Follow up histopathology results to physician Preoperative Phase Preoperative Assessment -​ The goal in the preoperative period is for the patient to be as healthy as possible -​ Consent -​ Health history is obtained -​ Nutritional and fluid status -​ Dentition -​ Alcohol and drug use -​ Respiratory status -​ Cardiovascular status -​ Hepatic, renal and endocrine function -​ Previous medication used Preoperative Nursing Interventions -​ Providing patient teaching -​ Deep breathing, coughing and incentive -​ Spirometry -​ Demonstrate how to take deep, slow breath and how to exhale slowly -​ Instruct patient to breathe deeply, exhale through mouth, take a short breath, and cough from deep in the lungs -​ Demonstrates how to use an incentive spirometer -​ Mobility and active body movement -​ Patient should be taught that early and frequent ambulation, exercise of the extremities and frequent change of position immediately postoperative as tolerated will help prevent complications -​ Pain management -​ Pain is instructed to take medication as frequently as prescribed during the initial postoperative period for pain relief -​ Reducing anxiety and decreasing fear -​ Assist patient to identify coping strategies that he/she has previously used to decrease fear -​ Managing nutrition and fluids -​ NPO overnight or longer to prevent aspiration -​ Specific recommendations depend on the age of the patient and type of food eaten -​ Bowel preparation -​ Enemas are not commonly prescribed preoperatively unless the patient is undergoing abdominal or pelvic surgery -​ Allow satisfactory visualization of the surgical site and to prevent trauma to the intestine or contamination of the peritoneum by fecal material -​ Cleansing enema or laxatives may be prescribed evening before the surgery and maybe repeated the morning of the surgery -​ Skin preparation -​ Goal is to decrease bacteria without injuring the skin -​ Cleanse the skin with soap containing detergent-germicide -​ If hair must be removed, electric clippers are used Immediate Pre-Op Nursing Interventions -​ Assist the patient in changing hospital gown -​ cover the head completely with a cap -​ Inspect the mount, dentures, and plates are removed -​ Remove all jewelries/body piercing -​ If the patient objects in removing wedding ring, secure it with tape -​ All valuable articles are given to family members or labelled it clearly and store it in a safe and secured place according to hospital policy -​ Patient should avoid first before going to the OR -​ If preanesthetic medication is administered, the patient is kept in bed with side rails raised -​ The completed chart accompanies the patient to the OR with the surgical consent form attached, along with all laboratory reports and nurse’s records -​ Transfer the patient to the holding area/presurgical suite 30-60 minutes before anesthetic agents is administered -​ Patient safety in the preoperative area is PRORITY
text.304: Surgical Positions -​ Supine (dorsal) position -​ patient is flat on the back, both arms are positioned at the side of the table, one with the hand placed palm down; the other is carefully positioned on an armboard to facilitate IV infusion of fluids, blood, or medications -​ Used for procedures of anterior surface of the body, such as abdominal, abdominothoracic and some lower extremities procedures -​ Shoulder or anterolateral procedures: the patient is on supine position with a small sandbag/water bag/roll/pad is placed under the affected side to elevate and expose the shoulder -​ Dorsal recumbent: for vaginal or perineal procedures -​ Modified dorsal recumbent (frog leg): surgical procedures in the groin lower extremities -​ Arm extension: surgical procedures of the breast, axilla, upper extremities or hand -​ Trendelenburg’s position -​ Usually used for surgery on the lower abdomen and pelvis to Oban good exposure by displacing the intestines into the upper abdomen -​ Reverse Trendelenburg's position -​ Used for thyroidectomy, laparoscopic gallbladder, biliary tract or stomach procedure -​ Fowler’s position -​ Used for shoulder, nasopharyngeal, facial and breast reconstruction procedure -​ Sitting position
text.305: -​ Occasionally used for otorhinologic and neurosurgical procedure -​ Prone position -​ Used for all procedures with dorsal or posterior approach -​ Modified prone procedure: used for neurosurgical and spine procedures -​ Kraske (Jack-Knife) position -​ Hips are positioned over the center break of the operating table between the body and leg section -​ The leg section of the operating table is lowered (usually 90) and the entire operating bed is tilted head downward to elevate hips above the rest of the body -​ Done for rectal procedures -​ Knee-Chest position -​ used for sigmoidoscopy or culdoscopy -​ Lateral position -​ Used for renal surgery Spaulding’s Classification of Instruments -​ Non-critical: items that come in contact with intact skin; immediate level disinfection -​ Stethoscope -​ BP cuffs -​ Tourniquet -​ Semi-critical: items that come in contact with mucous membranes and non-intact skin; sterilization (preferred)/high level disinfection -​ Anesthesia equipment -​ GI endoscopes -​ Speculum -​ Bronchoscopies -​ Laryngoscopes -​ Thermometer -​ Respiratory therapy equipment (endotracheal tube) -​ Critical: items that come in penetrate sterile tissues such as body cavity and vascular system; sterilization -​ Surgical instruments -​ IUD -​ Vascular catheters -​ Implants -​ Urinary catheter -​ IV needles, fluids
text.306: Classification of Instruments -​ Cutting and dissecting -​ Used to dissect, incise, separate or excise tissues -​ Scalpels -​ Blade 10, 11, 12 and 15 fits handle size 3 or 7 -​ Blade 20, 22, 25 fits handle size 4 -​ Blade 10 is used to open the skin -​ Blade 11 makes initial skin puncture for tiny deep incisions -​ Blade 12 is commonly used for tonsillectomy -​ Blade 15 is used for shallow short controlled incisions -​ Blade 20 same with 10 but larger in size -​ Scissors -​ Suture scissors are used to cut sutures -​ Wire scissors are used to cut wires -​ Bandage scissors are used to cut drains and dressings and to open items such as plastic packets -​ Sharp-tipped angled scissors with short jaws used for vascular surgery -​ Mayo scissors are used for cutting heavy fascia and sutures -​ Metzenbaum scissors are more delicate than mayo scissors and are used to cut delicate tissues -​ Curettes -​ Tissue from bone is removed by scraping with the sharp edge of the loop or scoop on the end of the curette -​ Grasping and holding -​ Tissues should be grasped held in position so surgeon can perform the design and the maneuver without injuring the surrounding tissues -​ Delicate forceps - hold fine tissues such as eye tissues -​ Adson forcep - used to pick up or hold soft tissues during closure -​ Smooth (thumb) forceps - used to prevent injury to the suture -​ Toothed forceps - hold on tough tissue -​ Allis forceps - used to hold tough tissue -​ Babcock forceps - end of each jaw is rounded to grasp tissue without injury -​ Lahey forceps - has sharp point tips to grasp tough organs or tumors -​ Stone forceps - grasp calculi in kidney and gallbladder -​ Clamping and occluding -​ instruments that apply pressure by clamping or occluding -​ Hemostatic forceps - used for occluding blood vessels -​ Crushing clamps - used to crush tissues or clamp blood vessels -​ Exposing and retracting -​ Soft tissues, muscles, and other structures should be pulled aside for exposure of the surgical site -​ Malleable retractors - maybe bent to the desired angle and depth for retraction -​ Hooks - commonly used to retract skin edges during a wide-flap dissection -​ self-retraining - inserted to spread the edges of an incision and hold them apart -​ Sutures -​ used for ligating, stitching, or approximating tissues -​ Absorbable sutures -​ Surgical gut - collagen derived from the submucosa or sheep’s intestine -​ Plain surgical gut - loses strength in 5-10 days and is digested within 70 days, used to ligate small vessels and sutures subcutaneous fats -​ Chromic surgical gut - support the wound for about 14 days and loses tensile strength up to 21 days and is absorbed within 90 days, used for ligation of lager vessels and sutures urinary/biliary tract -​ Synthetic absorbable polymers - are absorbed by a slow hydrolysis process in the presence of tissue fluids -​ Polydioxanone sutures (PDS) - useful in tissues in which would healing is slow, as in the fascia or where extended wound support is desirable -​ Poliglecaprone 25 (Monocryl) - loses all tensile strength by 21 days and absorption is between 91-119 days, used in soft tissues such as gynecologic, urologic and plastic surgery -​ Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) - absorbs rapidly within 90 days, uncoated polyglactin 910 is used for ophthalmic procedures -​ Non-absorbable sutures -​ Surgical silk - loses tensile strength when wet, used frequently in the serosa of the GI tract and to close fascia in the absence of infection -​ Surgical cotton - gains tensile strength when wet, used in most body tissues for ligating and suturing -​ Surgical stainless steel - used for abdominal wall or for retention suture to reduce the danger of wound disruption/dehiscence -​ Surgical needles -​ Point of the needle - honed to the configuration and sharpness desired of specific types of tissue -​ Cutting point is used when tissue is difficult to penetrate -​ Conventional cutting needles -​ Reverse-cutting needles -​ Side cutting needles -​ Trocar point -​ Taper (round) point is used when tissue such as intestines and peritoneum -​ Blunt point is used for suturing friable tissues
text.308: -​ Body of the needle -​ Straight needles are used in readily accessible tissues -​ Curved needles are used to approximately most tissue -​ French eye needle has a slit from the inside of the eye to the end of the needle through which the suture strand is drawn -​ Eyeless needle is a continuous unit with the suture strand, needle is swagged onto the end of the strand in the manufacturing process Potential Intraoperative Complications -​ Nausea and vomiting -​ administer antiemetics preoperatively or intraoperatively as ordered to counteract possible aspiration -​ If gagging occurs, turn the patient to side, the head of the table is lowered, and a basin is provided to collect the vomitus -​ Suction saliva and vomited gastric content -​ Respiratory complications -​ May lead to brain damage if not recognized -​ Be vigilant in monitoring the patient’s oxygenation status -​ Check peripheral perfusion frequently -​ Hypothermia -​ Patient’s temperature may fall during the anesthesia -​ may occur as a result of low temperature in the OR, infusions of cold fluids, inhalation of cold gases, open body wounds or cavities and decreased muscle activity -​ Environmental temperature in the OR can temporarily be set at 25-26.6C -​ Warm IV and irrigating fluids -​ Wet gowns and drapes are removed promptly and replaced with dry materials Preventing Intraoperative Positioning Injury -​ The patient should be in as a comfortable a position as possible, whether conscious or unconscious -​ The operative field must be adequately exposed -​ an awkward position, under pressure on a body part, or use of stirrups or traction should not obstruct the vascular supply -​ Respiration should not be impeded by pressure of arms, hands, and legs or feet can cause serious injury or paralysis. Shoulder braces must be well padded to prevent irreparable nerve injury, especially when the trendelenburg position is necessary -​ Precautions for patient safety must be observed, particularly with thin, elderly, or obese patient and those with a physical deformity -​ The patient may need light restraint before induction in case of excitement
text.309: Post-Operative Phase Care of Patient in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) -​ Phases of post-anesthesia care -​ Phase I: care of surgical patients immediately after surgery and for the patient whose condition warrants close monitoring and intensive care is provided -​ Phase II: surgical patient’s condition no longer requires close monitoring provided in phase I PACU. Patient is prepared for self-care or care in the hospital or extended care setting -​ Phase III: setting in which the patient is cared for immediate postoperative period and then prepared for discharge from the facility -​ Determining readiness for discharge from the PACU -​ many hospitals use a scoring system (Aldrete score) to determine the patient’s general condition and readiness for transfer from the PACU -​ Throughout the recovery period, the patient’s physical signs are observed and evaluated by means of a scoring system based on the set of objective criteria -​ The patient is assessed at regular intervals and a total score is calculated and recorded -​ Aldrete score is usually 8-10 before discharge from the PACU, the patient with the score of <7 must remain in the PACU until condition improves or they transferred to ICU -​ Areas of assessment in Adrete score includes: -​ Activity -​ Respiration -​ circulation -​ Consciousness -​ oxygen saturation -​ Priority #1: restoration of homeostasis and prevent complications -​ Priority #2: maintain and promote adequate airway and respiratory function -​ Priority #3: maintain adequate cardiac function and promote tissue perfusion -​ Priority #4: maintain adequate fluid and electrolyte balance and adequate renal function -​ Sufficient fluids to maintain extracellular fluids and blood volume -​ Prevent fluid overload with resultant -​ pulmonary congestion and edema -​ Monitor serum electrolyte -​ Accurate I&O recording -​ Instruct and support breathing exercise -​ Don't force fluid too soon -​ Priority #5: promote comfort and rest -​ Manage pain during variety of approaches: pharmacologic, comfort measures -​ Priority #6: promote adequate nutrition and elimination -​ normal peristalsis returns to 48 to 72 hours post op
text.310: -​ liquid diet -​ Early ambulation to prevent abdominal distention -​ Priority #7: promote wound healing and prevention of: -​ Dehiscence: total or partial disruption or separation in wound edges but underlying subcutaneous tissue has not parted -​ Evisceration: protrusion of viscera through an abdominal wound opening Post-Operative Complications Shock -​ One of the most serious postoperative complications, can result to hypovolemia and decreased intravascular volume -​ Primary intervention for hypovolemic shock is volume replacement -​ Administer oxygen -​ Continuously monitor patient’s condition has stabilized -​ Kepp the patient warm and maintain normothermia -​ Assessment: -​ SBP: <90 mmHg -​ Downward trend of 5 mmHg reading -​ Intervention: -​ Administer oxygen (1-2 LPM via nasal cannula) -​ Position: modified trendelenburg Hemorrhage -​ Is copious escape of blood from blood vessel -​ Classification of hemorrhage: -​ Primary: hemorrhage occurs at the time of surgery -​ Intermediary: hemorrhage occurs during the few hours after surgery when the rise of blood pressure to its normal level dislodges insecure clots from untied vessels -​ Secondary: hemorrhage may occur sometime after surgery if a suture slips because of the blood vessel was not securely tied, became infected, or was eroded by a drainage tube -​ Types of vessels: -​ Capillary: hemorrhage is characterized by a slow, general ooze -​ Venous: darkly colored blood bubbles out quickly -​ Blood is bright red and appears in spurts with each heartbeat -​ Visibility: -​ Evident: hemorrhage is on the surface and can be seen -​ Concealed: hemorrhage is in a body cavity and cannot be seen -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Patient presents with hypotension, rapid, thready pulse, disorientation, restlessness, oliguria, cold and pale skin -​ Feeling of apprehension, decreased cardiac output and vascular resistance and signifies that the patient is in the early phase of shcok -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Transfusing of blood or blood products and detrmining the cause of hemorrhage are the initial therapeutic measures -​ Inspect surgical site and incision, if bleeding is evident, a sterile gauze pad and a pressure dressing are applied, and the site of bleeding is elevated to heart is possible -​ Place the patient in shock position (flat on back, legs are elevated at 20 degree angle and kept straight) -​ If suspected for internal hemorrhage, patient is taken back to OR Deep Vein Thrombosis -​ DVT occurs in pelvic veins or in the deep veins of the lower extremities in postoperative patients -​ DVT is common after hip surgery -​ Venous thrombi located above the knee are considered as the major source of pulmonary emboli -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Homan’s sign: calf pain upon dorsiflexion -​ Painful, swelling of the entire leg -​ Slight fever, chills and perspiration -​ Marked tenderness over the anteromedial surface of the thigh -​ Intravascular clotting without marked inflammation may develop, leading to phlebothrombosis -​ Circulation distal to the DVT may be compromised if sufficient swelling is present -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Hydrate patient adequately postoperatuvely to prevent hemoconcentration -​ Encourage leg exercise and ambulate patient as soon as permitted by surgeon -​ Avoid restricting devices such as tight straps that can constrict and impair circulation -​ Avoid rubbing or massaging calves and thighs -​ Instrcut to avoid standing and sitting in one place for prolonged periods and crossing legs when seated -​ Assess the distal peripheral pulses, capillary refill and sensation of lower extremities -​ Check the positive Homan’s sign -​ Prevent the used of bed rokks or knee-gatch on the patients at risk because there is danger of constricting the vessels under the knee -​ Initiate anticoagulant therapy either IV, SQ, or orally as prescribed -​ Prevent swelling and stagnation of venous blood by applying approximately fitting elastic stockings or wrapping the legs from the toes or the groin with elastic bandage -​ Apply external pneumatic compression intraoperatuvely to patients of highest risk of DVT Pulmonary Embolism -​ Is caused by the obstruction of one or more pulmonary arteries by the embolus originating somewhere in the venous system or in the right side of the heart -​ Postoperatively, most emboli develop in the pelvic or in the iliofemoral veins before becoming dislodged and travelling to the lungs -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Dyspnea is the most frequent symptom -​ Chest pain (sudden and pleuritic in origin) -​ Anxiety, fever, tachycardia, apprehension, cough, diaphoresis, hemoptyssis, and syncope -​ Most frequent sign is tachypnea -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Administer oxygen -​ Calm the patient -​ Monitor visual signs, ECG, arterial blood gases -​ Treat for shock or heart failure as directed -​ Give analgesics or sedatives as directed to control pain or apprehension -​ Prepare for anticoagulation or thrombolytic therapy or surgical intervention (management depends on the severity) Urinary Retention -​ Intervention for bladder or urinary retention: foley catheter -​ Expected time patient will void: within 8 hours -​ Expected amount of urine voided: after surgery atleasr 200 ml -​ Bladder training start: -​ If without urge: clamp 2 ½ hours then release for 30 minutes, if no urge: reclamp -​ Repeat steps until urge occurs -​ If with urge: remove clamp for 30 minutes then reclamp until next urge -​ Indication for removal of foley catheter: 4-5 consistent urges (successive) -​ Kegels exercise: to promote bladder control -​ Expected time of urination after FC removal: within 4 hours -​ Interventions to stimulate urination: -​ Fluids: increase OFI -​ Sound: whooshing -​ Faucet: running water -​ Environment: comfort room as much as possible -​ Bedpan or commode: warm Wound Dehiscence/Evisceration -​ Dehiscence: partial or toral separation of wound edges -​ Evisceration: uncontrolled exteriozation of intra-abdominal contents -​ Onset: 5th to 8th post op (commonly) -​ Causes: -​ Surgical team: inadequate surgical closure -​ Patient activity: coughing, vomiting, valsalva manuuver, bleeding down -​ Signs: -​ Drainage: serosaguinous (pinkish) -​ Sensation: something let go -​ Management: -​ Initial management -​ Dehiscence: assist patient to go back to bed -​ Evisceration: lie down where they are then sterile gauze with PNSS -​ Position: dorsal recumbent -​ Subsequent management -​ WOF: shock -​ Anticipate return to OR -​ Prevention: -​ Coughing with splinting -​ Pillow -​ Antiemetics -​ Stool softener: colace -​ Changing wound dressing -​ Optimal times: not during meals and do it without visitors -​ Never touch dressing with ungloved hands -​ In removing tapes: moisten tape with sterile water -​ Wear gloves during -​ Clean gloves: removing old dressing -​ Sterile gloves: wound cleaning and applying nee dressing -​ WOF: sanguinous, purulent drainage
text.314: Immunology -​ Is the biological and medical study of an organism's immune system, focusing on its components, function, and how it protects against diseases like infections and cancer -​ Immunology nursing involves nurses applying knowledge of the complex immune system to provide specialized care for patients, focusing on immune-related diseases and conditions like allergies, autoimmune disorders, and immunodeficiency NURSING PRACTICE IV Neurology -​ Focused on the diagnosis and treatment of disorders affecting the nervous system Cranial nerve - found in brain stem Lowest part of the brain - medulla oblongata (controls RR, HR, swallowing, hiccups and vomiting) Nervous System -​ Central Nervous System (brain & spinal cord) -​ Peripheral Nervous System (ganglia) - cranial and spinal nerves -​ Voluntary (somatic NS) -​ Efferent (motor/down) and afferent (sensory/up) nerve -​ Involuntary (autonomic NS) -​ Sympathetic - increased all except GI & GU (fight or flight) -​ Catecholamine (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine) released by adrenal medulla -​ Anti-cholinergic/adrenergic effects -​ dilated pupils (mydriasis) - to be aware of surroundings -​ Increased BP & HR - vasoconstriction -​ Bronchodilation - increased oxygen -​ Increased RR -​ Dry mouth -​ Constipation & water retention -​ Fluid volume excess -​ Parasympathetic - decreased all except GI & GU (rest and digest) -​ Acetylcholine - decrease all bodily activities except GI & GU -​ Cholinergic/vagal effects -​ Constrict pupil (miosis) -​ Decreased BP & HR - vasodilation -​ Bronchonstriction - decreased RR -​ Increased salivation -​ Diarrhea & urinary frequency -​ Fluid Volume deficit Cranial Nerves Cranial Nerve Name Sensory/Motor Function Abnormalities I Olfactory Sensory Smell Anosmia (absence of smell) II Optic Sensory Vision Blurring of vision, blindness III Oculomotor Motor Eye movement (up, down, in) eyelid up, pupil constriction Horizontal & Vertical Diplopia, Ptosis (drooping of eyelids), Anisocoria (unequal pupil) IV Trochlear Motor (smallest) Eye movement (down, in) Vertical Diplopia V Trigeminal Both (largest) Maxillary nerve Ophthalmic (corneal reflex) Mandibular nerve (mastication) Trigeminal neuralgia VI Abducens Motor Eye movement (abduction) Horizontal Diplopia VII Facial Both Facial expression and taste, Anterior ⅔ Bell’s palsy VIII Vestibulocochlea r Sensory Hearing and balance Hearing Loss, tinnitus, vertigo, Nystagmus IX Glossopharyngea l Both Taste, posterior ⅓, gag reflex Dysphasia (risk for aspiration) X Vagus Both (longest) Gag reflex, PNS activation Dysphasia, abnormal PNS
text.316: (cholenergic) GI secretions XI Accessory Motor Neck and shoulder movement Accessory neuropathy XII Hypoglossal Motor Tongue movement Dysarthria, tongue protrusion/deviation Spinal Nerves Spinal Nerve Controls Cervical (8) Diaphragm, chest wall muscles, shoulders, arms Thoracic (12) Trunk stability, thoracic organs (sympathetic), heart lungs, GIT Lumbar (5) Lower body, bowel and bladder Sacral (5) Coccyx (1) Common Neurologic Illness Increased ICP -​ Increased pressure within the skull due to increase in one of the intracranial components (0-15 mmHg) -​ Predisposing Factors -​ Stroke (Hemorrhagic) -​ Tumor -​ Inflammation (Meningitis, encephalitis) -​ Trauma (surgery) -​ Cerebral edema (SIADH) -​ Hydrocephalus -​ Monro-Kellie Doctrine - the skull is a closed vault, an increase in one component will increase the ICP -​ Skull components: -​ 80% - brain mass -​ 10% - CSF -​ 10% - blood -​ Pathophysiology -​ Alteration in BM, C, B (trauma) -> brain compression/brain herniation -> MO will move to FM -> respiratory arrest -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Early signs -​ Blurred vision, decreased visual acuity, diplopia -​ change or decreased LOC -​ restlessness to confusion -​ Disorientation to lethargy -​ Sluggish pupils & eye movement -​ Monoparesis/hemiparesis (weakness) -​ Throbbing/dull headache -​ Late signs (Change in VS) -​ Systolic hypertension (systolic high, diastolic same) -​ wide pulse pressure (N) 40-50 -​ Decreased irregular RR (Cheyne’s stokes - hypercapnia with periods of apnea) -​ Increased temperature -​ Projectile vomiting -​ Abnormal posturing (decorticate (cortex) - abnormal flexion/decerebrate (brain stem) - abnormal extension) -​ (+) Babinski reflex -​ Hemiplegia -​ Seizure -​ Coma Cerebral Perfusion Pressure - 60-100mmHg -​ Formula: CPP= MAP - ICP -​ MAP = SBP + (DBP) 2 / 3 (N: 70-100mmHg) Management -​ Head of Bed: elevated (semi-fowler’s) 30-45 degree -​ Neutral neck position for venous drainage -​ Evaluate neurological status every 1-2 hours -​ Airway: check RR: 12-20 cpm -​ If GCS 8 = intubation -​ Avoid fever and chills (acetaminophen & blanket) -​ Avoid coughing (antitussives - 1 extremity only) -​ Aphasia -​ Dizziness & vertigo, tinnitus -​ Stroke in evolution - progression of signs and symptoms of stroke -​ Complete stroke - cheyne-stokes respiration -​ (+) Kernig's and Brudzinski (+) hemorrhagic stroke -​ Homonymous hemianopsia - 2nd & with history of seizure -​ Risk factors -​ Metabolic imbalance -​ Alcohol/drug withdrawal -​ Autism (brain developmental disorder) -​ Genetics -​ Infection -​ Injuries of the brain -​ Cerebral palsy -​ Stress - post - ictal sleep (the longer = status epilepticus) -​ Safety -​ Turn to side (during) -​ Unrestrained -​ Remove hazards -​ Nothing in mouth -​ Padded side rails - always up -​ Oxygen after seizure -​ Don’t leave patient -​ Avoid alcohol -​ + Dilantin = CNS depression -​ Aura -​ Activities - what occurred before seizure -​ Reduce stimuli (bright/flashing lights, noise) -​ Remain with patient - note the time when it began, how long it lasted -​ Reorient -​ Diagnostic Test -​ Patient history -​ CT Scan (brain lesion) -​ EEG (electroencephalography) -​ (+) Abnormal spike-and-waves -​ Wash hair first -​ No fasting -​ No stimulants - may alter brain waves -​ No sleeping (to trigger seizure) -​ Signs and Symptoms -​ Generalized seizure -​ Tonic-Clonic seizure - common -​ AURA - warning sign of impending seizure attack (no stimulus) -​ Epigastric pain (flashes of lights, noise, taste, smell) -​ Epileptic cry - fall -​ Loss of consciousness (3-5 minutes) -​ Tonic-clonic contractions -​ Extension of extremities - tonic (10-20 secs) -​ Contractions - clonic (30 secs - 2 mins) -​ Post-ictal sleep (5-30 minutes) - lethargy, drowsy and unresponsive, exhausted -​ PRIORITY: SAFETY -​ Petitmal/absence seizure - common in 12 y/o -​ blank stare -​ Decreased eye blinking -​ staring into space -​ pausing amidst conversation -​ loss of consciousness (5-10 secs) -​ Status epilepticus -​ Continuous seizure activity > 5mins (can be up to 30 minutes according to Saunders) -​ 2 or more seizure within 5 minute period -​ If untreated, coma/death -​ PRIORITY: AIRWAY (min. 15LPM high flow non-rebreather mask) -​ Medications: IV push slowly -​ Lorazepam (DOC) -​ Diazepam (or rectal) -​ Midazolam (IM, if no IV site) -​ If seizure > 30mins, not breathing (intubate) -​ Add IV thiamine if with alcohol withdrawal CNS PNS -​ Brain, brain stem, & Spinal cord -​ MS -​ Alzheimer’s -​ Parkinson’s -​ Huntington’s -​ Cranial and spinal nerve -​ MG -​ ALS (muscle weakness) -​ GBS
text.324: CNS Disorders Multiple Sclerosis -​ Chronic asymmetrical autoimmune disease that destroys the myelin sheath (oligodendrocytes) of neurons in CNS -​ Inflamed neuron -> decreased nerve impulse transmission -​ Common: women (20-50 y/o) -​ Cause: idiopathic -​ Pathophysiology -​ Immune system attacks -> myelin sheath -> communication breakdown -> sensory and motor dysfunction, cognitive dysfunction -​ Signs and Symptoms -​ Charcot’s Triad -​ Dysarthria - difficulty/unclear speech (damaged in brain stem due to plaque) -​ Nystagmus - involuntary rapid eye movement (plaque in eye nerves) -​ Optic nerve - blurring of vision (1st) -​ Optic neuritis -​ Diplopia - double vision -​ Scotomas - blind spots -​ Intention tremor - plaque in motor pathway -​ Tremors -​ Ataxia -​ Muscle weakness & spasms -​ Paralysis -​ Plaques in sensory pathway -​ Numbness & paresthesia -​ Plaques in ANS (autonomic NS) -​ Urinary retention or incontinence -​ Constipation -​ Decreased sexual activity -​ Higher order activities -​ Cognitive: poor memory & attention, problem-solving issues -​ Psychosocial: depression, anxiety, mood swings -​ Lhermitte’s sign - sudden electric-like shock sensation -​ From spine to limb upon bending neck forward -​ Uhthoff’s sign - heat makes s/sx worse -​ Diagnostic Test -​ CSF analysis via lumbar puncture
text.325: -​ Increased CSF proteins levels (oligoclonal bands) -​ Means CNS inflammation -​ MRI with contrast - confirmatory test -​ Site and extent of demyelination -​ Management -​ Supportive/palliative -​ Prevent Uhtoff’s sign -​ Assistive devices -​ Side rails up -​ Prevent complications of immobility -​ Assess in plasmapheresis -​ Removal of plasma (fluid part of the blood) specifically antibodies -​ Medication: for acute exacerbation -​ Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone IV) - decreased inflammation and prevent paralysis -​ Symptom management -​ Baclofen - muscle relaxant -​ Tizanidine - muscle relaxant -​ Amantadine - fatigue -​ Propranolol - tremors -​ Chronic treatment -​ immunosuppressants -​ Beta-interferon - increase function of regulatory T-cells -​ Avonex -​ Rebif Alzheimer’s Disease -​ Atrophy of the brain due to beta amyloid plaque deposits outside neurons which disrupts synapse and cause inflammation -​ Cognitive decline and neuron death -​ Decreased acetylcholine (learning & memory) -​ Cause: idiopathic -​ Common: women (elderly) -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Short term memory loss (antero) - initial sign -​ Amnesia - events -​ Anomia - can’t name everyday objects -​ Agnosia - can’t recognize familiar objects, persons, sounds, shapes or smell -​ Apraxia - cannot perform motor activities despite intact motor function
text.326: -​ Aphasia -​ Expressive: broca’s (left frontal) aphasia - can’t speak (common in stroke) -​ Receptive: wernicke’s (left temporal) aphasia - can’t understand spoken words (common in alzheimer’s) -​ Diagnostic Tests -​ CT Scan - progressive brain atrophy -​ Autopsy - confirmatory -​ Management -​ Supportive/palliative -​ DOC: donepezil (Aricept) - take at bedtime -​ Memantine (Namenda) -​ PRIORITY: SAFETY (risk for injury) Parkinson’s Disease -​ Degenerative disease -​ Movement disorder, no weakness -​ Pathophysiology -​ Dopamine (inhibitory) - smooth and coordinated muscle movement , acetylcholine (excitatory) - muscle contraction -​ Dopaminergic neuron degeneration (substantia nigra) -> decreased dopamine -> dopamine & acetylcholine imbalance -> resting tremor, akinesia, rigidity -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Tremors (resting) -​ Pill rolling (1st sign) -​ Rigidity & bradykinesia -​ mask-like facies - hypomimia -​ monotonous voice - hypophonia -​ dysphagia -​ Cogwheel rigidity -​ Reduced arm swing -​ Shuffling gait -​ Akinesia - difficulty starting movement -​ Postural instability - stooped posture, impaired balance -​ Management -​ Safety (Priority) -​ Assist in ambulation -​ non-skid shoes, no heels -​ Grab bars, walkers, canes -​ Medications (increases dopamine)
text.327: -​ Levodopa -​ + Carbidopa -​ = Sinemet -​ Ropinirole (dopamine agonist) - delays levodopa use -​ Amantadine - controls dyskinesias in long term use of levodopa -​ Interdisciplinary -​ Physical Therapist -​ Occupational Therapist -​ Nurse -​ Speech Therapist -​ Lifestyle changes -​ Exercise, high fiber, increase OFI -​ Encourage gait training - use metronome or music -​ Diet: -​ Decrease or no protein at all - it inhibits absorption of medication (AM) -​ Increased protein in PM to induce sleep due to tryptophan -​ Small frequent meal -​ Double swallowing -​ Chin-tuck maneuver -​ Surgery: deep brain stimulation (most common surgical treatment) -​ Anti-parkinsonian -​ Take before meals - to increase absorption -​ With meals if there is nausea and vomiting -​ Inform patient - urine, stool may be darkened -​ Delayed reaction (2-3 weeks) PNS Disorders Myasthenia Gravis -​ Grave muscle weakness, chronic autoimmune asymmetrical descending muscle weakness due to destruction of acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junction -​ Voluntary muscles -​ Common: women (20-40 y/o) -​ Cause: idiopathic -​ Pathophysiology -​ Acetylcholine -> ACH receptors -> antibodies blocks the receptors -> no muscle contraction -​ Signs and Symptoms -​ Ptosis (initial sign) -​ Diplopia -​ Mask-like facies -​ Dysarthria -​ Dysphagia -​ Laryngeal muscle weakness -​ Respiratory muscle weakness -​ Leg weakness -​ Fatigue -​ Paralysis -​ Diagnostic Test -​ Tensilon test (Edrophonium Chloride) -​ Strengthens muscle (5-10 minute) -​ Short term - cholinergic -​ Antidote: atropine sulfate -​ CSF analysis - increase cholinesterase level -​ Management -​ Supportive/palliative -​ Surgery: thymectomy (removal of thymus - T-cell maturation) -​ Medication -​ Cholinergics or anticholinesterase agents -​ Pyridostigmine -​ Neostigmine -​ Corticosteroids - to suppress immune response -​ Prednisone -​ Immunosuppressant -​ azathioprine -​ Methotrexate (RA) -​ Crisis -​ Myasthenic crisis -​ Causes -​ Under medication -​ Stress -​ infection -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Ptosis & diplopia -​ Dysphagia -​ Can't breathe -​ Management -​ Cholinergic agent
