arrhythmia -​ Medications -​ IV immunoglobulin - to fight GBS antibodies -​ Gabapentin - for neuropathic pain -​ Heparin - DVT prophylaxis -​ Anti-arrhythmic agents (amiodarone, beta blockers, calcium-channel blockers - verapamil & diltiazem) Fluids and Electrolytes -​ Fluid - 60% total body weight -​ Intracellular Fluid - about ⅔ (70%) -​ Extracellular Fluid - about ⅓ (30%) -​ Intravascular - fluid within the blood vessels (plasma) -​ Interstitial - fluid surrounds the cell -​ Electrolytes - substances that dissociate into ions when mixed with water and are crucial for maintaining fluid balance, electrical charge and proper organ function -​ ICF - potassium and phosphate -​ ECF - sodium and chloride Acid - Base Balance -​ pH: 7.35-7.45 -> blood -​ Lungs (PaCO2): 35-45 -​ Kidneys (HCO3): 22-26 -​ PaO2: 80-100 -​ ABG Analysis (1)​ Determine the pH (acidic/alkali) (2)​ Look for the culprit (ROME) (a)​ Lungs - respiratory (b)​ Kidneys - metabolic (3)​ look for compensation (a)​ Uncompensated - pH abnormal, PaCO2 or HCO3 abnormal (b)​ Partially compensated - all are abnormal (c)​ Fully compensated - pH normal, both are abnormal (d)​ Mixed - if all are acid/alkali Regulatory Mechanism (1)​ Osmosis - movement of fluid from an area of low solute concentration to high concentration to achieve equilibrium (2)​ Diffusion - movement of solutes from an area of high concentration to low concentration (3)​ Filtration - fluid movement from arterial capillary beds (hydrostatic pressure) into the interstitial fluid, carrying water and electrolytes (4)​ Active transport - uses energy (ATP) to move ions against the concentration gradient Sources of Normal Fluid Loss -​ Urine output - 1 - 2L daily, varying with hydration status and kidney function -​ Sensible losses (visible perspiration) - 0 - 100 ml/hr, increased with fever and activity -​ Insensible losses (evaporation) - 600 ml/day under normal conditions, increased with fever -​ GI losses - 100 - 200 ml/day through normal digestive processes Homeostatic Mechanisms (1)​ Renal System (a)​ Kidneys filter 170 L of plasma daily (b)​ Reabsorbs bicarbonate (HCO3), secrete hydrogen ions (c)​ Slow compensatory response (may take several days) (2)​ Pulmonary System (a)​ Lungs regulate carbon dioxide (CO2) and carbonic acid (H2CO3) to maintain acid-base balance (3)​ Cardiovascular System (a)​ Maintains adequate renal perfusion and supports fluid regulation (b)​ Essential for blood pressure control (4)​ Endocrine System (a)​ Pituitary gland secretes ADH (promotes water retention) (b)​ Adrenal gland secretes aldosterone (causes sodium retention and potassium excretion) (5)​ RAAS (Renin-Angiotensin-Adlosterone System) (a)​ Maintains blood pressure through fluid retention and vasoconstriction (b)​ Decreased BP or decreased sodium or decreased renal perfusion -> kidneys releasing Renin -> Renin acts on angiotensinogen (from liver) -> forms angiotensin I -> angiotensin I converted to angiotensin II by ACE (in lungs) -> angiotensin II effects -> vasoconstriction (increased BP) & stimulates adrenal glands (increased aldosterone) -> aldosterone promotes sodium and water retention and potassium excretion -> increased blood volume -> increased BP Hypovolemia -​ Fluid Volume deficit - excessive loss of water and electrolytes in equal proportion, leading to dehydration -​ Etiology: -​ Inadequate fluid intake -​ Excessive fluid loss: severe diarrhea, vomiting, blood loss -​ Third-space fluid shift: ascites, burns, pancreatitis -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Tented skin turgor, dry mucous membranes -​ Postural hypotension, increased HR -​ Extreme thirst, dizziness, weakness -​ Renal shutdown, coma (severe cases) -​ Diagnostic findings: -​ Urine specific gravity > 1.020 -​ elevated BUN disproportionately to serum creatinine -​ Elevated hematocrit -​ Nursing management: -​ Monitor I&O, urine specific gravity -​ Weight daily (same clothes, same time, same scale) -​ Provide hydration (oral or IV fluids) -​ Assess VS, LOC and skin color
text.333: Hypervolemia -​ Fluid Volume Excess - excessive retention of water and electrolytes, leading to fluid overload -​ Etiology: -​ Excessive fluid intake -​ Impaired fluid excretion (renal, liver disease) -​ Heart failure, corticosteroid therapy, excessive sodium intake -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Weight gain, dependent edema (feet, ankles, sacrum) -​ Dyspnea, crackles (especially in cardiac patients) -​ Bounding pulse, JVD -​ Change in mental status (due to hyponatremia) -​ Diagnostic findings: -​ Decreased BUN and hematocrit -​ Nursing management: -​ Monitor I&O, VS -​ Elevate HOB for dyspnea; encourage deep breathing -​ Administer diuretics as prescribed (furosemide, spironolactone) -​ Provide client education on sodium-restricted diet and fluid restrictions Electrolyte Imbalances Hyponatremia -​ Sodium deficiency - serum sodium level <135 mEq/L (Sodium deficiency) -​ Etiology: -​ Fluid loss: vomiting, diarrhea, diuretic therapy -​ Adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) -​ SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone) -​ Excessive water gain (psychogenic polydipsia) -​ Clinical manifestations -​ Anorexia, nausea, muscle cramps -​ Lethargy, confusion, seizures (neurologic) -​ Diagnostic findings: -​ Serum sodium <135 mEq/L -​ Urine sodium varies: low with sodium loss, high with SIADH -​ Nursing management: -​ Monitor I&O, weight daily -​ Administer sodium supplements
text.334: -​ Monitor neurological status, maintain seizure precautions Hypernatremia -​ Sodium excess - serum sodium level of >145 mEq/L (Sodium excess) -​ Etiology: -​ Water loss: diarrhea, fever, diabetes insipidus -​ Inadequate water intake: common in elderly, comatose patients -​ Excessive sodium intake -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Thirst, tongue dry, tented skin turgor, sticky mucous membranes -​ Elevated temperature, lethargy, restlessness -​ Diagnostic findings: -​ Serum sodium level >145 mEq/L -​ Serum osmolality >295 mOsm/kg -​ Nursing management: -​ Monitor I&O, weight daily -​ Increased fluid intake, administer hypotonic solutions -​ Monitor serum sodium levels and neurological status -​ Protect the client from injury Hypokalemia -​ Serum potassium level of <3.5 mEq/L (Potassium deficiency) -​ Etiology: -​ Inadequate potassium intake: low dietary intake of potassium-rich foods -​ Excessive loss of potassium (medications, GI losses, renal losses) -​ Metabolic alkalosis: causes potassium to shift intracellularly, leading to a reduction in extracellular potassium levels -​ Hyperaldosteronism: high aldosterone levels cause increased potassium excretion by the kidneys -​ Clinical manifestations: (1)​ Neuromuscular (a)​ Fatigue: the most common complaint (b)​ Muscle weakness: especially in the legs (c)​ Leg cramps: due to muscle cell dysfunction (d)​ Paresthesia: tingling or numbness in extremities (2)​ Cardiovascular (a)​ Cardiac arrhythmias: premature ventricular contractions (PCVs), U waves, flattened T waves, prolonged PR intervals
text.335: (b)​ Hypotension due to reduced cardiac output (3)​ Gastrointestinal (a)​ Anorexia, nausea and vomiting (b)​ Decreased bowel motility, leading to ileus or abdominal distention -​ Laboratory and diagnostic findings: -​ Serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L (typically <3 mEq/L is considered severe) -​ Electrocardiogram (ECG) -​ Flattened T wave -​ Prominent U wave -​ ST-segment depression -​ Prolonged PR interval -​ Nursing management: (1)​ Therapeutic intervention (a)​ Parenteral potassium (i)​ Administer IV potassium slowly (NEVER IV PUSH or IM), always dilute it in at least 100 ml of fluid (ii)​ Infuse via infusion pump and monitor ECG during the infusion (2)​ Client education (a)​ Dietary teaching: encourage consumption of potassium-rich foods such as bananas, oranges, cantaloupe, spinach, potatoes and tomatoes (b)​ Monitor digoxin levels: hypokalemia can increase digoxin toxicity. Clients taking digoxin should be monitored closely for signs of toxicity (3)​ Monitor for complications (a)​ Cardiac arrhythmia (b)​ Increased risk for diuretics (c)​ Assess paralytic ileus: hypokalemia can lead to intestinal obstruction, causing symptoms like bloating, constipation and abdominal pain Hyperkalemia -​ Serum potassium level >5.5 mEq/L (Potassium excess) -​ Etiology: (1)​ Decreased renal excretion (a)​ Renal failure: the kidneys are unable to excrete potassium properly, leading to accumulation in the bloodstream (b)​ Hypoaldosteronism: aldosterone deficiency results in reduced potassium excretion (2)​ Tissue injury (a)​ Severe tissue trauma: burns, massive infections, rhabdomyolysis or crush injuries can release intracellular potassium into the extracellular space (3)​ Acidosis (a)​ Metabolic acidosis causes potassium to shift from inside the cells to extracellular space (4)​ Excessive potassium intake (a)​ Overuse of potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes (b)​ Excessive potassium administration in IV fluids (rare, but possible) -​ Clinical manifestations (1)​ Cardiovascular - cardiac arrhythmias: severe hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation, heart block and asystole (2)​ Neuromuscular (a)​ Muscle weakness, particularly in the legs (b)​ Paresthesias or numbness (especially in the extremities) (c)​ possible paralysis (due to muscle and nerve dysfunction) (3)​ Gastrointestinal (a)​ Abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting (b)​ Diarrhea: this is due to increased motility in the intestines (4)​ Respiratory (severe hyperkalemia) (a)​ Shallow respirations (due to muscle weakness and impaired diaphragm function) -​ Laboratory and diagnostic findings -​ Serum potassium >5.5 mEq/L, severity increases as potassium exceeds 6 mEq/L -​ ECG -​ Tall, tented T waves -​ Prolonged PR interval and QRS duration -​ Absence of P waves -​ ST-segment depression -​ Nursing management -​ Therapeutic interventions -​ Cation-exchange resins (kayexalate) -​ Calcium Gluconate -​ Sodium bicarbonate -​ Insulin and glucose -​ Hemodialysis -​ Monitor for complications -​ Cardiac monitoring: closely monitor the ECG for arrhythmias -​ Muscle weakness: watch for signs of muscle weakness, which may indicate worsening hyperkalemia or paralysis -​ Lab results: regularly check potassium levels and renal function -​ Client education -​ Diet restrictions: advise patients to avoid high-potassium food such as bananas, oranges, tomatoes, dried fruits and potatoes
text.337: -​ Medications: warn clients on potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone) about the risk of hyperkalemia Hypocalcemia Functions of Calcium (1)​ Electrical energy for the nervous system (2)​ Electrical energy for muscular system (3)​ Strength for skeletal system -​ Serum calcium levels <8.5 mEq/L, leading to symptoms like muscle spasms, tetany and arrhythmias (Calcium deficiency) -​ Etiology -​ Primary or surgical hypoparathyroidism pancreatitis -​ Insufficient vitamin D intake or synthesis -​ Renal failure -​ Drug therapy -​ Insufficient dietary calcium intake -​ Clinical manifestations -​ Tetany (tingling in the fingers and circumoral area, muscle spasms in extremities and face) -​ (+) Trousseaus’s and Chvostek’s sign (Hallmark) -​ Carpopedal spasms -​ Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
text.338: -​ Seizures due to neuromuscular irritability -​ Laboratory and diagnostic findings -​ Serum calcium <8.5 mEq/L -​ ECG reveals prolonged QT interval -​ Nursing management (1)​ Prepare for therapy (a)​ Institute seizure precautions (b)​ Administer parenteral calcium (careful of tissue infiltration, which can cause necrosis) (c)​ Avoid adding calcium to parenteral solutions containing bicarbonate or phosphorus (d)​ Caution with digoxin: calcium increases its effects, risking cardiac arrest) (e)​ Maintain a quiet, relaxed environment to promote rest (2)​ Administer vitamin D: this helps increase calcium absorption from the GI tract (3)​ Client education (a)​ Encourage a calcium-rich diet (1000 to 15000 mg/day) from foods like milk, green leafy vegetables and oysters (b)​ Avoid excessive alcohol or caffeine as they inhibit calcium absorption (c)​ Osteoporosis prevention: ensure adequate calcium intake and exercise to prevent bone loss Hypercalcemia -​ Serum calcium >10.5 mEq/L (Calcium excess) -​ Etiology -​ Excessive calcium intake or administration -​ Calcium moving from bones to serum -​ Hyperparathyroidism -​ Thiazide diuretic therapy -​ Clinical manifestations -​ Anorexia, nausea and vomiting -​ Constipation -​ Muscular weakness and incoordination -​ Altered LOC (slurred speech, confusion, lethargy, coma) -​ Polyuria and polydipsia -​ Cardiac arrhythmias -​ Hypoactive deep tendon reflexes -​ Laboratory findings -​ Serum calcium >10.5 mEq/L -​ ECG: shortened QT interval, bradycardia, heart blocks
text.339: -​ Nursing management (1)​ Prepare for therapy (a)​ Administer parenteral saline solution to dilute serum calcium and inhibit reabsorption (b)​ Administer parenteral phosphate to promote calcium deposition in bones (c)​ Use furosemide (Lasix) to increase calcium excretion (d)​ Treat underlying causes: use calcitonin for hyperparathyroidism, mithramycin and corticosteroids for cancer-related hypercalcemia (2)​ Maintain normal bowel elimination (a)​ Assess dehydration and mental confusion (b)​ Encourage fluids (3-4 quarts/day) and dietary fiber to prevent constipation (3)​ Injury prevention (a)​ for clients with mental confusion, ensure bedside rails are up and the bed is in low position (b)​ Reposition the client frequently and secure all invasive lines (4)​ Provide client education (a)​ Promote early ambulation to reduce calcium loss from the bones (b)​ Encourage daily weight bearing activities to prevent further calcium loss from bones Hypomagnesemia Function of Magnesium (1)​ Neuromuscular function (2)​ Carbohydrate and protein metabolism (3)​ Nerve function (sedative effects) -​ Magnesium serum level <1.3 mEq/L (Magnesium deficiency) -​ Etiology -​ Poor nutrition: insufficient intake of magnesium-rich foods -​ Alcoholism: impaired absorption and increased renal excretion of magnesium -​ GI and renal losses: diarrhea, vomiting, or renal disorders without adequate replacement -​ Clinical manifestations (1)​ Neuromuscular irritability: muscle spasms and tremors due to low magnesium (2)​ (+) Trousseaus's sign and Chvostek's sign: indicative of neuromuscular excitability (3)​ Insomnia - difficulty in sleeping due to neuromuscular hyperactivity (4)​ Mood changes: including irritability and anxiety (5)​ Cardiac arrhythmias: irregular heartbeats due to changes in electrical activity -​ Laboratory and diagnostic findings -​ Serum magnesium <1.3 mEq/L -​ ECG: flattened T wave, prominent U wave, ST-segment depression
text.340: -​ Nursing management (1)​ Prepare for therapy (a)​ Administer parenteral magnesium carefully using an infusion pump to prevent rapid administration and reduce the risk of cardiac arrest (b)​ Monitor for magnesium toxicity: look for signs such as hot, flushed skin, diaphoresis, hypotension, anxiety, lethargy, and laryngeal stridor (c)​ Monitor ECG and pulse for abnormalities (2)​ Prevent injury (a)​ Institute seizure precaution to prevent injury due to neuromuscular irritability (b)​ Ensure safety measures for mental confusion (c)​ Assess swallowing ability before administering oral medications as magnesium depletion can cause dysphagia (d)​ Monitor clients on digoxin closely, as magnesium deficit increases the risk of digoxin toxicity (3)​ Provide client and family education (a)​ Dietary sources of magnesium: encourage foods like nuts, whole grains, spinach, bananas, and oranges (b)​ Increase dietary magnesium to meet daily intake requirements Hypermagnesemia -​ Elevated magnesium serum level of >2.5 mEq/L (Magnesium excess) -​ Etiology -​ Renal failure -​ Overuse of magnesium-containing antacids -​ Excessive magnesium administration -​ Overuse of enemas or laxatives containing magnesium -​ Severe dehydration, as occurs in diabetic ketoacidosis -​ Clinical manifestations -​ Hot, flushed skin -​ Hypoactive reflexes -​ Hypotension, bradycardia -​ Depressed respirations, lethargy, drowsiness, and absent deep tendon reflexes with increasing magnesium level -​ Cardiac arrhythmias -​ Laboratory and diagnostic findings -​ Serum magnesium >2.5 mEq/L -​ ECG: prolonged QT interval and atrioventricular blocks -​ Nursing management (1)​ Prepare for therapy
text.341: (a)​ Discontinue all magnesium sources: stop parenteral and oral magnesium (b)​ Administer IV calcium Gluconate to counteract the neuromuscular effects of magnesium (c)​ Prepare the patient for hemodialysis to remove excess magnesium from the bloodstream (d)​ Administer diuretics and 0.45% normal saline to increase magnesium excretion (2)​ Provide client and family education (a)​ Educate the client about the adverse effects of overusing magnesium-containing antacids or laxatives (b)​ Read OTC drug labels carefully for magnesium contents (c)​ Monitor dietary intake of magnesium to avoid excessive levels Hypophosphatemia -​ Serum phosphorus level of <2.5 mEq/L (Phosphorus deficiency) -​ Etiology -​ Inadequate intake or administration -​ Obsessive intake or administration of carbohydrates/calories -​ Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) administration without proper phosphorus supplementation -​ Metabolic disturbances -​ Prolonged intense hyperventilation -​ Alcohol withdrawal and diabetic ketoacidosis -​ Respiratory alkalosis -​ Severe dehydration (common in diabetic ketoacidosis) -​ Clinical manifestations (1)​ Neurological and muscular symptoms (a)​ Irritability, apprehension, weakness (b)​ Numbness, confusion, seizures, coma (c)​ Muscle weakness, muscle pain (2)​ Systemic effects (a)​ Hypoxia leading to increased respiratory rate and respiratory alkalosis (b)​ chronic phosphorus loss may cause bruising and bleeding due to platelet dysfunction (c)​ Increased susceptibility to infection -​ Laboratory and diagnostic findings -​ Serum phosphorus level <2.5 mEq/L -​ Possible ECG changes or other abnormal findings related to cellular function due to low phosphorus levels -​ Nursing management

production -​ D vitamin activation Organs of the Urinary System -​ Kidneys: main filtration organ -​ Cortex - glomerulus -> inside Bowman’s capsule -​ Medulla - loop of Henle -​ Renal Pelvis - collects the urine -> ureters -​ Main parts: -​ Glomerulus -​ Bowman’s capsule -​ Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) - reabsorption -​ Loop of Henle - concentrates urine -​ Distal Convoluted Tubule exits the body Micturition reflex: bladder fills (500ml) -> stretch receptors fire -> spinal cord reflex -> detrusor muscle contracts -> internal sphincter relaxes -​ Laboratory and Diagnostic Test -​ Retention and Incontinence Feature Urinary Retention Urinary Incontinence Main Problem Inability to empty the bladder even when full Inability to control urine flow - leakage occurs involuntarily text.347: Genito-Urinary Tract Disorders Urinary Tract Infection -​ UTI is an infection and inflammation of any part of the urinary tract -​ Upper UTI - pyelonephritis (kidney infection) -​ Lower UTI - cystitis (bladder), urethritis (urethra), ureteritis (ureter) -​ Women are more prone due to shorter urethras -​ Incidence increases with age, especially in women; in men, rises after age 50 -​ Etiology -​ Caused by bacteria, most commonly E.coli -​ Risk factors -​ Sexual activity -​ Urinary catheter -​ urine retention or stasis -​ Mucosal damage -​ Poor hygiene -​ Diabetes -​ Pathophysiology -​ An upper UTI is a bacterial infection of the renal pelvis, tubules, and interstitial tissue of one or both kidneys that occurs because of reflux of urine into the ureters -​ A lower UTI is an infection that typically ascends from the urethra to the bladder and possibly to the ureter -​ Assessment findings -​ Signs and symptoms -​ Upper UTI -​ Flank pain, fever, chills -​ Nausea, malaise -​ Dysuria, urgency, frequency -​ Cloudy or bloody urine -​ Costovertebral angle tenderness -​ Lower UTI -​ Burning during urination -​ Frequency, urgency, nocturia -​ Painful urination -​ Inflammation at urethral opening
text.348: Cystitis -​ Infection of urinary bladder -​ Usually caused by ascending bacterial infection (E.coli) -​ Most common route is transurethral -​ Female - shorter urethra, childbirth, anaotmic proximity of urethra to rectum) -​ Male - due to epididymitis, prostatitis, renal calculi) -​ Predisposing factors: -​ Microbial invasion - E. coli -​ High risk - women -​ Obstruction -​ Urinary retention -​ Increase estrogen levels -​ Sexual intercourse -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Pain - flank area -​ Hematuria -​ Nocturia -​ Dysruria -​ Pyuria -​ Fever -​ Urgency -​ Chills -​ Suprapubic pain -​ Urinary frequency -​ Diagnostic test -​ Urine culture and sensitive: (+) E. coli -​ Management: -​ Pharmacologic -​ Antibiotics (Co-trimazole - DOC) -​ Antispasmodics -​ Analgesics -​ Nursing intervention -​ Force fluid/hydration -​ Diet -​ Cranberry/oranage juice -​ Avoid urinary tract irritants (coffee, tea, alcohol) -​ Warm sitz bath -​ Empty bladder after sexual intercourse -​ Good hygiene

text.356: Nephrotic Syndrome -​ Renal pathology characterized by increased glomerular permeability and is manifested by massive proteinuria -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Damage glomerular capillary membrane -> loss of plasma protein (albumin) -​ -> stimulates synthesis of lipoproteins -> hyperlipidemia -​ -> hypoalbuminemia -> decreased oncotic pressure -> shifting of fluids from IV to IS -> activation of RAAS -> sodium retention -> edema -​ -> proteinuria -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Pathognomonic sign: anasarca (generalized edema) -​ Edema (soft and pitting) -​ Periorbital edema -​ Dependent edema (sacrum, ankle, and hands) -​ Ascites -​ Irritability -​ Headache -​ Malaise -​ Assessment and Diagnostic test: -​ Proteinuria -​ Increased WBC in urine -​ Needed biopsy of the confirmatory exam -​ Complications: -​ Infection -​ Thromboembolism -​ Pulmonary emboli -​ Acute renal failure -​ Accelerate atherosclerosis -​ Management: -​ Pharmacologic -​ Diuretics -​ ACE inhibitors -​ Lipid lowering agents -​ Nursing intervention -​ Monitor VS, I&O, daily weight and urine specific gravity -​ Dietary restriction of sodium, fluid and protein -​ Carbohydrates are given liberally to provide energy and reduce the catabolism of protein -​ Provide special skin care
text.357: -​ WOF: renal failure, cardiac failure, hypertensive encephalopathy -​ Monitor urinalysis, BUN, creatinine levels -​ Promote rest and regular activity when hematuria and proteinuria resolve Acute Renal Failure -​ Acute tubular necrosis (ATN), renal parenchymal failure, acute tubule-interstitial nephritis -​ Reversible condition characterized by: -​ A sudden reduction of cessation of renal function -​ Retention of waste products -​ Increased BUN and creatinine -​ Causes -​ Pre-renal -​ Hypoperfusion of kidney -​ Volume depletion -​ Impaired cardiac efficiency -​ Vasodilation -​ Intra-renal -​ Actual damage to kidney tissue -​ Prolonged renal ischemia -​ Nephrotoxic agents -​ Infectious process -​ Post-renal -​ Obstruction to urine flow -​ Urinary tract obstruction -​ Calculi (stones), tumors -​ Benign prostatic hyperplasia -​ Blood clots -​ Phases -​ Onset -​ Benign with initial insult and ends when oliguria develops -​ Initial phase of injury 1-3 days -​ Oliguric phase -​ The oliguria period is accompanied by an increase in the serum concentration of substances usually excreted by the kidney -​ Urine output <400 cc/24 hours for 3 days - 2 weeks -​ Elevated BUN, creatinine -​ Edema, hypertension -​ Hyperkalemia -​ Hyponatremia -​ Hyperphosphatemia -​ Metabolic acidosis -​ Diuretic phase -​ The diuresis period is marked by a gradual increase in urine output which signals that glomerular filtration has started to recover -​ Urine output (3-5 L/days for 10 days) -​ Elevated BUN and creatinine -​ Elevated BP -​ Hypokalemia -​ Last for 1 week -​ Recovery phase -​ The recovery period signals the improvement of renal function and may take 3-12 months -​ Avoid nephrotoxic drugs -​ May lead to CRF -​ Diagnostic and laboratory findings: -​ Hyperkalemia -​ Hyperphossphatemia -​ Hypocalcemia -​ Metabolic acidosis -​ Azotemia -​ Proteinuria -​ Urinalysis (Cast, RBC, WBC) -​ Signs and symptoms: -​ Irritability -​ Headache -​ Anorexia -​ Tingling of extremities -​ Lethargy that can progress to stupor and coma -​ Sudden dramatic drop in urinary output -​ Restlessness, twitching, convulsions -​ Skin pallor, anemia, and increased bleeding time -​ Ammonia odor breath and perspiration -​ Generalized edema -​ Hypertension which can progress to pulmonary edema and CHF -​ Management: correct the underlying cause -​ Pharmacologic -​ Volume expanders (dopamine) to restore renal perfusion in hypertensive client -​ Loop diuretics -​ ACE inhibitors for hypertension

the study of body’s immune system, its functions and how it protects against disease Immunology nursing - focuses on the care of patients with disorders of the immune system including autoimmune diseases, allergies and immunodeficiency Immune System -​ Immunity: the body’s specific protective response to a foreign agent or organism -​ Immune system: functions as the body’s defense mechanism against invasion and allows a rapid response to foreign substances in a specific manner -​ Anatomy of Immune System: -​ Bone marrow: the WBC involved in immunity are produced in the bone marrow. Lymphocytes are generated from stem cells (undifferentiated cells) -​ Types of lymphocytes -​ B cells/lymphocytes -​ T cells/lymphocytes -​ Lymphoid tissue -​ Spleen: composed of red and white pulp acts somewhat like a filter -​ Red pulp: the site where old and injured RBCs are destroyed -​ White pulp: contains concentrations of lymphocytes -​ Lymph nodes: remove foreign material from lymph system before it enters the bloodstream -​ Centers for immune cell proliferation -​ Contain immune cells that defend the body’s mucosal surfaces against microorganisms -​ Function of the immune system -​ Remove foreign antigens such as viruses and bacteria to maintain homeostasis -​ General types: -​ Natural (innate): or nonspecific immunity is present at birth -​ Provides a broad spectrum of defense against and resistance to infection -​ First line of host defense following antigen exposure becayuse it protects the host without remembering prior contact with an infectious agent -​ Monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, basophils, eosinophils and granulocytes -​ Acquired (adaptive): or specific immunity develops after birth -​ Usually develops due to prior exposure to an antigen through immunization or by contracying a disease, both of which generate a protective immune response -​ Divided into two mechanism: -​ The cell-mediated response involving T-cell activation -​ Effector mechanisms, involving B-cell maturation and production of antibodies -​ Types of acquired immunity: -​ Active acquired immunity: refers to immunologic defenses developed by the person’s own body -​ Passive acquired immunity: temporary immunity transmitted from a source outside the body that has developed immunity resulting from the transfer of antibodies from mother to an infant in utero or through breastfeeding or receiving injections of immunoglobulin -​ Three means of defense: -​ Phagocytic immune response: primarily involves the WBCs (granulocytes and macrophages) which ingest foreign particles and destroy the invading agent -​ Humoral immune response (antibody response): begins with the B lymphocytes, which can transform themselves into plasma cells that manufacture antibodies -​ Bacterial phagocytosis and lysis -​ Anaphylaxis -​ Allergic hay fever and asthma -​ Immune complex disease -​ Bacterial and some viral infections -​ Cellular immune response: involves T lymphocytes which can turn into special cytotoxic (or killer) T cells that can attack the pathogens -​ Transplant rejection -​ Delayed hypersensitivity (tuberculin reaction) -​ Graft versus host disease -​ Tumor surveillance or destruction -​ Intracellular infections -​ Viral, fungal and parasitic infection Immune System Disorders Disorder Description Autoimmunity Normal protective immune response paradoxically turns against or attacks the body leading to tissue damage Hypersensitivity Body produces inappropriate or exaggerated responses to specific antigen Gammopathies Overproduction of immunoglobulin Primary Immune Deficiences Deficiency results from improper development of immune cells or tissues usually congenital or inherited Casual is defined as any time of day without regard to time since the last meal. The classic symptoms include polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss 2.​ Fasting plasma glucose greater than or equal to 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/L). Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for 8 hours 3.​ Two-hour postprandial glucose equal to or greater than 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/L) during an oral glucose tolerance test. The test should be performed as described by WHO, using a glucose load containing the equivalent of 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in water Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus -​ Cause: Autoimmune, congenital -​ Characterized by destruction of pancreatic beta cells -​ Abnormal response in which antibodies are directed against normal tissues of the body responding to these tissues as if they were foreign -​ destruction of the beta cells cells results in decreased insulin production, unchecked glucose production by the liver, and fasting hyperglycemia -​ Glucose derived from food cannot be stored in the liver but instead remains in the bloodstream and contributes to postprandial (after meals) hyperglycemia -​ If the concentration of glucose in the blood exceeds the renal threshold for glucose, usually 180-200 mg/dl (9.9 to 11.1 mmol/L), the kidneys may be reabsorbed all the filtered glucose; the glucose then appears in the urine (glycosuria) -​ When excess glucose is excreted in the urine, it is accompanied by excessive loss of fluids and electrolytes this is called osmotic diuresis -​ Fat breakdown occur, resulting in an increase production of ketone bodies which are the byproducts of fat breakdown -​ Ketone bodies are acids that disturb the acid-base balance of the body when they accumulate in excessive amounts, this results to diabetic ketoacidosis -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ <30 years of age -​ Thin, recent weight loss -​ Hyperglycemia (>140 mg/dl) -​ Polyuria (osmotic diuresis) -​ Polydipsia (increased thirst) -​ Polyphagia (increased appetite) -​ Poor wound healing (poor circulation) -​ Blurred vision -​ Management: -​ Test blood sugar -​ Administer insulin -​ Eat - Avoid exercise in extreme heat or cold. Inspect feet daily after exercise. Avoid exercise during periods of poor metabolic control -​ Pharmacological -​ Oral hypoglycemic agents (OHA) -​ Sulfonylureas -​ stimulate beta cell of the pancreas to secrete insulin; may improve binding between insulin and insulin receptors or increase the number of insulin receptors -​ Glipizide, Glicazide - increase insulin sensitivity -​ Biguanide -​ Inhibits production of glucose by the liver -​ Increase body tissues sensitivity to insulin -​ Decrease hepatic synthesis of cholesterol -​ the only biguanide in the market: metformin (Glucophage) - increase insulin sensitivity (DOC) -​ Never mix with alcohol (lactic acidosis & damaged kidney) -​ Never mix with contrast agent (hold 24 hours before and 48 hours after) - lactic acidosis + AKI -​ Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor -​ Delay absorption of complex carbohydrates in the intestine and slow entry of glucose into systemic circulation -​ Non-sulfonylureas secretagogues (Meglitinides and phenylalanine derivatives) -​ Stimulate pancreas to secrete insulin -​ Thiazolidinediones (Glitazone) -​ Sensitized body tissue to insulin; stimulate receptor sites to lower blood glucose and improve action of insulin -​ Dipeptide-pepidase-4 (DDP-4) inhibitors
text.407: -​ Increase and prolongs the action of incretin, a hormone that increases insulin release and decreases glucagon levels which result to improve glucose control -​ Meglitinides (Repaglinide) - increase pancreatic insulin -​ Insulin (PRN) Cause of Morning Hyperglycemia Characteristic Treatment Insulin Warning - progressive rise in blood glucose from bedtime to morning Increase evening (pre-dinner or bedtime) dose of intermediate acting or long acting insulin or institute a dose of insulin before the evening meal if one is not already part of treatment regimen Dawn Phenomenon - relatively normal blood glucose until about 3 AM, when the level begins to rise Change time of injection of evening intermediate acting insulin from dinner time to bedtime Somogyi Effect - normal or elevated blood glucose at bedtime, a decrease at 2-3 am to hypoglycemic levels and a subsequent increase caused by the production of counter regulatory hormones Decrease evening (pre-dinner or bedtime) dose of intermediate acting insulin or increase bed time snack Insulin Therapy -​ In type 1 diabetes, exogenous insulin must be administered for life because the body loses the ability to produce insulin Time Course Agent Onset Peak Duration Indication Rapid - acting Lispro (Humalog) Aspart (Novolog) Glulisine (Apidra) 15-30 mins 30 mins - 1 hr 2-4 hours Used for rapid reduction of glucose Level to treat postprandial Hyperglycemia and/or to prevent nocturnal hypoglycemia Short - acting Regular (Humalog R, Novolin R, Iletin II Regular) 30 mins - 1 hr 1-2 hours 4-8 hours Usually administered 20-30 minutes before meals; maybe taken alone or in combination with long - acting insulin Can be incorporated to an IV infusion Intermediate - acting NPH (Neutral Protamine Hagedorn) Humulin N, Iletin II Lente, Iletin II NPH 1-2 hours 2-4 hours 8-16 hours Usually taken after food Long - acting Glargine (Lantus) Detemir (Levemir) 1-2 hours Continuous (no peak) 24-48 hours Use for basal dose -​ Human insulin preparations have a shorter duration of action than insulin from animal sources because the presence of animal protein triggers an immune response that results an in binding of animal insulin -​ Short acting insulin is called regular insulin (marked R on the bottle). Regular insulin is a clear solution and is usually administered 20-30 minutes before a meal. Regular insulin is the only insulin approved for IV use -​ Intermediate acting insulins are called NPH insulin or Lente insulin -​ “Peakless” basal or very long acting insulin is absorbed very slowly over 24 hours and can be given once a day Complications of Insulin Therapy -​ Local allergic reactions -​ Redness, swelling, tenderness and induration or 2-4 cm wheal may appear at the injection site 1-2 hours after the insulin administration -​ Systemic allergic reactions -​ When they occur, there is an immediate local skin reaction that gradually spreads into generalized urticaria (hives) -​ These are rare reactions are occasionally associated with the generalized edema or anaphylaxis -​ Insulin lipodystrophy -​ Lipodystrophy refers to localized reaction in the form of either lipatrophy or lipohypertrophy occurring at the site of insulin injection -​ Lipatrophy is loss of subcutaneous fat; it appears as slight dimpling or more serious pitting of subcutaneous fat -​ Resistance to injected insulin -​ Most patients have some degree of insulin resistance at one time or another. The most common being obesity, which can overcome weight loss -​ Morning hyperglycemia -​ an elevated blood glucose level on arising in the morning is caused by an insufficient level of insulin, which may be caused by several factors; the dawn phenomenon, the somogyi effect or insulin warning Things to Take Note in Administering Insulin -​ Storing insulin -​ Vials not in use, including spare vials should be refrigerated -​ Insulin should not be allowed to freeze and should not be kept in direct sunlight -​ the insulin in use should be kept at room temperature to reduce local irritation at the injection site -​ The patient should be instructed to always have spare vials of the type or types of insulin he/she uses -​ Cloudy insulins should be thoroughly mixed by gently inverting the vial or rolling it between the hands before drawing the solution into a syringe or a pen -​ Bottles of intermediate acting insulin should be also be inspected for flocculation which is frosted whitish coating -​ Mixing insulins -​ Long acting insulins must be mixed thoroughly before drawing in the syringe -​ Regular insulin should be drawn first -​ Withdrawing insulin -​ Inject air into the bottle of insulin equivalent to the number of units of insulin to be withdrawn -​ Selecting and rotating the injection site -​ The four main areas for injection are abdomen, upper arm (posterior surface), thighs (anterior surface) and hips -​ The speed of absorption is greatest in the abdomen and decreases progressively in the arm, thighs and hips respectively -​ systemic rotation of injection within an anatomic area is recommended to prevent localized changes in fatty tissues (lipodystrophy) -​ Administer each injection 0.5-1 inch away from the previous injection. Another approach to rotation -​ Patient should try not to use the same site more than once in 2-3 weeks -​ Insulin should not be injected into the limb that will be exercised because this will cause the drug to be absorbed faster which may result to hypoglycemia -​ Preparing the skin -​ They should be cautioned to allow the skin to dry after cleansing with alcohol -​ The alcohol may be carried into the tissues, resulting in a localized reddened area and a burning sensation -​ Inserting the needle -​ For a normal or overweight person, a 90 degree angle is the best insertion angle -​ Aspiration is generally not recommended with self-injection of insulin
text.410: -​ Disposing of syringe and needles -​ used sharps should be placed in a puncture-resistant container Diabetes Mellitus Complications Hypoglycemia -​ Occurs when the blood glucose falls to less than 50-60 mg/dl (2.7 to 3.3 mmol/L) because of too much insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, too little food, or excessive physical activity -​ Clinical manifestions: -​ Mild -​ sweating -​ Tremor -​ tachycardia -​ Palpitation -​ nervousness -​ hunger -​ Moderate -​ Inability to concentrate -​ headache -​ Lightheadedness -​ confusion -​ memory lapses -​ Numbness of the lips and tongue -​ slurred speech -​ impaired coordination -​ Emotional changes -​ Irrational or combative behaviors -​ Double vision -​ Drowsiness -​ Severe -​ Patient needs the assistance of another person for treatment of hypoglycemia -​ Disoriented behavior -​ Seizures -​ Difficulty arousing from sleep -​ Loss of consciousness -​ Emergency measures: -​ Injection of glucagon 1mg (SQ or IM)
text.411: -​ A concentrated source of carbohydrate followed by a snack should be given to the patient on awakening -​ In hospitals and ED, for patients who are unconscious or cannot swallow, 25-50 ml of 50% dextrose in water (D50W) may be administered IV -​ Assuring patency of the IV line because (D50W) is very irritating to the veins -​ Taking additional food when physical activity is increased -​ Routine blood glucose tests are performed -​ Wear an identification bracelet or tag stating that they have diabetes -​ Learn to carry some form of simple sugar with them at all times -​ Refrain from eating high-calorie, high fat dessert foods Diabetes Ketoacidosis -​ caused by a sense or markedly inadequate amount of insulin. His deficit in available insulin results in disorders in the metabolism of carbohydrate, protein and fat -​ Hyperglycemia -​ dehydration and electrolyte loss -​ Acidosis -​ Clinical Manifestation: -​ Polyuria -​ polydipsia -​ blurred vision -​ Weakness -​ headache -​ orthostatic hypotension -​ Weak and rapid pulse -​ Anorexia -​ nausea and vomiting -​ abdominal pain -​ Acetone breath -​ Kussmaul’s respiration (rapid, deep breathing) -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ Blood glucose levels may vary between 300 and 800 mg/dl -​ serum bicarbonate (0-15 mEq/L) -​ Low pH (6.8 to 7.3) -​ A low partial pressure of carbon dioxide -​ PCO2: 10-30 mmHg -​ increased level of creatinine -​ Increased BUN -​ Increased hematocrit
text.412: -​ Management: -​ Rehydration -​ 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline solution) 0.65 to 1Uh for 2-3 hours -​ Half strength normal saline (0.45%) - hypernatremia -​ Monitoring fluid volume status -​ VS -​ Lung assessment -​ I&O -​ Plasma expanders - severe hypotension -​ Monitor signs of overload -​ Restoring electrolytes -​ serum potassium levels must be monitored frequently -​ As much as 40 mEq/h may be needed for several hours -​ Frequent (every 2-4 hours initially) ECGs and laboratory measurements of potassium are necessary -​ Because a patient’s serum potassium level may drop quickly as a result of rehydration and insulin treatment, potassium replacement must begin once potassium levels drop to normal -​ Reversing acidosis -​ Insulin is usually infused intravenously at a slow continuous rate -​ bicarbonate infusion to correct severe acidosis is avoided during the treatment of DKA because it precipitates further sudden decrease potassium levels -​ When mixing the insulin drip , it is important to flush the insulin solution through the entire IV infusion se and to discard the first 50 ml of fluid -​ Insulin molecules adhere to the inner surface surface of IV infusion sets, therefore the initial fluid may contain a decreased concentration of insulin Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar Nonketotic Syndrome (HHNS) -​ Serious condition in which hyperosmolarity and hyperglycemia predominate with alterations of the sensorium (sense of awareness) -​ Ketosis is usually minimal or absent -​ persistent hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis which results in losses of water and electrolytes -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Hypotension -​ Profound dehydration (dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor) -​ Tachycardia -​ Alteration in sensorium -​ Seizures -​ Hemiparesis -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ blood glucose - 600 to 1200 mg/dl -​ Osmolality exceeds 350 mOsm/kg -​ Management: -​ Fluid replacement -​ Correction of electrolyte imbalance -​ Insulin administration -​ fluid treatment is started with 0.9% or 0.45% NS -​ central venous or hemodynamic pressure monitoring -​ potassium is added to Iv fluids -​ Insulin plays less important role in the treatment of HHNS because it is not needed for reversal of acidosis Characteristic DKA HHNS Patient most commonly affected Can occur in type 1 or type2 ; more common in type 1 diabetes More common in type 2 diabetes especially elderly patients with type 2 diabetes Precipitating event Omission of insulin; physiologic stress (infection, surgery, CVA, MI) Physiologic stress (infection, surgery, CVA, MI) Onset Rapid (<24h) Slower (over several days) Blood glucose levels Usually >250 mg/dl (>3.9 mmol/L) Usually >600 mg/dl (>33.3 mmol/L) Arterial pH level 7.3 Normal Serum and urine ketones Present Absent Serum osmolality 300-350 mOsm/L >350 mOsm/L Plasma bicarbonate levels <15 mEq/L Normal BUN & Creatinine Elevated Elevated Mortality rate <5% 10-40% Gastroenterology Gastroenterology - a branch of medicine focused on the digestive system and its diseases Gastroenterology nursing - focuses on the care of patients with conditions affecting the gastrointestinal system including the stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas and related organs Gastrointestinal System Definition: 23-26 foot long pathway including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines, rectum and anus -​ Esophagus -​ Located in the mediastinum, anterior to the spine and posterior to the trachea -​ approximately 25 cm in length -​ Tube connecting the mouth and stomach -​ Stomach -​ Distensible pouch into which food bolus passes to be ingested by gastric enzymes -​ Hollow muscular organ with a capacity of approximately 1500ml -​ stores food during eating -​ Small intestine -​ Longest segment of the GI tract where the process of absorption of nutrients take place -​ Consisting of three parts: duodenum, jejunum and ileum -​ Large intestine -​ The portion of the GI tract into which waste materials from the small intestine passes as absorption continues and elimination begins -​ Consist of several parts: ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon and rectum Function of Digestive System -​ Digestion: occurs when the digestive enzymes and secretions mix with ingested food and when proteins, fats, and sugars are broken down into their component smaller molecules -​ Absorption: occurs when small molecules, vitamins, and minerals pass through the walls of the small and large intestine and into the bloodstream -​ Elimination: occurs after digestion and absorption, when waste products are evacuated from the body -​ Chewing and swallowing -​ 1st process of digestion -​ Approximately 1.5L of saliva is secreted daily from the parotid, the submaxillary, and the sublingual glands -​ Salivary amylase: an enzyme that begins the digestion of starches -​ Swallowing begins as a voluntary act that is regulated by the swallowing center in the medulla oblongata of the CNS -​ Gastric function -​ Secretes highly acidic fluid in response to the presence of anticipated ingestion of food (HCl) -​ Intrinsic factor: secreted by the gastric mucosa, combines with dietary vitamin B12 -​ Pepsin: an important enzyme for protein digestion; end product of the conversion of pepsinogen from the chief cells -​ Food remain in the stomach for variable length of time, from 30 minutes to several hours, depending on the volume, osmotic pressure, and chemical composition of gastric contents -​ Small intestine function -​ Secretions contain digestive enzymes -​ Amylase: aids in digesting starch -​ Lipase: aids in digesting fats -​ Trypsin: aids in digesting protein -​ Bile: aids in emulsifying ingested fats -​ secreted by the liver and stored in the gallbladder -​ Making them easier to digest and absorb -​ Intestinal secretions total approximately 1L/day of pancreatic juice, 0.5L/day of bile and 3L/day of secretions from gland of small intestine -​ Types of contractions in the small intestine -​ Segmentation contractions -​ produce mixing waves that move the intestinal contents back and forth in a churning motion -​ Intestinal peristalsis -​ Propels the contents of the small intestines toward the colon -​ Colonic function -​ Bacteria assist in completing the breakdown of waste materials especially undigested or unabsorbed proteins and bile salts -​ The slow weak peristaltic activity along the tract allows for efficient reabsorption of water and electrolytes which is the primary purpose of the colon -​ Intermittent, strong peristaltic waves propel the contents and eventually reach the rectum, usually in about 12 hours Physical Assessment Inspection, Auscultation, Percussion, Palpation (IAPePa) -​ Order of palpation -​ Right lower quadrant -​ Right upper quadrant -​ Left upper quadrant -​ Left lower quadrant Organs in specific places -​ Right hypochondriac -​ Right lobe of the liver -​ Gallbladder -​ Part of duodenum -​ Hepatic flexure of colon -​ Upper half of the right kidney -​ Suprarenal gland -​ Epigastric -​ Aorta -​ Pyloric end of stomach -​ Pancreas -​ Part of liver -​ Left hypochondriac -​ Stomach -​ spleen -​ Tail of pancreas -​ Splenic texture of the colon -​ upper half of left kidney -​ Suprarenal gland -​ Right lumbar -​ Ascending colon -​ Lower half of right kidney -​ Part of duodenum and jejunum -​ Umbilical -​ Omentum -​ Mesentery -​ Lower part of duodenum -​ Part of jejunum and ileum -​ Right inguinal -​ cecum -​ Appendix -​ lower end of ileum -​ Right ureter -​ right spermatic cord -​ Right ovary -​ Hypogastric -​ Ileum -​ Bladder (if enlarged) -​ Uterus (if enlarged) -​ Left inguinal -​ Sigmoid colon -​ Left ureter -​ Left spermatic cord -​ Left ovary Diagnostic Studies -​ Upper GI series -​ Delineates the entire GI tract after the introduction of contrast agent (Barium swallow) -​ Enables the examiner to detect or exclude anatomic or functional derangement of the upper GI organs or sphincters -​ Also aids in the diagnosis of ulcers, varices, tumors, regional enteritis and malabsorption syndromes -​ Nursing interventions: -​ Clear liquid diet with NPO from midnight the night before the study -​ Smoking, chewing gum and mints can stimulate gastric motility so the nurse advises against these practices -​ Increase fluid intake to facilitate evacuation of stool and the radiopaque liquid -​ Typically, oral medications are withheld on the morning of the study and resumed that evening but each patient’s medication regimen is evaluated on an individual basis -​ Lower GI series -​ Visualization of the lower GI tract -​ with introduction of barium enema -​ The procedure usually takes about 15 minutes to 30 minutes during which time x-ray images are obtained -​ The patient must be assessed for allergy to iodine or contrast agent -​ Nursing intervention: -​ Emptying and cleansing the lower bowel prior to the procedure -​ Low residue diet 1-2 days before the test -​ clear liquid diet, NPO after midnight; and cleansing enemas until returns to clear the following morning -​ Laxative is given before and after the procedure -​ Increased fluid intake after the procedure -​ Evaluation of bowel movement for evacuation of barium -​ Esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD) -​ Direct visualization of esophageal, gastric and duodenal mucosa through a lighted endoscope -​ After the patient is sedated, the endoscope is lubricated with a water-soluble lubricant and passed smoothly and slowly along the back of the mouth and down into the esophagus -​ The procedure usually takes about 30 minutes -​ The patient may experience nausea, gagging and choking -​ Use of topical anesthetic agents and moderate sedation makes it important to monitor and maintain the patient’s oral airway during and after the procedure -​ Precautions must be taken to protect the scope, because the fiberoptic bundles can be broken if the scope is bent at an acute angle -​ Nursing interventions: -​ The patient should be NPO for 8 hours prior to the examination -​ before the introduction of the endoscope, the patient is given a local anesthetic gargle or spray -​ Midazolam (Versed) a sedative that provides moderate sedation and relieves anxiety during the procedure -​ Atropine may be administered to reduce secretions and glucagon may be administered to relax smooth muscle -​ The patient is positioned left lateral position to facilitate clearance of pulmonary secretions and provide smooth entry of the scope -​ After gastroscopy, assessment includes LOC, VS, oxygen saturation, pain level -​ Monitor signs of perforation such as pain, bleeding, unusual difficulty of swallowing, rapidly elevated temperature -​ After the patient’s gag reflex has returned, lozenges, saline gargle and oral analgesics agents may be offered to relieve minor throat discomfort -​ Patients who were sedated for the procedure must remain in bed until fully alert -​ Endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography (ERCP) -​ Visualization of the common bile duct, the pancreatic, hepatic duct, through the ampulla of vater in the duodenum -​ Uses the endoscope in combination with x-ray techniques to view the ductal structures of the biliary tracts -​ Colonoscopy -​ Direct visual inspection of the large intestine -​ Therapeutically, the procedure can be used to remove all visible polyps with a special snare and cautery through the colonoscope -​ Laparoscopy -​ Direct visualization of the organs and structures within the abdomen, permitting visualization and identification of an growths, anomalies and inflammatory processes -​ A pneumoperitoneum (injecting carbon dioxide into the peritoneal cavity to separate the intestines from the pelvic organs) is created -​ Biopsy samples can be taken from the structures and organs as necessary -​ Laparoscopy usually requires general anesthesia and sometimes requires that the stomach and bowel decompressed
text.419: Gastrointestinal Disorders Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) -​ Excessive backflow of gastric and duodenal contents into the esophagus due to incompetent lower esophageal sphincter -​ Causes: -​ Weak LES (lower esophageal sphincter/cardia) - smooth muscle -​ Slow motility -​ Pyloric stenosis -​ Pyloric sphincter -​ Open: Gastric emptying (2-5 hours after meals) -​ Close: Food intake -​ Clinical manifestations: “Indigestion burns throat, larynx and esophagus” -​ Burning sensation (pyrosis/heartburn) - commonly after meal and in the evening -​ Dyspepsia (Nausea, vomiting, stomach, bloating) -​ Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) -​ Odinophagia (painful swallowing) -​ Globus (feeling of fullness in the throat; lump) -​ Laryngitis (hoarseness, dry cough) -​ Note: the symptoms may mimic those of heart attack -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ Endoscopy -​ Visualize the esophageal lining (check for inflammation) -​ Can also to take biopsy (barret’s esophagus) -​ Normal: squamous cells -​ Abnormal: columnar epithelial cells (intestine) - increased risk of esophageal cancer -​ Pre-procedure: NPO (prevent aspiration) -​ Post-procedure: WOF: bleeding (frequent swallowing) & perforation -​ Esophageal pH monitoring (probe) -​ Measures amount and frequency of acid reflux -​ Normal esophageal pH: >4 or slightly acidic -​ GERD: 24 hours -​ Confirmation: total of 58 minutes of exposure to acid (<4 pH) -​ Barium Swallow: barium sulfate (X-ray) -​ Evaluates anatomical abnormalities (weak LES) -​ Pre-procedure: assess for allergies, kidney function (creatinine 0.6-1.2 & BUN 10-20), NPO -​ Post-procedure: increased OFI (2000-3000 ml for 24 hours), white stool (normal for 24-72 hours after the procedure) -​ Management: “Food should go down” -​ Pharmacologic -​ Antacids “carbonate/hydroxide” -​ Neutralize pH -​ Examples: aluminum hydroxide -​ H2 receptors antagonist “tidine” -​ Decreases amount of HCl produced by stomach by blocking action of histamine receptors of parietal cells in the stomach -​ Example: ranitidine -​ Proton pump inhibitors “zole/prazole” -​ Decrease gastric acid secretion by slowing the ATpase pump on the surface of the parietal cells -​ Examples: omeprazole -​ Prokinetic agents -​ Enhancing colonic transit by increasing propulsive motor activity -​ Example: metoclopramide -​ Nursing intervention -​ Diet: -​ Fluids: in between meals (lessens abdominal distention) -​ Fiber: high (delays gastric emptying -> increases satiety (feeling of fullness) -> prevents overeating) -​ Meal: small frequent feedings (6-10 meals per day) -​ Position: -​ HOB: elevated at least 30-45 degrees -​ Turned to: left side lying -​ Avoid: -​ Coffee (relaxes LES) -​ Citrus fruits (naturally acidic) -​ Cigarette (nicotine - increases HCl; decreases saliva production) -​ Carbonated drinks (causes abdominal distention) -​ Chocolate (theobromine - muscle relaxant -> relaxes LES) -​ Alcohol (irritates esophagus) -​ Fatty foods (slowest food to digest) -​ Peppermint (muscle relaxant) -​ Spicy foods (worsens the signs of symptoms of GERD particularly the heartburn) -​ Increases intra-abdominal pressure -​ Straining (valsalva maneuver) -​ Tight fitting clothes -​ Heavy lifting -​ Bending below the waist -​ Drugs: decreased motility and increased HCl -​ Aspirin (increases HCl) -​ NSAIDs (inhibits prostaglandin synthesis -> decreased mucus) -​ Anti-cholinergic/Antispasmodics (decreases motility) -​ CCB (smooth muscle relaxant) -​ Surgical management -​ Nissen fundoplication: most common -​ Stomach wraps fully around esophagus -​ Dor fundoplication -​ Stomach wraps around the front of esophagus -​ Toupet fundoplication
text.422: -​ Stomach wraps around the back of esophagus Barrett’s Esophagus -​ A condition in which the lining of the esophageal mucosa is altered -​ Associated with GERD -​ Reflux causes causes changes in the lining of the lower esophagus -​ The cells that are laid to cover the exposed area no longer squamous in origin -​ Precursor to esophageal cancer -​ Clinical manifestations -​ Burning sensation in the esophagus (pyrosis) -​ Dyspepsia -​ Dysphagia -​ Hypersalivation -​ Esophagitis -​ Diagnostic test -​ Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) -​ Biopsy -​ Management -​ Photodynamic therapy - laser thermal ablation; destroy the metaplastic cells -​ Esophagectomy - total resection of the esophagus with the removal of the tumor plus wide tumor=free margin of the esophagus and the lymph nodes in the area Hiatal Hernia/Diaphragmatic Hernia -​ The opening in the diaphragm through which the esophagus passes becomes enlarged and part of the upper stomach tends to move up into the lower portion of the thorax -​ Most common structure: gastroesophageal junction - connects the esophagus to the stomach -​ Factor: -​ Increases intra-abdominal pressure -​ Pregnancy -​ Ascites -​ obesity -​ tumor -​ Types -​ Sliding - upper stomach and the gastroesophageal junction are slide displaced upward to the esophagus -​ Most common -​ May be asymptomatic -​ GERD-like symptoms
text.423: -​ Paraesophageal/Rolling - all or part of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm beside the esophagus, gastroesophageal junction stays in place -​ Rare -​ May be asymptomatic -​ (-) GERD-like symptoms -​ Fundus = herniates next to the esophagus -​ Feeling of fullness -​ Complications: strangulation -> decreased blood flow -> necrosis -​ Clinical manifestation -​ Heartburn -​ Regurgitation -​ Dysphagia -​ Sense of fullness after eating or chest pain -​ Diagnostic tests -​ Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) - confirmatory test -​ X-ray studies -​ Barium swallow -​ Fluoscopy -​ Management -​ Pharmacologic -​ Same pharmacological management with GERD -​ Nursing Intervention -​ Small frequent feeding -​ Patient is advised not to recline for 1 hour after eating -​ Elevate HOB -​ Surgery is indicated in about 15% of patients -​ Surgical: Fundoplication (reinforce LES) -​ Nissen fundoplication: most common -​ Stomach wraps fully around esophagus -​ Dor fundoplication -​ Stomach wraps around the front of esophagus -​ Toupet fundoplication -​ Stomach wraps around the back of esophagus Gastritis -​ Inflammation of the stomach lining or gastric mucosa -​ Causes -​ Food: highly seasoned -​ Medications: overuse of aspirin and other NSAIDS (aspirin/NSAID-induced gastritis) -​ Vices: excessive alcohol intake, smoking -​ Disease: gastric ulcer -​ Therapy: radiation and chemo - localized inflammation -​ Substance: ingestion of strong acid or alkali -​ Infection: bacteria (helicobacter pylori) -​ Types: -​ Acute - sudden inflammation -​ Hiccups -​ Epigastric pain -​ Anorexia -​ Dyspepsia -​ WOF: bleeding - emergency -​ Chronic - repeated inflammation resulting to formation of scars that destroys parietal cells -​ Halitosis (bad breath due to growth of bacteria) -​ Reflux -​ Sour taste -​ Early satiety -​ Anorexia -​ Epigastric pain -​ WOF: pernicious anemia (vitamin B12 deficiency) -​ Assessment and Diagnostic test -​ Achlorhydria or hypochlorhydria (absence or low levels of HCl) -​ Can be determined by an upper GI series or endoscopy -​ Tissue specimen (Biopsy) -​ Management -​ Acute: bleeding (rest the GI) -​ 1st: NPO to facilitate healing -​ 2nd: ice chips, liquid diet, solid food -​ Diet: bland - decreases HCl -​ Pharmacologic (same to PUD) -​ H2 blockers -​ Antibiotics -​ PPI -​ Antacid -​ Cytoprotective -​ Supplements: Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) -​ Avoid causes/factors -​ Surgical
text.425: -​ Gastrojejunostomy - anastomosis of jejunum to stomach to detour around the pylorus Peptic Ulcer Disease -​ Excavation that forms in the mucosa wall of the stomach, in the pylorus or in the duodenum -​ Factors: -​ Stress (chronic) -> PNS -> vagus nerves -> ACTH -> stimulates parietal, enterochromaffin & G-cells -> increases acid secretion -​ Drinks -​ Caffeinated & decaffeinated -> coffee beans -> roasted -> peptide -> increase HCl production -​ Vices -​ Smoking -​ Alcohol -​ Drugs -​ Aspirin -​ NSAIDs -​ Infection -​ H. Pyloric (raw meat) - most common cause -​ Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome - consists of severe peptic ulcers, extreme gastric hyperacidity, and gastrin-secreting benign or malignant tumors -​ Diagnostic Test -​ Upper endoscopy - direct visualization of GIT (inflammation & ulcers) -​ Serum test - detects antibodies to H. Pyloric -​ Fecal Occult Blood Test (FOBT) - detects duodenal ulcer -> hidden blood in stool -​ Urea Breath Test - ingest urea + specialized carbon isotope, collection bag (blows air) = labeled CO2 -​ If H. Pyloric is present: breaks down ingested agents = ammonia & labeled CO2 -​ Types: -​ Gastric ulcer -​ Pain triggered by food intake (persistent gnawing pain) -​ Pain relieved by vomiting with hematemesis (vomitus + blood_ -​ Duodenal ulcer -​ Pain triggered by gastric emptying (burning pain) -​ Pain relieved by food intake with melena (old blood in stool) Gastric Ulcer Duodenal Ulcer EpigastricPain Gnawing Burning Time Food intake Gastric emptying Relief of Pain Vomiting Food intake Bleeding Hematemesis Melena -​ Management: “stomach distention is directly proportional to HCl production” -​ Pharmacologic -​ H2 blockers - reduce HCl production “tidine” -​ Time: before meals (onset: 90 minutes) -​ Ranitidine -​ Antibiotics - kills the H. pylori -​ Combined with PPI (reduced HCl) + bismuth (increased mucus) subsalicylate (decreased inflammation) - ex. Pepto Bismol -​ 2 antibiotics: tetracycline & metronidazole DOC -​ Amoxicillin & clarithromycin -​ PPI - reduce HCl production “zole, prazole” -​ Time: 30 minutes before meals -​ Omeprazole -​ Antacid - neutralizes pH “carbonate/hydroxide” -​ Time: 1-2 hours after meals -​ Sodium bicarbonate - S/E: metabolic alkalosis -​ Calcium carbonate - S/E: hypercalcemia, constipation -​ Aluminum hydroxide - S/E: constipation -​ Magnesium hydroxide - S/E: diarrhea -​ Note: Aluminum and Magnesium hydroxide can be taken together to decrease side effects -​ Do not drink water for 30 minutes for effectivity -​ Gastric protestants/Cytoprotectants - creates a viscous substance in the presence of gastric acid that forms a protective barrier, binding to the surface of the ulcer and prevents digestion of pepsin -​ Sucralfate - provides gastric barrier -​ Time: before meals -​ Misoprostol - protaglandin analogue -> increases mucus production -​ Time: with meals -​ CI: pregnant women (can cause abortion) -​ Cytotec - dilates cervix -​ Surgical -​ Vagotomy - transecting nerves (vagus nerve) that stimulate acid secretion Gastrectomy - removal of stomach
text.427: -​ Total: removal of esophagus to small intestine -​ Subtotal/antrectomy: removal of lower portion of stomach -​ Anatomosis - reconnecting/reattaching -​ Billroth I (Gastroduodenostomy) - removal of the lower portion of the antrum of the stomach as well as the small portion of duodenum segment; upper portion of the stomach anastomosed to duodenum (surgery of choice) -​ Billroth II (Gastrojejunostomy) - removal of lower portion (antrum) of the stomach with anastomosis to jejunum; a duodenal stump remains and is oversewn -​ Nursing intervention -​ Meal: small frequent feeding -​ Diet: -​ Active phase: “painful” -> bland -> reduced HCl -​ Chew slowly and thoroughly -​ Milk restricted/limit (200-400 ml/day) -​ Avoid factors Dumping Syndrome -​ Partially the result of rapid gastric emptying, which prevents adequate mixing with the pancreatic and biliary secretions -​ It is an unpleasant set of GI symptoms that sometimes occur in patients who have gastric surgery or a form of vagotomy -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Large amount of foods -> increased concentration of food -> vasodilation -> fluids (fluid shifting) -​ -> small intestine -> increased fluid volume -​ -> decreased blood volume -> shock-like symptoms -​ Early: 5-30 minutes after meals -​ Rapid gastric emptying -> increased absorption -> elevated glucose -> pancreas -> increased insulin -> postprandial hypoglycemia -​ Late: 1-2 hours after meals -​ Clinical manifestations -​ Small intestine - increased fluids -​ Distended abdomen -​ Borborygmi sound -​ Diarrhea -​ Nausea and vomiting -​ Shock-like symptoms
text.428: -​ Pallor -​ Hypotension -​ Tachycardia -​ Hypoglycemia -​ Weakness -​ Diaphoresis -​ Lightheadedness -​ Management “food should stay” -​ Nursing intervention -​ Diet: -​ Protein: high (3-4 hours after meals) -​ Fiber: high (delays gastric emptying), if with diarrhea: low -​ Carbohydrate: low (1-2 hours after meals) -​ Meals: SFF -​ Fluids: in between -​ Avoid: concentrated foods (sweet, salty, milk and coffee) -​ Position: supine (lie down after meals for 20-30 minutes - to delay gastric emptying) -​ Pharmacologic -​ Medications: anti-cholinergic/antispasmodic - reduced motility -​ Vitamin B12: given IM monthly to prevent loss of intrinsic factor (produced by parietal cells) -​ Intrinsic factor helps absorbs vitamin B12 Diverticular Disease -​ A sac-like herniation of the lining that of the bowel that extends through a defect in the muscle layer -​ Commonly occurred in the sigmoid colon (LLQ) -​ Types: -​ Diverticulosis - multiple diverticula (outpouching) are present without inflammation or symptoms -​ Cause: low fiber intake = constipation -​ Diagnostic: colonoscopy -​ Diverticulitis - results when food and bacteria retained in a diverticulum produce infection; diverticulosis with inflammation; alternating diarrhea (active phase) and chronic constipation -​ Cause: increased in bacterial growth -​ Diagnostics: abdominal CT scan with contrast dye/medium - to detect peritonitis -​ Clinical manifestations
text.429: -​ Inflammation: -​ Cramping abdominal pain at LLQ -​ Infection -​ Fever, increased WBC -​ Injury - possibility of rupture of diverticula -​ Hematochezia (fresh blood in the stool) -​ Obstruction - increased in gas formation -​ Bloating or flatulence -​ Management -​ Diverticulosis: constipation -​ Fiber diet: high -​ Fluid intake: high -​ Medication: laxatives/lactulose -​ Diverticulitis: constipation & active phase (diarrhea) -​ Fiber: high, low -​ Fluid: high, high -​ Monitor for: peritonitis (rigid/board-like abdomen), paralytic ileus (no bowel sound, movement, flatus) -​ Medication: laxatives, anti-diarrheal (loperamide) Appendicitis -​ Inflammation of appendix (RLQ) -​ Causes: -​ Fecalith/fecal obstruction -​ Ruptured appendicitis: -​ Increased peristalsis -​ increased intra-abdominal pressure -​ Vasodilation -> increased blood flow -> increased swelling & edema -​ Diagnostics: ultrasound & CT scan -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ McBurney's sign/point: pain ⅓ from the iliac region -​ Rovsing’s sign: palpation in the LLQ will cause pain in the RLQ -​ Dunphy’s sign: pain triggered by coughing -​ Blumberg’s sign: rebound tenderness -​ Psoas sign : pain on passive extension of the right thigh -​ Obturator sign: eliciting pain on passive internal rotation of the hip with the knee flexed -​ WBC: high -​ Bowel sound: decreased or absent (late sign) -​ Absent - ruptured -> paralytic ileus, no pain
text.430: -​ Fever: present -​ Management -​ Suspected appendicitis -​ (-) analgesics - it will mask the pain or rupture -​ Decreased GI activity (NPO, bed rest) -​ Avoid causes of rupture -​ (+) cold compress -​ (-) hot compress -​ Position: low/semi-fowler’s - minimized movement -> decreased peristalsis -​ Diagnosed appendicitis -​ (+) analgesics -​ Surgery: Appendectomy -​ Laparoscopic (closed) -​ Laparotomy (open) -​ If there is an abscess: delay the surgery -> to avoid sepsis -​ Drain the abscess first -> continue the surgery -​ Post-operative: -​ Position: High fowlers - decreased tension incision -> decreased pain -​ Medication: morphine -​ Fluids: 1st 24 hours - IV -​ Foods: return of bowel movement/peristalsis (passage of flatus) & gag reflex (to prevent aspiration) -​ Ambulation: day of the surgery (1 day post op) Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) -​ Functional disorder (organs are not functioning but during diagnostic tests all are normal) -​ Cause: idiopathic -​ Factor: stress -> visceral hypersensitivity -> increased pain in normal GIT activity (food intake, peristalsis, defecation) -​ Types: -​ IBS-C: constipation -​ IBS-D: diarrhea -​ IBS-M: mixed -​ IBS-U: unidentified -​ Assessment: -​ Abdominal pain related to/associated with: -​ Change in frequency and appearance (Bristol stool chart) -​ Defecation: before and during -​ Common complain: -​ Abdominal -​ Pain -​ Triggered: food intake -> reristalsis (GIT activity) -​ Relieved defecation (no GIT activity) -​ Distention -​ Management: -​ Avoid stress -​ Diet: -​ Fiber: IBS- C - high; IBS-D: low -​ Food diary: to avoid triggers -​ Fluids: in between meals -​ Low-FODMaP (foods that can cause bloating/diarrhea and ferments in the colon causing gas formation/discomfort) -​ Fermentable Oligosaccharide (gas-forming) -​ Disaccharides (lactose/milk) -​ Monosaccharides (high fructose) -​ Polyols (stone fruits -> sugar alcohol -> poorly absorbed) -​ Pharmacologic -​ Antispamodic: decreases motility -​ Dicyclomine -​ Peppermint oil -​ Diarrhea (IBS-D) -​ Aldosteron -​ Constipation (IBS-C)
text.432: -​ Lubiprostone -​ Probiotics - decrease gas, diarrhea Hemorrhoids -​ Swollen, enlarged veins that form inside and outside the anus and rectum -​ Causes: -​ Straining -​ Dilation of varicosed veins (enlarged/swollen) -​ Portal hypertension -​ Increased in intra-abdominal pressure (at risk pregnant women) -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Increased venous pressure -> congestion of blood -> increased anorectal pressure -​ Two types: -​ External: below anal sphincter, visible upon inspection -​ Internal: above anal sphincter -​ Manifestations -​ Pain -​ Itching -> swelling of BV -> irritation of nerve endings -> triggers itching sensation -​ Bleeding upon defecation (bright red) -​ External: thrombosis -​ -> congestion of blood -> stasis of blood -> clots/thrombus -​ Internal: painless unless it prolapse -​ Management: -​ Good personal hygiene -​ Avoid straining upon defecation (internal -> causes prolapse) -​ Regular bowel movement -​ Increased fiber -​ increased fluids -​ Ambulation/exercise -​ Comfort/reduced engorgement -​ Sitz bath (after bath/defecation) -​ Cold compress (external hemorrhoids) -​ Pharmacologic -​ Hydrophilic bulk-forming agents (stool softeners) -​ Psyllium husk -​ Analgesics ointment - topical -​ Lidocaine -​ Suppositories - prevent straining upon defecation -​ Astringents - dehydrates hemorrhoids -​ Witch hazel -​ Surgery -​ Sclerotherapy - inject sclerosing agent (Phenol) to the dilated veins/tissue -​ shrink and hardening of hemorrhoids preventing prolapse -​ Rubber band ligation - application of rubber band in hemorrhoids -> decreases blood flow -> necrosis -> detaches itself -​ Stapled Hemorrhoidopexy - surgically staples prolapsed hemorrhoids -​ Hemorrhoidectomy - removal of hemorrhoids; indicated only if all of the conservative treatment are not working -​ Post-operative intervention: -​ Position: side lying/prone - decrease anal pressure -​ Ice packs: 1st 24 hours = vasoconstriction -> decreases bleeding -​ Sitz bath: temperature 31-41C, frequency: 3-4 times daily, duration: max of 20 mins to prevent burns -​ Avoid: prolonged sitting -> increased anal pressure -​ Stool softener: psyllium husk/docusate sodium (safe to pregnant women) Hepatobiliary Hepatobiliary nursing - focuses on the care and support of patients with disorders affecting the liver, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas and duodenum Hepatobiliary System -​ Liver
text.434: -​ Largest gland of the body -​ Divided into four lobes -​ Right -​ Left -​ Caudate -​ Quadrate -​ Contains several cell types including hepatocytes and Kupffer’s cells -​ Regulating blood glucose level by making glycogen which is stored in hepatocytes -​ Converting ammonia produced from gluconeogenetic by-products and bacteria to urea -​ Gall bladder -​ Pear-shaped organ attached to the liver under the right lobe -​ Normally holds 30-50 ml of bile and can hold up to 70 ml when fully distended -​ Pancreas -​ A slender, fish-shaped organ that lies horizontally in the abdomen behind the stomach and extends roughly from the duodenum to the spleen -​ Endocrine and exocrine functions has pancreatic juice: -​ Amylase -​ Lipase -​ Trypsin Hepatobiliary Disorders Hepatitis -​ Inflammatory disorder of the liver parenchyma -​ Occuring in Hepatitis A, B, C, D, E and toxic or drug-induced hepatitis -​ Hepatocellular damage results from the body’s immune response to the virus or toxin and is characaterized by diffuse inflammatory infiltration with local necrosis -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Pre-icteric stage -​ Earliest symptoms are not specific -​ Flu-like symptoms -​ Malaise -​ Fatigue -​ Heache -​ Myalgias -​ Anorexia -​ Nausea and vomiting -​ Diarrhea -​ Icteric stage -​ Few days to weeks after pre-icteric stage -​ Jaundice -​ Dark-colored urine -​ Light-colored stool -​ Steatorrhea -​ Enlarged liver -​ Post-icteric stage -​ Convalescent stage lasting a few weeks -​ Fatigue decreases -​ Appetite returns Viral Hepatitis Mode of Transmission Incubation Outcome Hepatitis A Fecal-oral route 15-50 days Usually mild with recovery Hepatitis B Parenterally; perinatal: sexual 28-160 days May be severe Hepatitis C Blood transfusion: sexual transmission 15-160 days Frequent occurrence of chronic hepatic cancer carrier state and chronic liver disease Hepatitis D Parenterally; perinatal: sexual 21-140 days May be severe but greater likelihood of carrier state Hapatitis E Fecal-oral route 15-65 days Usually mild with recovery except severe in pregnant women -​ Diagnostic tests: -​ Liver function test results are elevated -​ Serum bilirubin level is increased -​ Urinalysis reveals increased bilirubin levels -​ Management: -​ Administer prescribed medications which may include: -​ Immunoglobulins -​ Immunization -​ Antiviral -​ Prevent transmission of infection -​ Promote adequate rest without complications
text.436: -​ Encourage proper nutrition Liver Cirrhosis -​ Chronic liver disease marked by diffuse destruction and fibrotic regeneration of hepatic cells -​ Classification: -​ Laennec’s cirrhosis -​ Commonly caused by alcoholism and chronic nutritional deficiences -​ Biliary cirrhosis -​ Caused by bile duct disorders that suppress bile flow -​ Post-hepatic cirrhosis -​ Caused by various types of hepatitis -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Enlarged, firm liver -​ Chronic dyspepsia -​ Constipation or diarrhea -​ Gradual weight loss -​ Ascites -​ Splenomegaly -​ Spider telangiectasis -​ Caput medusae -​ Dilated abdominal blood vessels -​ Portal hypertension -​ Mental deterioration -​ Laboratory and Diagnostic findings: -​ Liver biopsy -​ Liver scan -​ Liver function test (ALT, AST) -​ Serum protein levels -​ Prothrombin time -​ Management: -​ Administer diuretics to decrease ascites -​ Promote adequate nutrition (vitamins and nutritional supplements to promote healing of damaged liver cells) -​ Prevent threats to skin integrity -​ Minimize risk of bleeding -​ Antacid/H2 antagonist to minimize possibility of GI bleeding -​ Limit visitors and orient the client to date, time and place -​ Avoid drinking alcoholic beverages -​ Institute safety measures such as raising side rails and assisting ambulation
text.437: -​ Diet: -​ Early phase: high protein diet to promote healing of the liver -​ Late phase: low protein diet to decrease ammonia levels Portal Hypertension -​ Elevated pressure in the portal vein associated with increased resistance to blood flow through the portal venous system -​ Obstruction of portal venous flow through the liver lead to: -​ Formation of esophageal and hemorrhoidal varicosities due to: -​ Increased venous pressure -​ Accumulation of fluid in the abdominal cavity -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Ascites -​ Rapid weight gain -​ Shortness of breathing -​ Fluid wave on abdominal percussion -​ Liver dullness -​ Dilated abdominal vessels radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae) -​ Enlarged, palpable spleen -​ Fluid and electrolyte imbalance -​ Management: -​ Bed rest -​ Administering medications which may include diuretics -​ Measure and record abdominal girth and body weight daily -​ Promote measures to prevent or reduce edema -​ Assist the health care provided with paracentesis -​ Monitor serum ammonia and electrolyte levels Esophageal Varices -​ Hemorrhagic process involving dilated, tortuous veins in the submucosa of the lower esophagus -​ Caused by portal hypertension -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Hematemesis and melena -​ Massive hemorrhage occurs -​ Signs of hepatic encephalopathy -​ Dilated abdominal veins -​ Ascites -​ History of alcohol abuse
text.438: -​ Diagnostic and laboratory tests: -​ Endoscopy -​ AST, ALT, Bilirubin (increased) -​ Portal hypertension measurements -​ Management: -​ Assess for ecchymosis, epistaxis, petechiae, and bleeding gums -​ Monitor level of consciousness, VS, urinary output to evaluate fluid balance -​ Monitor client during blood transfusion -​ Provide nursing care for client undergoing prescribed tamponade to control bleeding -​ Sengstaken-Blakemore Tube -​ Four openings: -​ Gastric aspirations -​ Esophageal aspiration -​ Gastric balloon inflation -​ Esophageal balloon inflation -​ The instrument at the bedside: scissors (cut the tube in case of respiratory distress) -​ The patient being treated with balloon tamponade must remain under close observation in the ICU because of the risk of serious take complications -​ Precautions must be taken to ensure that the patient not pull on or inadvertently displace the tube -​ Vasopressin - initial mode of therapy -​ Sclerotherapy - after treatment for acute hemorrhage, the patient must be observed for bleeding, perforation of the esophagus, aspiration pneumonia, and esophageal stricture -​ Variceal band ligation -​ A modified endoscope loaded with an elastic rubber band is passed through a band directly on the varix (or varices) to be banded -​ Complications: -​ Superficial ulceration -​ Dysphagia -​ Transient chest discomfort -​ Esophageal stricture Hepatic Encephalopathy -​ Neurologic syndrome that develops as a complication of liver disease -​ It may be acute and self-limiting and progressing or chronic -​ Incidence is similar to cirrhosis due to: -​ Severe liver damage -​ Hepatocellular failure -​ Increased serum ammonia levels from: -​ GI bleeding -​ High protein diet -​ Bacterial growth in the intestine -​ Uremia -​ Pathophysiology: -​ Hepatic insufficiency -> inability to detoxify toxic by-product of metabolism (ammonia) -> ammonia enters the brain -> excites peripheral benzodiazepine-type receptors on astrocyte cells -> stimulates GABA -> depression of CNS -> Encephalopathy -​ Clinical manifestations: -​ Neurological dysncfunction progressing from minor aberrations and motor disturbances to coma -​ Flapping tremors/liver flap (asterixis) -​ The patient is asked to hold the arm out with the hand held upward (dorsiflexed).
