benchmark against which to plan, to implement and assess quality of services -​ Negligence -​ Refers to the commission or omission of an act, pursuant to a duty, that a reasonably prudent person in the same or similar circumstance would or would not do, and acting or the non-acting of which is the proximate cause of injury to another person or his property -​ Elements -​ Existence of duty -​ Failure to meet the standard of due care/breach of duty -​ Foreseeability of harm/proximate cause -​ Injury of the plaintiff -​ Specific examples -​ Failure to report observations to attending physicians -​ Failure to exercise the degree of diligence which the circumstances of the particular case demands -​ Mistaken identity -​ Wrong medicine, wrong concentration, wrong route, wrong dose -​ Defects in the equipment such as stretchers, and wheelchairs may lead to falls thus injuring the patients -​ 3 conditions to establish negligence without proving specific conduct -​ Injury was of nature that it would not normally occur unless there was a negligent act -​ Injury was caused by an agency within control of the defendant -​ Plaintiff himself do not engage in any matter that would tend to bring about the injury -​ Malpractice -​ Improper or unskillful care of a patient by a nurse; also denotes stepping beyond one’s authority with serious consequences -​ Term for negligence of professional personnel (professional negligence) -​ Used properly only when it refers to a negligent act committed in the course of professional performance -​ Incompetence -​ Lack of ability, or legal qualifications and being unfit to discharge the required duty -​ Types of Incompetence -​ Gross Incompetence – A serious lack of knowledge, skill, or judgment that endangers a patient’s safety. -​ Professional Incompetence – Failure to meet the standards of practice expected of a nurse. -​ Technical Incompetence – Inability to properly perform nursing procedures or use equipment safely. -​ Moral or Ethical Incompetence – Failure to uphold ethical principles or professional values in nursing practice. -​ Doctrine: -​ Force Majeure -​ An irresistible force, one that is unforeseen or inevitable -​ Respondeat Superior -​ Let the master answer for the acts of the subordinate -​ Liability is shared between the employee and employer; not a shift of liability from the subordinate to the master -​ Captain of the ship: Surgeon -​ Res Ipsa Loquitor -​ The thing speaks for itself -​ Means that the injury could not have happened, if someone was not negligent that no further proof is required -​ Elements: -​ Injury will not normally occur unless negligence -​ Agency/Instrumentality within the control of the defendant/nurse -​ Patient did not participate Consent to Medical and Surgical Procedures -​ Consent -​ Free and rational act that presupposes knowledge of the thing to which consent is being given by a person who is legally capable to give consent -​ Must be obtained from the patient or his authorized representative who may be his parent or guardian -​ In case of emergency: consent is waived; consent does not apply -​ Nature -​ Nurse secures consent of the patient upon admission -​ Physician obtains the consent -​ To substantiate the patient’s consent, a written consent form is needed as proof against any liability -​ Elements -​ Diagnosis and explanation of the condition -​ Fair explanation of the procedures to be done and used and the consequences -​ Description of alternative treatments or procedures -​ Description of the benefits to be expected -​ Material rights if any -​ Prognosis, if the recommended care, procedure is refused -​ Proof of consent -​ Consent form is signed to show that the person consents and he/she understands the nature of the procedure, the risks involved and the possible consequences -​ Who must consent? -​ Minor -​ Parents or someone standing in their behalf -​ If the minor is married or otherwise emancipated, parental consent is not needed -​ Mentally ill -​ Parents or legal guardian -​ Emergency situation -​ No consent is necessary because the inaction at such time may cause greater injury -​ Implied consent -​ Consent for sterilization -​ Husband and wife, if the operation is primarily to accomplish sterilization -​ Patient alone, if only because of medical necessity and the sterilization is an incidental result Medical Records -​ Purposes -​ Saves duplication in future cases and aids in prompt treatment -​ Supplies rich material for medical and nursing research -​ Serves as a legal protection for the hospital, doctor and nurse by reflecting the disease or condition of the patient and his management -​ Remember -​ If it was not charted, it was not observed or done -​ Nurses’ notes -​ Should be written, fully, accurately, legibly, and promptly -​ Not only includes medications and treatments but also physical and emotional symptoms exhibited by the patient -​ Aids to medical diagnosis and in understanding the patient’s behavior -​ Nurses’ role -​ Safeguarding the patient’s record from loss or destruction or from access by persons who are not legally authorized to read such -​ Medical records in legal proceedings -​ It is usually the medical records librarian, by virtue of a subpoena duces tecum, who testifies that the patients’ records are kept and protected from unauthorized handling and change Advance Directives -​ Living will: directive given by the patient as to type of treatment he wants to receive if and when he gets into respiratory arrest -​ Durable power of attorney or health care proxy: when the patient legally assigns a person, who will decide in his behalf for his treatment Crimes, Misdemeanors and Felonies -​ Crime: defined as an act committed or omitted in violation of the law -​ Elements -​ Criminal act -​ Evil/criminal intent -​ Conspiracy -​ Principal -​ Direct part in the execution of the act -​ Directly force or induce others to commit it -​ Mastermind of a crime: principal by inducement -​ Accomplice -​ Cooperates in the execution of the offense by previous or simultaneous act -​ Had knowledge of the criminal intention of the principal -​ Accessory -​ Have knowledge of the commission of the crime -​ Take part subsequent to its commission by profiting themselves or assisting the offender to profit from the effects if the crime -​ Provides the exit strategy -​ Felony -​ Committed with deceit and fault -​ Major public offense for which a convicted person is liable to be sentenced to death or to be imprisoned in a penitentiary or prison -​ According to degree to act -​ Consummated -​ All the elements necessary for its execution and accomplishment are present -​ Frustrated -​ When the offender performs all acts or execution which will produce the felony -​ Did not produce felony by reason of causes independent of the will of the perpetrator -​ Attempted -​ Offender commences the commission of the same directly by overt acts -​ Does not perform all the acts or execution which shall produce the felony Circumstances Affecting Criminal Liability -​ Justifying circumstance -​ No criminal liability because the act itself is justified as reasonable -​ Examples -​ Self defense -​ Elements -​ Unlawful aggression -​ Necessity of the means employed -​ No sufficient provocation of the attacker -​ If one of the three elements is lacking, this becomes incomplete self-defense and it becomes a mitigating circumstance -​ Fulfillment of a lawful order or duty -​ State of necessity -​ Exempting circumstance -​ No criminal liability because the person who committed the crime is exempted -​ Examples -​ Insane or imbecile -​ Insane person lacks intelligence, the ability to determine what is right or what is wrong -​ Imbeciles are people who have abnormalities in development who also do not possess adequate intelligence -​ Person below 9 years old -​ Parents would pay damages -​ Force majeure/natural calamity causes injury -​ Lucid interval: person has normal state of mind during a lucid interval -​ Mitigating circumstance -​ Decreases criminal liability because of equity and justice -​ Examples -​ Voluntary surrender -​ Confession of guilt -​ Provoked -​ Age of convict -​ Below 18 years old -​ Above 70 years old -​ Blind, deaf and mute -​ Because they cannot defend themselves in court -​ Aggravating circumstance -​ Increase criminal liability -​ Examples -​ Abuses -​ Cruelty -​ Abuse of authority -​ Crimes in times of calamity (looting, profiteering) -​ Treachery
text.513: -​ Insult to authority -​ Premeditation -​ Alternative circumstance -​ Degree of education -​ Degree of intoxication -​ Relationship Leadership and Management Leadership - the act of influencing and motivating others toward achieving a common goal Management - the process of planning, organizing, coordinating and directing the work of others to meet organizational goal Leadership Management -​ Do not have delegated authority and may be employed in a variety of positions -​ Involves empowering others -​ Have common goals that may or may not reflect those of the organization -​ Influencing, Motivating -​ DFF -​ Legitimate source of power due to the delegated authority -​ Emphasizes control, decision making and solving problems -​ Greater formal responsibility and accountability -​ Organization goal -​ Planning, Organizing, Directing, Controlling -​ Class president Leadership Theories Classic Autocratic (Authoritarian) -​ Determining policies, giving orders and directions -​ Needs for creativity, autonomy, and -self-motivation are not met -​ Often used in urgent decision making when group members cannot or do not wish to participate in decision making, completing a project quickly Democratic (Participative, Consultive) -​ Group discussions and decisions making are encouraged -​ Assumes that individuals are internally motivated, capable of making decisions and value independence -​ Allows self-motivation and productivity and calls for coordination and cooperation among members
text.514: Laissez-faire (Non-directive, Permissive) -​ Recognizes the group’s need for autonomy and self-regulation -​ Assumes a “hands-off” approach -​ Used in groups whose members have both personal and professional maturity -​ “Trusts” someone who is personally and professionally mature -​ Judge Bureaucratic -​ Does not trust self or others to make decisions -​ Rely on established rules, procedures, regulations -​ Dura lex Sed lex “The law is hard, but the law is the law” Situational -​ Adapts leadership style to the situation -​ Adapts to the readiness and willingness of the individual or group members to perform the assigned task Contemporary Charismatic -​ Charming personality Transactional -​ Relationship with followers is based on an exchange for some resource valued by the followers (giving incentives to promote loyalty and performance Transformational -​ Promotes creativity, risk - taking, commitment and collaboration. Involves empowering and inspiring others to contribute in the organization’s vision Shared leadership -​ Co-leadership; distributes decision making among group of people (shared governance) involves principle of unity of command Effective Leadership -​ Vision: mental image of a possible or desirable future state -​ Power: capacity to influence -​ Influence: gaining cooperation through excellent communication and persuasion based on trust Types of Power Legitimate Based on hierarchy in an organization, derived from formal position or office Reward Based on incentives (promotion, time-off from work, attractive work assignment)
text.515: Coercive Based on fear of retribution of withholding of rewards (dismissal, demotion, low rating) -​ RA 7877 - Anti-Harrassment Law -​ Work, education, training -​ Moral ascendency -​ Sexual Expert Based on high level of competence, knowledge, personality abilities or skills Referent Admiration and respect for the leader based on charisma and success Levels of Management Top Level - organizational executives; establishing goals and developing strategic plans (Chief Nurse) Middle Level - supervise first-level managers and activities in the department they supervise (Supervisor) -​ With most gathered information First Level - manages work of non- managerial personnel and day to day activities of specific work group/groups (Head Nurse) Principles of Management Manager -​ Authority - legitimate right to direct the work of others -​ Responsibility - obligation to complete task -​ Accountability - ability and willingness to assume responsibility for one’s actions and accept consequence of one’s behavior -​ Criminal Case - people of the Philippines (article 365) regular court -​ Civil Case - money, resources (damages) regular court -​ Administrative Case - license (suspension - 4 years sec. 23 RA 9173) PRC Principle of Unity of Command An employee is answerable to one boss Principle of Requisite Authority When a responsibility for a particular task is delegated to a subordinate, subordinate must also be given authority over resources needed for task accomplishment Principle of Continuing Responsibility when the performance of a task is delegated, the delegator retains accountability for the outcome Principle of Organizational Centrality Workers who interact with the greatest amount of work-related information (middle level)
text.516: Notable Theories of Management Frederick Taylor - Scientific Management Douglas McGregor - Theory X & Y Theory X Theory Y Dislikes work and avoids it Views work as natural as work and play Avoids responsibility and seeks direction Accepts responsibility and seeks it Security is valued over ambition Individuals capable of innovation Coerced, controlled, threatened Possesses self-direction and self-control Max Weber - Social and economic organization Henry Fayol - Modern Management:14 Principles of Management (1)​ Division of labor - division of work (2)​ Authority and responsibility - principles of management (3)​ Discipline - applying penalty after due process/judicious application of penalty (4)​ Remuneration - salary (5)​ Unity of command - one boss (6)​ Unity of direction - an organization with common goal (7)​ Subordination of individual interest - general interest over individual interest (8)​ Equity - equality based on situation “less in life, more in law” (9)​ Order - a place for everything and everything in its place (10)​ Scalar chain - the greater the power, the greater the responsibility (11)​ Degree of centralization - person/group that has authority (12)​ Esprit de corps - team building (13)​ Initiative - take action on your own (14)​ Stability of tenure - regularization General Management Roles -​ Interpersonal role -​ Symbol: signing of papers/documents -​ Facilitator: hires, trains, fires, remunerates and judges -​ Liaison: link to community, suppliers and the organization -​ Informational role -​ One who monitors information -​ Disseminates information from both external and internal sources -​ Spokesperson or representative of the organization -​ Decisional role
text.517: -​ An entrepreneur or innovator -​ A trouble shooter -​ A negotiator Fundamental Skills of Managers -​ According to Katz -​ Technical: proficiently in performing an activity in the correct manner with the right technique -​ Human: dealing with people and how get along with them -​ Conceptual: ability to see individual matters as they relate to the total picture and to develop big problems and discarding irrelevant facts -​ According to Summer -​ Knowledge factors: refer to ideas, concepts, or principle -​ Attitude factors: beliefs, feelings, and values -​ Ability factors: skills, art, judgement and wisdom Management Functions Planning -​ Assessing a situation, establishing goals and objectives based on assessment of the situation, developing a plan of action that identifies priorities, delineates who is responsible, determines deadlines -​ Deciding what, when, where, how to do it, by whom, and what resources Organizing -​ Determining responsibilities, communicating expectations, and establishing the chain of command for authority and communication Directing -​ Process of getting the organization’s work accomplished -​ Assigning and communicating expectations about the task to be completed, providing instructions and guidance and on-going decision-making Coordinating -​ Ensuring that plans are carried out and evaluating outcomes Planning -​ It is a continuous process of assessing, establishing goals and objectives, implementing and evaluating them and subjecting these to changes -​ Deciding in advance what to do; who is to do it; how, when and where it is to be done -​ Characteristics of a good plan -​ A well-developed plan should:
text.518: -​ Be precise with clearly-worded objectives -​ Be guided by policies and/or procedures affecting the planned action -​ Indicate priorities -​ Develop actions that are flexible and realistic -​ Develop a logical sequence of activities -​ Include the most practical methods for achieving each objective -​ Pervade the whole organization Strategic Planning -​ 3-5 years in the future -​ Set overall goals and policies -​ Nursing directors, chief nurses, director of nursing 1.​ Vision: descriptive picture of a desired FUTURE STATE 2.​ Mission: identifies the REASON an organization exists and what it DOES to achieve its vision 3.​ Goals and Objectives: ends toward which the organization is working 4.​ Philosophy: integrated set of beliefs and values that guides actions 5.​ Policies and procedures -​ Policies: plans reduced to instructions or statements -​ Procedures: process that implements a policy according to a specific task 6.​ Standards: professionally desirable norms 7.​ Rules: describe situations that allow only one choice of action; fairly inflexible Intermediate Planning -​ 6 months-2 years -​ Formulation of policies, rules and regulations, methods and procedures for intermediate level planning for on-going activities is done in coordination with the top management and those with the lower level -​ Nursing supervisors Operational Planning -​ Department plans, maintenance and improvement goals -​ Daily and weekly plans for administration or direct patient care -​ Head nurses Budgeting: Financial Plan -​ Budget: a financial road map that estimates future costs and a plan for utilization of resources -​ Components -​ Operating budget -​ Daily revenue and expenses including -​ Salaries -​ Supplies -​ Contractual services -​ Employee benefits -​ Laundry services, drug and pharmaceuticals -​ In-service education -​ Revenue budget -​ Summarizes the income -​ Expense budget -​ Salaries, supplies, utilities, maintenance -​ Cash budget -​ Forecasts the amount of money received -​ In consist of the beginning cash balance, estimates of the receipts and disbursements and the estimated balance for a given period -​ Prepared by estimating the amount of money to be collected from patients and allocating it to cash disbursement required to meet obligations promptly as they come -​ Capital expenditure budget -​ Major expenditures -​ Consists of accumulated data for fixed assets that are expected to be acquired during the budget period -​ Replacement or expansion of the plant, major equipment and inventories -​ Flexible budget -​ Composed of budgets that adjust automatically over the course of the year depending on variables such as volume and labor costs -​ Zero-based budgeting -​ Major advantage of this type is that it forces managers to set priorities and justify -​ Disadvantage: time consuming Organizing -​ It is a process of establishing formal authorities that involves -​ Setting up the organizational structure through identification of groupings, roles and relationships -​ Determining the staff needed and distributing them in various areas -​ Elements -​ Organization structure -​ Staffing -​ Scheduling -​ Developing job description -​ Authority: the right to act or make decisions without the need for approval of higher administration -​ Terms used in organizing authority -​ Accountability: taking full responsibility for the quality of work and behavior -​ Responsibility: obligation to perform the assigned task -​ Principles -​ Unity of command: there can only be one superior -​ Scalar principle/hierarchy/chain of command: flow from higher to lower authority -​ Departmentalization: grouping of workers with similar assignments -​ Span of control: the number of people that reports directly to a manager -​ Centralization: the staff all report to one person that is higher than them -​ Decentralization/delegation: transferring specified decision making to lower levels of the organization -​ Organization: the structure and process which allows an agency to enact its philosophy and achieve its goals -​ Types -​ Line organization -​ It is the simplest and most direct type of organization -​ Each position has general authority over the lower positions in the hierarchy -​ Advantages -​ Maintain simplicity -​ Encourages speedy action -​ Makes a clear division of authority -​ Disadvantages -​ Neglects special training -​ Overworks key people -​ Depends upon retention of few key people -​ Staff organization -​ It is purely advisory to the line structure with no authority to put recommendations into action -​ Advantages -​ Frees the line executive of detailed analysis -​ Affords young specialists a mass training -​ Enables specialist to give expert advise -​ Disadvantages -​ Reduces expert power to place recommendation into action -​ Tends towards centralization of the organization -​ Continues the organization even if its functions are not clear -​ Functional organization -​ It is one where each unit is responsible for a given part of the organization’s workload -​ There is a clear delineation of roles and responsibilities which are actually interrelated -​ Advantages -​ Relieves line executive of routine specialized decision -​ Provides frameworks for applying expert knowledge -​ Disadvantages -​ Makes relationship more complex -​ Makes limits of authority of each specialists a difficult coordination -​ Organizational chart -​ It is a diagrammatic representation of the organizational structure -​ Five major characteristics -​ Division of work -​ Chain of command -​ Type of work to be performed -​ Grouping of work segment -​ Levels of management -​ Forms of organizational chart -​ Vertical chart -​ Also known as tall chart -​ Depicts the chief executive at the top with line of authority flowing down the hierarchy -​ Horizontal chart -​ Depicts structure side to side -​ Useful for showing processes or equal authority distribution -​ Concentric chart -​ Also known as circular chart -​ Shows outward flows of communication from center
text.522: Staffing -​ It is the process of determining and providing the acceptable number and mix of nursing personnel to produce a desired level of care to meet the patient’s demand -​ Purpose: to provide each nursing unit with an appropriate and acceptable number of workers in each category to perform the nursing tasks required -​ Schedule: a timetable showing planned workdays and shifts for nursing personnel -​ Types -​ Centralized -​ Done by the chief nurse -​ He/she assigns the nursing personnel to the various units of the hospital -​ Decentralized -​ The shift and off duties are arranged by the nurse supervisors or senior nurse of the particular unit -​ Cyclical -​ Covers a designed number of weeks as one cycle, which is repeated there on -​ Advantages -​ It is fair to all -​ Saves time -​ Enables employees to plan ahead of time -​ Scheduled leaves are more stable -​ Productivity is improved The Hospital Nursing Service Administration Manual of the DOH has recommended the following nursing care hours for patients in the various nursing units of the hospital Cases/Pt NCH/Pt/Day Prof to Non-prof Ratio General medicine 3.5 60:40 Medical 3.4 60:40 Surgical 3.4 60:40 Obstetrics 3.0 60:40 Pediatrics 4.6 70:30 Pathologic Nursery 2.8 55:45 ER/ICU/RR 6.0 70:30 CCU 6.0 80:20

text.524: Secondary 60:40 Tertiary 65:35 Specialized 70:30 or 80:20 Distribution per Shift AM 45% PM 37% Night 18% Staffing Formula 1.​ Categorize according to the level of care needed. Multiply the total number of patients by the percentage of patients at each level of care 2.​ Find the total number of nursing care hours needed by the patients at each category level a.​ Find the number of patients at each level by the average number of nursing care hours needed per day b.​ Get the sum of the nursing care hours needed at the various levels 3.​ Find the actual number of nursing care hours needed by the given number of patients. Multiply the total nursing care hours needed per day by the total number of days in a year 4.​ Find the actual number of nursing care hours rendered by each nursing personnel per year a.​ Multiply the number of hours on duty per day by the actual working days per year 5.​ Find the total number of nursing personnel needed a.​ Divide the total number of nursing of nursing care needed per year by the actual number of working hours rendered by an employee per year b.​ Find the number of relievers. Multiply the number of nursing personnel needed by 0.15 (40 hours per week) or by 0.12 (48 hours per week) c.​ Add the number of relievers to the number of personnel need 6.​ Categorize the nursing personnel into professional and non-professionals. Multiply the number of personnel according to the ratio of professionals to non-professionals 7.​ Distribute by shifts Directing -​ Issuance of orders, assignments and instructions that enable the nursing personnel to understand what are expected
text.525: -​ Involves command and coordination -​ Elements -​ Communication -​ Delegation -​ Supervision -​ Coordination -​ Staff development -​ Decision-making Communication -​ Transmission of information, opinions and intentions between and among individuals -​ Types -​ Verbal -​ Oral -​ Written -​ Non-verbal -​ Facial expression -​ Tone of voice -​ Body language -​ Touch -​ Line of Communication -​ Downward -​ From superior to subordinate -​ Examples -​ Policies -​ Rules and regulations -​ Memorandum -​ Employee -​ Handbooks -​ Performance appraisal -​ Upward -​ From subordinates upward -​ Examples -​ Incident report -​ Grievance report -​ Horizontal -​ Between peers, personnel or departments on the same level -​ Examples -​ Endorsements
text.526: -​ Conferences -​ Nursing rounds -​ Outward -​ From caregivers to patient and their relatives -​ Examples -​ Discharge teaching -​ Diagonal -​ From individuals or departments that area not in the same level or the hierarchy -​ Examples -​ Nutrition department to nursing department -​ Grapevine -​ Informal communication; often rapid and subject to much distortion -​ Example -​ Gossip -​ hearsay Delegation -​ Process by which a manager assigns specific tasks/duties to workers with commensurate authority to perform the job -​ Principles -​ Select the right person is to be delegated -​ Delegate both interesting and uninteresting tasks -​ Provide subordinates with enough time to learn -​ Delegate gradually -​ Delegate in advance -​ Consult before delegating -​ Avoid gaps and overlaps -​ What cannot be delegated -​ Overall responsibility, authority and accountability for satisfactory completion of all activities in the unit -​ Authority to sign one’s name is never delegated -​ Evaluating the staff and/or taking necessary corrective or disciplinary action -​ Responsibility for maintaining morale or the opportunity to say a few words of encouragement to the staff especially to new ones -​ Jobs that are too technical and those that involve trust and confidence -​ Responsibilities -​ Registered Nurse -​ IV medications -​ Health teaching
text.527: -​ Assessment -​ Evaluation -​ Overall accountability unstable/critical patients -​ Licensed practical nurse -​ Medications (IM, SC, ID except IV) -​ Wound cleansing -​ Blended feeding -​ Suctioning -​ Nursing assistant -​ Routine activities -​ VS -​ Application of pulse oximeter sensor -​ Post-mortem -​ Stable/ambulatory/MGH Nursing Care Assignments -​ Can also be called modalities of nursing care, systems of nursing care, or patterns of nursing care 1.​ Functional nursing a.​ This kind of nursing modality is task-oriented in which a particular nursing function is assigned to each worker b.​ Divides work to be done and every member is responsible for his actions c.​ Best system that can be used if there are many patients and professionals d.​ Advantages i.​ Work is done fast ii.​ Workers learn to work fast e.​ Disadvantages i.​ Fragmentation of nursing care; therefore holistics not achieved ii.​ Patient cannot identify who their real nurse is iii.​ Nurse-patient relationship is not fully developed iv.​ Evaluation of nursing care is poor v.​ Outcomes are rarely documented vi.​ It is hard to find a specific person to answer relative question 2.​ Total care nursing a.​ One nurse is assigned to one patient for the delivery of total care 3.​ Team nursing a.​ One nurse leads a group of nursing personnel in providing nursing needs to a group of patients b.​ Decentralized system of care c.​ Advantages
text.528: i.​ Team effort ii.​ Frees patient care coordinator to manage the unit iii.​ Nursing care conferences help problem solve and develop staff iv.​ Nursing care plan d.​ Disadvantages i.​ Time needed to coordinate delegated work 4.​ Primary nursing a.​ RN is responsible for the total care of a small group of patients (4-6) from admission to discharge b.​ RN remains responsible for the care of those patients 24 hours per day c.​ Advantages i.​ Patient and family are able to develop trusting relationship with the RN ii.​ Assures continuity of care iii.​ Improves communication with the members of the health team and eliminates the use of nursing aides in the provision of direct nursing care d.​ Disadvantages i.​ High cost because there is higher RN skill ii.​ Proximity of patient assignment iii.​ Overlapping of staff function iv.​ Nurse-patient ratio must be realistic 5.​ Case method a.​ One is to one nurse patient ratio b.​ Advantages i.​ Consistency of one individual caring for the whole shift ii.​ More opportunity to observe and monitor the patient c.​ Disadvantages i.​ The nurse must not have the same patient the next day ii.​ It does not serve the purpose of decentralization 6.​ Modular method a.​ Also termed as district nursing b.​ Modification of team and primary nursing c.​ It is sometimes used when there are not enough RNs to practice nursing d.​ It differs from the team nursing in that the RN provides direct nursing care with the assistance of aides Supervision -​ It is providing guidelines for the accomplishment of a task or activity with initial direction and periodic inspection of the actual accomplishment coordination, and synchronization of services -​ Principles of good supervision

text.539: -​ Professionalism -​ Accountability -​ Social relevance of nursing -​ Research & decision making Ultimate Goal of Research: To improve the practice/client care/patient care/health care/nursing care/profession (if general) Sources of knowledge: -​ Tradition (stories from one generation to another generation) -​ Authority (people who are experts) -​ Logical reasoning (use of logic and reason) -​ Experience (best teacher) and trial & error (try and try until succeed) -​ Scientific method/experiment (discover something all by yourself) Types of Research -​ According to Purpose: -​ Basic/Pure research -​ To increase general knowledge -​ Formulate/refine a theory -​ General principles of human behavior -​ Applied research -​ Find solution to existing problem -​ Focus on intervention to achieve desired goal -​ How principles can be used to solve problems in nursing practice -​ According to Levels of Investigation (General) -​ Level I: Exploratory - identify the variables (opinion) “quality”/census -​ Level II: Descriptive - describe whether the variables are associated or related (facts/issues/study/analysis) -​ Descriptive - describe the variables as it is -​ Correlational - describe the relationship of the variables to each other -​ Comparative - describe the comparison of the variables to each other (similarities/differences) -​ Level III: Experimental - to find out the cause and effect of the variables to each other (effect/manipulation) -​ According to Design -​ Non-Experimental - without manipulation -​ Historical - study of the past issues (descriptive)

previous researches (least being used) 4.​ Criteria of a Good Research Problem a.​ Significance of the study (address it to the people, society at large, profession) b.​ Availability of the subjects c.​ Limitation of subjects d.​ Time allotment and research ability e.​ Limitation of tools f.​ Interest of the researcher g.​ Novelty (newness/freshness of the idea) iii.​ Problem statement 1.​ Articulate the problem to be addressed and indicates the need for a study through the development of an argument iv.​ Research questions 1.​ Are the specific queries researcher wants to answer addressing the research problem b.​ Reviewing the related literature i.​ Provides a foundation on which to base new evidence and usually is conducted well before any data are collected ii.​ Synthesis of previous studies iii.​ Purpose of RRL: To get an idea or the background of the study iv.​ Types of Sources 1.​ primary source 2.​ descriptions of studies written by the researchers who conducted them 3.​ Mostly recommended 4.​ secondary source - description of studies prepared by someone other than the original researcher c.​ Undertaking a clinical fieldwork i.​ To get an idea or the background of the study ii.​ Complements & support RRL d.​ Defining the framework and developing conceptual definition i.​ Framework is the overall conceptual underpinnings of the study 1.​ Conceptual framework a.​ Deals with the abstraction that are assembled by virtue of their relevance to common theme b.​ It is the study that has roots in a specified conceptual mode (topic) 2.​ Theoretical framework - it is a study based on theory 3.​ Conceptual definition - presents the abstract or theoretical meaning of the concepts being studied 4.​ Operational definition - specifies the operation that researchers must perform to collect and measure the required information/define the variables on how they are used on their study e.​ Formulating hypothesis i.​ Hypothesis - is a statement of the researcher’s expectations about relationships between study variable/tentative prediction of the relationship between variables ii.​ 4 Parts of Hypothesis 1.​ Independent variable (cause) 2.​ Dependent variable (effect) 3.​ Relationship 4.​ Population to which it applies a.​ Population - include all characteristics b.​ Set (2 or more sets) - concentrate on characteristics that differentiate them) i.​ Set characteristic (fixed) - independent variable ii.​ Vary - dependent variable c.​ Set (1 set) i.​ Eliminate the population since 1 set ii.​ Go back and ask what is being studied iii.​ Fixed - independent variable iv.​ Vary - dependent variable d.​ Manipulation - anything that is given (independent variable) iii.​ Research hypothesis - statement of expected relationships between variables 1.​ Non-directional - predicts a relationship or difference between variables without specifying the direction of that relationship 2.​ Directional - predicts the specific direction of a relationship or difference between variables iv.​ Null hypothesis - state that there is no relationship between the independent and dependent variables 2.​ The design and planning phased (most used of your time) a.​ Selecting a research design b.​ Developing the protocols for the intervention (optional, only for experimental research) c.​ Identifying the population to be studied i.​ People who provide information to the researchers or investigators are: 1.​ Subjects 2.​ study participants 3.​ Respondents 4.​ Informants (qualitative study) ii.​ Population - all the individuals or objects with common defining characteristics iii.​ Accessible/source population - aggregate of cases that conform to designated criteria and that are accessible as subjects for a study iv.​ Target population - aggregate of cases about which the researcher would like to generalize v.​ Sample - subset of population elements vi.​ Element - most basic unit about which information is collected vii.​ Pilot study - small-scale version or trial run designed test the methods to be used in a larger, more rigorous study called parent study d.​ Designing the sampling plan i.​ Sampling - the process of selecting a portion of the population to represent the entire population so that interferences about the population can be made ii.​ Representatives - the key consideration in assessing a sample in quantitative study 1.​ Probability sampling - involves random selection of elements a.​ simple random sampling - most basic probability sampling design b.​ Stratified random sampling - it subdivides the population into homogenous subsets from which an appropriate number of elements are selected at random c.​ cluster sampling (muti-stage sampling) - involves the successive selection of random samples from larger to smaller units by either simple random or stratified random methods d.​ Systematic sampling - involves the selection of every nth case from the list, such as every tenth person on a patient list 2.​ Non-probability sampling - elements are selected by non-random methods a.​ Convenience/accidental sampling - entails using the most conveniently available people as study participants b.​ Snowball/network/chain sampling - variant of convenience sample, every sample members are asked to refer other people to meet the eligibility criteria c.​ Quota sampling - one in which the researcher identifies population strata and determines how many participants are needed from the stratum d.​ Purposive/judgemental sampling - the researcher selects units to be sampled based on their knowledge and professional judgement e.​ Specifying the methods on how to measure research variables - tools/instruments for data collection f.​ Developing a method on how to safeguard human/animal rights g.​ Reviewing and finalizing the plan 3.​ The empirical phase (longest phase) a.​ Collecting the data i.​ Data saturation - involves sampling to the point at which no new information is obtained and redundancy is achieved ii.​ Major Forms of Data Collection 1.​ Observation - way of gathering data by watching behavior, events, or noting physical characteristics in their natural setting a.​ Phenomena (amenable to observation) i.​ characteristics and condition of the subject ii.​ activities and behaviors of the subjects iii.​ skill attainment and performance (performance appraisal) iv.​ environmental characteristics v.​ verbal communication vi.​ non-verbal communication b.​ Types of observation i.​ Overt - everyone knows they are being observed ii.​ Covert - no one knows they are being observed and the observer is concealed c.​ Types of observer i.​ Non-participant/direct observation - is where data are collected by observing behavior without interacting with the participants ii.​ Participant observation - is where data are collected by interacting with, and therefore experiencing the phenomenon being studied d.​ Advantages of observation i.​ Collect data where and when an event or activity is occurring ii.​ Does not rely on people’s willingness or ability to provide information iii.​ Allows you to directly see what people do rather than relying on what people say they did e.​ Disadvantages of observation i.​ Susceptible to observer bias ii.​ Susceptible to hawthorne’s effect (people usually perform better when they know they are observed though indirectly) iii.​ Can be expensive and time-consuming compared to other data collection method iv.​ Does not increase your understanding of why people behave as they do 2.​ Self-Reports (widely used form) - disadvantage: accuracy and validity a.​ Questionnaires - is a research instrument consisting of questions and other prompts for the purpose of gathering information from the respondents i.​ Types of questions 1.​ Closed-ended - is a question format that provide respondents with a list of answer choices from which they must choose to answer the question 2.​ Open-ended - designed to encourage a full, meaningful answer using the subject’s own knowledge or feelings ii.​ Advantages 1.​ Cost - less costly, less time and energy to administer 2.​ Anonymity - offer possibility of complete anonymity 3.​ Interviewer bias - absence of an interviewer ensures that there will be no interviewer bias b.​ Interview - is a conversation between two people where questions obtain information from the interviewee i.​ Types of interview 1.​ Structured - require adherence to a very particular set of rules. Each question that is outlined should be ready word for word by the researcher without any deviation from the protocol 2.​ Semi-structured - using this type are still expected to cover every question in the protocol, they have some wiggle room to explore participant responses by asking for clarification or additional information 3.​ Unstructured - need only a checklist of topics to be covered during the interview ii.​ Advantages 1.​ Response rates - tend to be high in face to face interview 2.​ Audience - many people cannot fill up questionnaire, interview is feasible with most of the people 3.​ Clarity - interviews offer some protection against ambiguous or confusing questions 4.​ Depth of questioning - open-ended questions are used mostly in interviews 5.​ Missing information - less likely to give missing information in the interview 6.​ Order of question - in interviews, researchers have control over question ordering 3.​ Biophysical measurements (use of equipment and gadgets) a.​ In Vivo - measurement directly on the subject (pulse oximeter) b.​ In Vitro - measurement performed outside (laboratories) c.​ Criteria: i.​ Validity - venture what is supposed to be measured ii.​ Reliability - consistency or the repeatability of the tool iii.​ Sensitivity - detect small variations or find differences 4.​ Pre-existing data (any forms of records) b.​ Preparing for data analysis 4.​ The analytic phase a.​ Analyzing the data b.​ Interpreting the result - interpretation is the process of studying the results and examining their implications (inferential statistics) i.​ Parametric test - are characterized by three attributes 1.​ They involve the estimation of a parameter 2.​ they require measurement on at least an interval scale 3.​ They involve several assumptions, such as the assumption that variables are normally distributed in the population a.​ Interval - occurs when the researcher can specify the rank-ordering of the objects on an attribute and can assume equivalent distance between them (fahrenheit temperature scale) b.​ Ratio - provides information concerning the ordering of objects on the critical attribute, the intervals between objects and the absolute magnitude of the attribute (scores in board exam) ii.​ Non-parametric tests - they involve less restrictive assumptions about the shape of the variable’s distribution than do parametric tests 1.​ Levels of measurement a.​ Nominal - involves assigning numbers to classify characteristics into categories (gender, blood type, marital status) b.​ Ordinal - involves sorting objects based on their relative ranking on an attribute (mid, moderate, severe) iii.​ Measurements 1.​ Chi-square test - to test hypothesis about the proportion of cases that fall into different categories as when a contingency table has been created 2.​ T-test - assess whether the means of two groups are statistically different from each other 3.​ Analysis of variance (ANOVA) - testing differences between means when there are three or more groups iv.​ Descriptive Statistics 1.​ Measures of condense a.​ Frequency distribution - a systematic arrangement of values from lowest to highest together with a count of the number of times each value was obtained b.​ Percentage - a way of expressing a number, especially a ratio as a fraction of 100

Orbital Fracture (+) Battle’s sign & Racoon eyes Scope of Nursing Practice -​ Promoting health and wellness -​ A process that engages in activities and behaviors that enhance quality of life and maximize personal potential -​ Activities that enhance healthy lifestyles -​ Improving nutrition and physical fitness -​ Preventing drug and alcohol misuse -​ Restricting smoking -​ Preventing accidents and injury at home and workplace -​ Preventing illness -​ Goal of illness prevention program is to maintain optimal health by preventing disease which includes -​ Immunization -​ Prenatal and infant care -​ Prevention of STI -​ Restoring health -​ Focuses on the ill client and it extends from early detection of disease through helping the client during the recovery period -​ Activities include -​ Providing direct care to the ill client -​ Performing diagnostic and assessment procedures -​ Teaching clients about recovery activities -​ Rehabilitating clients to their optimal functional level -​ Caring for dying -​ Comforting and caring for people of all ages who are dying which includes -​ Helping clients live as comfortably as possible until death -​ Helping support persons to cope with death Standard of Nursing Practice -​ Assessment: collect comprehensive data pertinent to the patient’s health or situation -​ Diagnosis: analyzes the assessment data to determine the diagnosis or issue -​ Outcome identification: identifies expected outcomes for a plan individualized to the patient or the situation -​ Planning: develops a plan that prescribe strategies and alternatives to attain expected outcomes -​ Implementation: implements the identified plan -​ Evaluation: evaluates progress towards attainment of outcomes -​ Quality practice: systematically enhance the quality and effectiveness of nursing practice -​ Education: attains knowledge and competency that reflects current nursing practice -​ Professional practice evaluation: evaluate one’s own practice in relation to professional practice standards and guidelines, relevant statutes, rules and regulation -​ Collegiality: interacts with and contributes to the professional development of peers and colleagues -​ Collaboration: collaborates with patients, family and others in the conduct of nursing practice -​ Ethics: integrates ethical provisions in all areas of practice -​ Research: integrates research findings into practice -​ Resource utilization: considers factors related to safety, effectiveness, cost and impact on practice on the planning and delivery of nursing services -​ Leadership: understanding of the situations to appropriate actions -​ Inclined to take a certain action because “it felt right” Communication in Nursing -​ Interchange of information between two or more people: exchange of ideas and thoughts -​ In addition, thoughts are conveyed to others not only by spoken or written words but also by gestures or body actions -​ Verbal: uses spoken or written words
text.604: -​ Non-verbal: uses gestures, facial expressions, posture/gait, body movements, physical appearance, eye contact and tone of voice -​ Components -​ Sender: the person who encodes and deliver message -​ Message: the content of the communication, may contain verbal, non-verbal and symbolic language -​ Receiver: the person who receives and decodes the message -​ Channel: means of conveying and receiving messages through visual, auditory and tactile senses -​ Response/feedback: message returned by the receiver to the sender Characteristics of Communication -​ Simplicity: use of commonly understood words -​ Pace and intonation: modifies the feeling and the impact of the message -​ Clarity and brevity: message that is direct and simple -​ Timing and relevance: require choice of time and consideration of client’s interest and concern -​ Adaptability: message needs to be altered in accordance with behavioral cues from the client -​ Credibility: means worthiness of belief, trustworthiness and reliability -​ Humor: used to help client adjust to difficult and painful situation Documentation -​ Written or computer based -​ Served as a permanent record of client’s record/SOMR) -​ Each person or department makes notations in a separate section/s of client’s chart -​ Specific information is easier to locate -​ Components -​ Admission sheet -​ Face sheet -​ record -​ Nurses notes -​ Client discharge plan and referral summary -​ Initial nursing assessment -​ Problem-oriented medical record -​ Data about the client are recorded and arranged according to the sources of the information -​ Records integrates all data about the problem, gathered by members of health team -​ 4 basic components -​ Database -​ Contains all information from the patient when he first entered the agency -​ It includes nursing assessment, physician’s history, social and family data, results of physician’s examination -​ Problem lists -​ Contains all the aspects of the person’s life requiring health care -​ Kept in the front of the chart -​ Problems are listed in order, which they are identified -​ Continually updated as new problems are identified and others are resolved -​ Initial list of orders or plan of care -​ Made with reference to the active problems and are generated by the person who lists the problem -​ Progress notes -​ Includes nurses narrative text.606: -​ May be written in a pencil to ease in recording frequent change in details of client care -​ A series to flip cards usually kept in portable life Recording -​ General guidelines -​ Date and time -​ For legal reasons and client’s safety -​ Record the time in conventional manner or according to 24 hour clock to avoid confusion about whether the time was am or pm -​ Timing -​ Adjust the frequency as per client’s condition indicates -​ No recording should be done BEFORE providing nursing care -​ Documenting should be done as soon as possible after assessment/intervention -​ Legibility -​ All entries must be easy to read to prevent interpretation errors -​ Permanence -​ Records are made in the dark permanent ink -​ Use of accepted terminology -​ Use only commonly accepted abbreviation, symbols and terms that are specified by the agency -​ Correct spelling -​ Is essential for accuracy in recording -​ If unsure how to spell, look it up in a dictionary or other resource book -​ Signature -​ Each recording in nursing notes is signed by the nurse making it -​ Include name and title -​ Accuracy -​ Client’s name should be written on each page of the clinical record -​ Accurate notations consists of facts/observations rather than opinions or interpretation -​ When recording MISTAKE is made, draw a line through it and write the words “mistaken entry” (avoid writing the word “error”) above or next to the original entry with your initials and name -​ Do not erase, blot out or use correction fluid -​ Write every line but not between the line -​ If a blank appears in the notation, draw a through the blank space and sign the notation -​ Sequence
text.607: -​ Document events in the order which they occur -​ Appropriateness -​ Record only information that pertains to the client’s health problems and care -​ Recording irrelevant information may be considered an invasion of the client privacy -​ Completeness -​ Information needs to be complete and helpful to the client and health care professionals -​ Care that is omitted because of client’s refusal of treatment must also be recorded -​ Document what and why it is omitted and who was notified -​ Conciseness -​ Recording needs to be brief as well as completed to save time in communication -​ Legal prudence -​ Accurate and complete documentation should be a legal protection to the client and health care team -​ Confidentiality -​ Only the health professionals who participate in the care of the client are allowed to read the chart Reporting -​ Takes place when two or more people share information about client care, either face to face via telephone -​ Types -​ Change of shifts report or endorsement -​ For continuity of care of clients by providing quick summary of health care needs and details of care to be given -​ It is not merely reciting the content or the kardex -​ Telephone reports -​ Provide clear, accurate and concise information -​ Date and time -​ Name of the person giving the information -​ Subject of information received -​ Name and signature of the receiver -​ Person receiving the information should repeat it back to the sender to ensure accuracy -​ Telephone orders -​ Only RNs may receive telephone orders -​ Another RN should listen in another telephone line to countercheck the details -​ Write the date and time the telephone order was received -​ Write the complete order and read it back -​ Question primary health care provider about any order that is unusual or contraindicated to client’s condition -​ The order should be countersigned by the physician who made the order within the prescribed period of time (within 24 hours) -​ Transfer report -​ Done when transferring a client to other unit Nursing Process -​ Purpose -​ To identify client’s health status -​ Actual health problem -​ Potential health problem or needs -​ To establish plans to meet identified needs -​ To deliver specific nursing care and improve the quality care -​ Characteristics of nursing care -​ Cyclical (regularly repeated events) and dynamic (continuously changing) -​ Client centered: organizes the plan or care according to client’s problems rather than the nursing goal -​ Focused on problem solving: nursing process is directed towards a client’s responses to disease and illness -​ Decision making: involved in every phase of nursing process -​ Interpersonal and collaborative -​ Communicates with the client and family -​ Collaborates with other members of the health care team -​ Universally applicable: used in all types of health care setting with the clients of all age group -​ Nurses must use a variety of critical thinking skills to carry out the nursing process -​ Components -​ Assessment -​ Diagnosis -​ Planning -​ Implementation -​ Evaluation Nursing Assessment -​ A systematic and continuous collection, organization, validation and documentation of data about the client health status -​ Purpose: establish a database -​ Activities during assessment -​ Data collection: gathering information about client, considering the physical, psychological, emotional, social-cultural, and spiritual factors that may affect his/her health status -​ Sources of data -​ Client (primary) -​ Support people (secondary) -​ Family members, friends, and caregivers who know the client well -​ Client records -​ Medical records: past and present health and illness patterns -​ Records of therapies: social workers, nutritionist, dieticians, physical therapists -​ Laboratory record -​ Health care professionals -​ Literature -​ Data collection methods -​ Observing: gathers data by using senses -​ 2 aspects -​ Noticing the data -​ Selecting, organizing, and interpreting data -​ Interviewing: is a planned communication or a conversation with a purpose -​ 2 approaches -​ Directive -​ Highly structured and elicits specific information -​ Uses closed-ended questions -​ The nurse establishes the purposes and control the interview -​ Used when you need to elicit specific data -​ Used in emergency situation -​ Non-directive (rapport building) -​ Nurse allow the client to control the purpose, subject matter and pacing -​ Uses more open-ended questions -​ Advantage: allows the patient to explain certain information -​ Stages of interview -​ The opening -​ Most important -​ Establish rapport -​ Orientation -​ The body -​ The client communicates what he/she thinks, feels, and perceives in response to the question -​ The closing -​ Termination of interview -​ Data organization -​ clustering /organizing of facts into group of information -​ Nurse uses a written/computerized data systematically -​ Validating data -​ Double checking or verifying data to confirm that it is accurate and factual -​ Documenting data -​ Accurate documentation is essential and should include all data collected about the client’s health status -​ 4 types of assessment -​ Initial assessment -​ Perform within the specified time after admission -​ Main purpose is to create database for problem identification reference and future comparison -​ Problem-focused assessment -​ Integrated throughout the nursing process -​ Purpose is to determine the status of a specific health -​ Emergency assessment -​ Done during an acute physiologic and psychologic crisis of the client -​ Purpose is to identify life-threatening conditions and to identify new or overlooked problems -​ Framework and principle in emergency assessment -​ Airway -​ Breathing -​ Circulation -​ Use either Maslow’s hierarchy of needs or ABC principles -​ Time-lapsed assessment -​ Done several months after the initial assessment -​ Purpose is to compare clients current status to baseline data previously obtained

client’s potential or actual alteration of health status -​ It uses the critical thinking skills of analysis and synthesis -​ Basic 2 part statements -​ Problem (statement of the client’s response) -​ Signs and symptoms (defining characteristics by the client) -​ 1 part statement -​ Consists of NANDA label only -​ Collaborative problems -​ Suggested that all collaborative problems begging with the diagnosing label “potential complications” -​ Purpose of NANDA -​ To define, refine and promote taxonomy of nursing diagnostic terminology of general use to professional nurses -​ Members -​ Staff nurses -​ Clinical specialists -​ Faculty, directors of nursing -​ Deans, theorists, and researchers -​ Types -​ Actual diagnosis -​ Client problem that is present at the time of the nursing assessment -​ Risk diagnosis -​ Clinical judgement that a problem does not exist, but the presence of risk factors indicates that a problem is likely to develop unless nurses intervene -​ Wellness diagnosis -​ Describes human responses to levels of wellness in an individual, family or community that have a readiness for enhancement -​ Possible diagnosis -​ Evidence about a health problem is incomplete or unclear -​ Syndrome diagnosis -​ Associated with a cluster of other diagnoses Planning -​ Deliberative, systematic phase of nursing process that involves decision making and problem Types -​ Initial planning -​ Done by the nurse who performs the admission assessment -​ Ongoing planning -​ Done by all nurses who work with the client -​ Occurs at the beginning of a shift as the nurse plans the care given that day -​ Discharge planning -​ Process of anticipating and planning for needs after discharge, is a crucial part of comprehensive care -​ Begins at first client contact and involves comprehensive and ongoing assessment to obtain information about client’s ongoing needs -​ Planning process -​ Setting priorities -​ Establishing client goals/desired outcomes -​ Selecting nursing interventions -​ Writing individualized nursing interventions on care plans -​ Guidelines for writing nursing care plans -​ Date and sign the plan -​ Use category headings -​ Use plan contains interventions for ongoing assessment of the client -​ Include collaborative and coordination activities in the plan -​ Include plans for the client’s discharge and home care needs -​ Characteristics of the planning process -​ Client-centered -​ Specific -​ Measurable -​ Attainable -​ Realistic -​ Time bound Implementation -​ Doing and documenting the activities that are specific text.615: -​ Therapeutic use of self -​ Right attitude Evaluation -​ Collecting data, comparing data and relating nursing activities to outcomes -​ Drawing conclusions about problem status -​ Continuing, modifying or terminating the NCP -​ Types -​ Ongoing/formative evaluation -​ Done during or immediately after the intervention -​ Allows the nurse to decide and make on the spot modification/s in an intervention -​ Intermittent evaluation -​ Done at a specified time and it shows the extent of progress of the patient -​ Enables the nurse to correct deficiencies and modify the NCP -​ Terminal/summative evaluation -​ Done at or immediately before discharge -​ Importance: it determines whether the goals are met, partially met, or unmet -​ When goals have been partially met or when goals have not been met, two conclusions may be drawn -​ The care plan may be need to be revised, since the problem is only partially resolved -​ The care plan does not need revision, because the client merely needs more time to achieve the previously established goal/s Concepts of Health and Illness -​ Health is state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO) -​ Health is the ability to maintain homeostasis or dynamic equilibrium. Homeostasis is regulated by the negative feedback mechanism (Walter Cannon) Models of Health and Illness -​ Travis’ illness-wellness continuum -​ The illness-wellness continuum developed by Travis ranges from high-level wellness to premature death -​ The model illustrates two arrows pointing in opposite directions and joined at a neutral point -​ Movement to the right of the neutral point indicates increasing levels of health and well-being for an individual -​ This is achieved in three steps -​ Awareness -​ Education -​ Growth -​ In contrast, movement to the left of the neutral point indicates progressively decreasing levels of health -​ Health belief model -​ The model of Becker (1975) which describes the relationship between a person’s belief and behavior -​ Individual perceptions and modifying factors may influence health beliefs and preventive health behavior -​ Individual perceptions include the following -​ Perceive susceptibility to illness -​ Perceive seriousness of an illness -​ Perceive threat of an illness -​ Modifying factors include the following -​ Demographic variables -​ Socio-psychologic variables -​ Structural variables -​ Cues to action -​ Smith’s model of health -​ Clinical model: identifies health as absence of signs of symptoms of disease or injury -​ Role performance model: health is identified in terms of individual’s ability to perform his/her work -​ Adaptive model: health is a creative process; disease is a failure in adaptation; focuses on the ability of the person to cope -​ Eudemonistic model: health is seen as a condition of actualization or realization of person’s potential -​ Leavell and Clark’s Agent-Host-Environmental model (ecologic model) -​ States that there three interactive factors that affect health and illness -​ Agent: any factor or stressor than can cause or lead to illness -​ Host: person who may or may not be at risk of acquiring the disease -​ Environment: any factor external to the host that may or may not be predispose the person to the development of the disease -​ Illness: is the state in which the person’s physical, emotional, intellectual, social, developmental, or spiritual functioning is diminished or impaired compared with previous experiences
text.617: -​ Disease: an alteration in body functions resulting in reduction of capacities or a shortening of the normal life span -​ Common causes of disease -​ Biological agents -​ Inherited genetic defects -​ Developmental defects -​ Physical agents -​ Chemical agents -​ Tissue response to injury -​ Faulty chemical/metabolic process -​ Emotional/physical reaction to stress Stages of Illness -​ Symptom experiences -​ Person comes to believe something is wrong -​ Physical: experience of symptoms -​ Cognitive: the interpretation of the symptoms in terms that have some meaning to the person -​ Emotional: fear and anxiety -​ Assumption of the sick role -​ Acceptance of the illness -​ Excused from normal duties and role expectations -​ Confirmation from family and friends -​ Medical care contact -​ Seek advice of the health professionals for validation of real illness, explanation of symptoms, and reassurance or prediction of what the outcome will be -​ Dependent patient role -​ Client becomes dependent on the health professionals for help -​ Accepts/rejects health professional’s suggestions -​ Later becomes more passive and accepting -​ May regress to an earlier behavior stage -​ Recovery or rehabilitation -​ Client is expected to relinquish the dependent role and resume former roles and responsibilities -​ Risk factors: any situation, habit, environmental physiologic/psychologic condition or other variable that increases the vulnerability of the individual to illness or accident -​ Genetic and physiological factors -​ Age
text.618: -​ Environment -​ Lifestyle Levels of Prevention -​ Primary prevention -​ To encourage optimal health and to increase the person’s resistance to illness -​ Seeks to prevent a disease or a condition at a pre-pathologic state -​ Health promotion -​ Specific protection -​ Quit smoking -​ Avoid/limit alcohol intake -​ Exercise regularly -​ Eat well-balanced diet -​ Reduce fat intake and increase fiber in the diet -​ Secondary prevention -​ It is also known as health maintenance -​ Seeks to identify specific illnesses or conditions at an early stage with prompt intervention to prevent or limit disability -​ Early diagnosis/detection/screening -​ Prompt treatment to limit disability -​ Have annual physical examination -​ Regular pap smear test for women -​ Monthly BSE for women -​ Tertiary prevention -​ Occurs after a disease or disability has occurred and the recovery process has begun -​ Intent to halt the disease or injury process and assist the person in obtaining an optimal health status -​ Rehabilitation -​ Self-monitoring of blood glucose level among diabetics -​ Physical therapy after CVA -​ Undergoing speech therapy after laryngectomy Physiologic Responses to Stress and Illness -​ Stress -​ Is a universal phenomenon, all person experience it -​ Is a condition in which the person responds to changes in the formal balanced state -​ Stressor
text.619: -​ When a person faces stress, responses are called coping strategies, coping responses, or coping mechanism -​ Sources of stress -​ Internal stressor: originate within the person -​ External stressor: originate outside the individual -​ Developmental stressor: occur at predictable times throughout an individual’s life -​ Situational stressor: unpredictable and may occur at any time during life may be positive or negative Response Based Model of Stress -​ Adaptation -​ The adjustments that a person make in different situations -​ Types -​ General adaptation syndrome (GAS) -​ Alarm reaction/stage of alarm -​ Alerts the body’s defense -​ The person becomes aware of the presence of threat or danger -​ Levels of resistance are decreased -​ Adaptive mechanism are mobilized -​ If the stress in intense enough even at the stage of alarm, death may be ensure -​ Shock/resistance phase -​ The stressor may be perceived consciously by the person -​ Autonomic nervous system reacts, and large amount of epinephrine and cortisone are released into the body -​ Fight or flight -​ This primarily response is short, lasting from 1 minute to 24 hours -​ Counter-shock/exhaustion phase -​ The changes produced in the body during the shock phase are reversed -​ The person is best mobilized to react during the shock phases of the alarm reaction -​ Stage of Resistance -​ Is when the body’s adaptation takes place -​ The body attempts to cope with the stressor and limit the stressor to the smallest area of the body that can deal with it -​ The person moves back to homeostasis -​ Stage of exhaustion -​ The adaptation that the body made during the second stage cannot be maintained -​ The ways used to coped with the stressors have been exhausted -​ If adaptation has not overcome the stressors, the stress affects may spread to the entire body -​ At the end of this stage, the body may either rest and return to normal, or death may be the ultimate consequence -​ Local adaptation syndrome (LAS) -​ Man may respond to stress through a particular body part or body organ -​ Homeostasis -​ A state of dynamic equilibrium; stability, balance; uniformity -​ It is now more commonly referred to as hemodynamics because it is characterized by constant change -​ It is regulated by negative feedback mechanism -​ Concepts -​ Sympatho-adreno-medullary response (Walter Cannon) -​ SAMR or flight response -​ Adreno-cortical response -​ Neurohypophyseal response -​ Local physiologic response to stress -​ Inflammation involves mobilization of specific and nonspecific defense mechanism in response to tissue injury or infection -​ Purpose of inflammation -​ To localize tissue injury -​ To protect tissue from injury -​ To prepare tissue tissue to repair -​ Cellular response -​ Neutrophils: first to be launched at the site of injury -​ Monocytes: perform phagocytosis in chronic tissue injury -​ Lymphocytes: responsible for immune responses -​ Process involved -​ Marginal/pavementation: phagocytes line up at the peripheral walls of blood vessels -​ Emigration/diapedesis: phagocytes shift out of the blood vessels -​ Chemotaxis: impaired tissues release substances which exert magnet-like force to the phagocytes to bring them to the areas of injury -​ Phagocytosis: phagocytes ingest or engulf the antigens -​ Exudate production -​ Inflammatory exudate is produced, consisting of fluid that escaped from the blood vessels, dead phagocytic cells, and dead tissue cells and producta\s that they release
text.621: -​ Plasma protein fibrinogen, thromboplastic and platelets together form an interlacing network to wall off the area, and prevent spread of the injurious agent -​ During this stage, the injurious agent is overcome, and the exudate is cleared away by lymphatic drainage -​ Healing process (reparative phase) -​ Regeneration: involves replacement of damaged tissue cells by new cells which are identical in structure or function -​ Scar formation: involves replacement of damaged tissue cells by fibrous tissue formation -​ Granulation tissue -​ Cicatrix scar -​ Healing may also be classified as: -​ First intention: occurs in clean-cut wound. The wound edges are approximated and there is minimal ir no scar tissue formation -​ Second intention: occurs when the wound is extensive and there is a great amount of tissue. The repair time is longer and the scarring is greater -​ Third intention: occurs when there is delayed surgical closure of infected wound Vital Signs Temperature -​ Body temperature: balance between heat produced by the body and heat loss from the body -​ Types: -​ Core temperature: temperature of the deep tissues of the body -​ Surface temperature: temperature of the skin, SQ tissues and fat, rises and falls in response to the environment -​ Processes involved in heat loss -​ Radiation: transfer of heat from surface to surface of one’s object to surface of another without contact -​ Conduction: transfer of heat from one surface to another through direct contact -​ Convection: dispersion of heat by air currents -​ Evaporation: vaporization of moisture from the respiratory tract, mucosa of the mouth and skin -​ Factors affecting body temperature -​ Age -​ Diurnal variation (circadian rhythms) -​ Highest temperature: 4pm-6pm -​ Lowest temperature: 4am-6am -​ Exercise -​ Hormones -​ Stress -​ Environment -​ Alterations in body temperature -​ Pyrexia/hyperthermia/fever -​ Body temperature is above the usual range -​ Hyperpyrexia: very high fever, 41C (105.8F) and above -​ Hypothermia -​ Core body temperature is below the lower limit of normal -​ May be caused by excessive heat loss, inadequate heat production or impaired hypothalamic thermoregulation -​ Types of fever -​ Intermittent: body temperature alternates at regular intervals between periods of fever and normal and subnormal temperature (within 24 hours) -​ Remittent: wide range of temperature fluctuations more than 2C for over 24 hours, all of which are above normal -​ Relapsing: short febrile periods of a few days are interspersed with periods of 2-3 days of normal temperature, saddle back shape -​ Normal temperature in dengue: low platelet (risk for bleeding) -​ Constant fever: body temperature fluctuates minimally but always remains above normal (40-41C: unresponsive to antipyretics) -​ Kawasaki Disease: unknown, autoimmune, vasculitis -​ DOC: aspirin + IVIG -​ Fever spike (staircase): temperature rises to fever level rapidly following a normal temperature then returns to normal within a few hours -​ Assessing body temperature -​ Oral -​ Considered to be the most convenient and most accessible -​ Wait for 30 minutes before taking oral temperature if the client has taken cold or hot drinks/food or smoked -​ Contraindicated to patients with: -​ Oral lesions/surgery -​ Dyspnea -​ Cough -​ O2 therapy -​ Nausea and vomiting -​ Presence of oro-nasal pack, NGT, ET -​ Seizure prone -​ Very young children (<5 years old) -> febrile seizure -​ Safety -​ Airway/O2 -​ Take duration of seizure -​ Restless, disoriented, confused (ALOC) -​ Clean the thermometer before use (bulb to stem) and after use (stem to bulb) -​ Place the bulb of thermometer on either side of the frenulum -​ Take oral temperature for 2-3 mins -​ Normal range: 35-37.5C -​ Rectal -​ Considered to be very accurate -​ Contraindicated to patients with: -​ Anal or rectal conditions/surgery -​ Diarrhea -​ Hemorrhoids -​ Increased ICP -> at risk for brain herniation -​ Monro-Kellie Doctrine (3 constant in the skull) -​ Brain volume: meningitis/cerebral edema -​ CSF: continuously produced and absorbed (400-600 ml/day) -> brain herniation -​ Intracerebral blood: hematoma -​ Quadriplegia and myocardial infarction -> bradycardic -​ Morphine -​ Oxygen -​ Nitroglycerin -​ Aspirin -​ + laxative -​ Wear clean gloves and assists the client to assume lateral/sim’s position -​ Lubricate thermometer before insertion -​ Instruct the client to take a slow deep breath during insertion -​ Never force the thermometer if resistance is felt -​ Insert 15 cm (6 in) in adults and 11 cm for children -​ Hold the thermometer in place for 2 mins -​ Normal range: 36-37.8C -​ Axillary -​ Safest and non-invasive -​ Pat dry the axilla -​ Rubbing causes friction that may increase surface temperature -​ The bulb is placed in the center of axilla -​ Place the arm tightly across the chest to keep the thermometer in place and leave it for 9 mins
